Can a positive mindset protect us from the sniffles?

New Scientist October 16, 2026

The threat seems to be everywhere. On the tube, on the bus, as I the queue for coffee, I find that I am surrounded by coughs and sneezes, spreading diseases.

I eat healthily, exercise and try to get 8 hours of sleep to fend off the dreaded lurgy. It is only recently, however, that I started wondering whether our mental life might also play a part in our body’s defences. And the more I dug into the available literature, the more convinced I have become that it is critical.

Too busy to meditate? Microdosing mindfulness has big health benefits

Our attitudes, I have discovered, can subtly shape our immune system’s activity, which directly influences how likely we are to develop symptoms. If we want to fend off infection, we would do well to look after our minds as well as our bodies.

Advertisement

One of the first studies to explore this possibility arrived in the early 2000s, when Sheldon Cohen at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, and his colleagues recruited 334 plucky volunteers who were willing to be infected with the common cold. In the month before the trial, they took regular questionnaires about their feelings throughout the day, noting emotions both positive (cheerful, at ease, energetic) and negative (sad, on edge, hostile).

On infection day, the scientists gave each participant a nasal drop containing one of two rhinoviruses known to cause sniffles, then held them in quarantine for five more days to observe whether any symptoms developed – quantified through objective measures. The team estimated the participants’ mucus production, for example, by collecting and weighing the snotty tissues they had used.

Cohen’s results were unequivocal. People with a sunnier emotional style were about a third less likely to develop symptoms than those who were less positive. Quite amazingly, the influence of the positive feelings was independent of the negative feelings – meaning that people who managed to feel both cheerful and anxious, for instance, were still less likely to develop symptoms than those who were neither cheerful nor anxious. This may sound counterintuitive, but it is perfectly possible to feel multiple emotions at the same time, and Cohen’s results seemed to suggest that positive feelings play the greatest role in our health.

I might have been sceptical if this were the only evidence, but multiple other studies have since confirmed and extended these findings. Cohen and his colleagues have shown that a so-called positive emotional style (PES) could also protect participants from influenza, for example – even after they controlled for a host of factors including age, sex, education, race and body mass.

While the exact mechanisms are unclear, it almost certainly comes down to stress, which is known to throw our defences into disarray. Someone under a lot of pressure may struggle to summon the resources to identify the virus when it first takes hold, leading to a suppressed immune response. Alternatively, the immune system may leap into action too quickly and too eagerly, bombarding the body with the inflammation that lies behind many of our symptoms.

How important is thinking about your breath for calming yourself down? We now know that slow breathing is effective even without conscious involvement

In the case of the common cold, it seems that the second potential mechanism is the most relevant. Someone with a more positive frame of mind may find it easier to cope with life’s stresses, meaning that the body becomes less inflamed when they face a pathogen. Along these lines, Cohen has found that people’s symptoms, such as a runny nose, are directly correlated with their levels of IL-6, a pro-inflammatory signalling protein called a cytokine, after infection. This was much lower among those with a PES. A group of researchers led by Sara Puig Pérez at Valencian National University, Spain, meanwhile, found that optimists have lower levels of another pro-inflammatory cytokine, TNFα, which has been linked to the fatigue and lethargy that often accompanies our sniffles, and this seemed to be reflected in fewer overall symptoms. It seems that the optimist’s body is simply better able to fine tune its response to the threat at hand.

As fascinating as this is, I’m mostly interested in the ways that I might use this information to protect myself, so I was delighted to find a trial of an eight-week mindfulness course by Bruce Barrett at the University of Wisconsin-Madison and his colleagues. Like Cohen, Barrett looked for objective evidence of infection, with blood tests, cheek swabs and nasal washes, rather than relying solely on reported symptoms.

The mindfulness course had previously been shown to cultivate a more positive mindset – and this had the desired effect on the participants’ health. The participants were generally less likely to develop a respiratory illness after practicing mindfulness. And for those who did develop signs of an infection, the symptoms were less severe. The benefits were comparable to those of exercise, which is also known to increase the efficiency of the immune system. The meditators were also less likely to take time off work due to illness than the control group, who had been put on a waiting list for the course.

Mindfulness may not be your thing. As I’ve written previously, I’ve personally struggled with it in the past, although I’m now finding new ways to incorporate it into my life. Given the very general link to good feelings, I’m sure that plenty of other kinds of self-care would bring similar protection. Social connection also seems to boost the immune response, so you might try to reach out to the people who matter most to you, for instance.

With the nights drawing in over the northern hemisphere, it is very easy to succumb to the winter blues, so now could be the perfect time to focus on the things that bring you comfort. A sneeze-free sniffle season may just be one of many benefits.

Will physics be the next field to be turned upside down by AI?

New Scientist October 16, 2026

AI has grown so adept at solving mathematical puzzles that critics fear the flood of new proofs it creates will overwhelm academics and actually set the field back. Until now, AI has had limited impact on other areas of science, but there are signs that physics may be about to experience a similar upset.

John Sous at Yale University says AI models may have an unfairly bad reputation when it comes to physics because of the way they are tested. Cutting-edge models have previously scored as low as 30 per cent on six different tests designed specifically to assess AI’s ability on tough physics problems, but this doesn’t square with the successes Sous and his colleagues have seen when using them, he says.

Checking the problems in the benchmark revealed a litany of errors and ambiguous definitions. Once corrected, scores soared to as high as 94 per cent. The problem didn’t lay with AI, but in the tests not providing the necessary information.

Advertisement

“I think anything that’s well defined, even if it’s very hard, I suspect that AI will be very good at it – arguably better than the best experts,” says Sous. “This is backed up by our data.”

But while some parts of physics can be very well defined – physicist Vladimir Arnold once said that mathematics is the part of physics where experiments are cheap – many aren’t. And it is in the new, uncharted, fuzzy and cutting-edge parts of physics where AI may struggle.

arXiv might not survive AI slop onslaught, warn mathematicians

Sous says that interesting physics comes when we find something confusing, some phenomenon we observe in nature, a material or the cosmos that we don’t understand. It is then a physicist’s job to create a model, an approximation or a simulation that captures and predicts that phenomenon.

“That’s a very artistic, a very creative process,” says Sous. “Can AI really take the next step and do the full job of a theoretical physicist? Do end-to-end research: define, create, explore, test? The picture is not clear yet.”

One reason mathematics has been at the tip of the spear of AI progress is formalisation. This technique turns a mathematical idea into computer code that can be methodically checked; the process is so thorough that if a theorem comes through intact, it is considered correct beyond all reasonable doubt. It allows AI to process a problem and know when it has arrived at a correct solution.

Subscriber-only newsletter

While some advances have been made in using formalisation to test physics, it is early days in comparison to mathematics. And physics problems can often be messier and harder to pin down.

What is clear is that AI is already being used by physicists, not only to write computer code and do maths, but even to design and run experiments. Logan Wright, also at Yale University, is now teaching a course on using AI in physics research, and says that the syllabus is constantly changing to catch up with developments.

The key, says Wright, is to create experiments where the inputs and outputs can be computer controlled. Then that control can be handed over to an AI that is able to pull the appropriate levers to explore the problem space and arrive at meaningful results.

“It doesn’t have hands, it doesn’t have eyes, it just interacts with the world through language and code,” says Wright. “So if we can set up an experiment in which all the observations are reduced to code, and all the actions are reduced to code… then AI can actually be very helpful.”

Mathematicians and AI in behind-the-scenes battle over what’s true

One such experiment currently underway in Wright’s laboratory involves analysing how different shapes of laser pulses affect a rubidium atom. The researchers use Anthropic’s AI Claude to control the laser pulses and gather data on their effects.

“Claude can now basically say ‘I think this laser pulse is gonna produce this output’, right,” says Wright. “And it can test that.”

Wright says that such experiments can run overnight and complete as much work as a human would in a week – and human physicists can even use an app on their phone to suggest ideas that come to them while they are away from the lab, and get the results when they return.

“It’s not going to be [the case that] all of the universe can be explored in that way. It’ll be like very constrained domains,” says Wright. “I think part of the next frontier of physics will be to make as much progress as we can in those domains.”

Wright says that it is already entirely possible that AI will soon design an experiment that humans don’t understand, ask humans to build it and generate exciting new results. “But just to be clear, just like in math, there’s a debate about does it count as science if we get a result that we don’t understand anything about,” says Wright.

Tūrangi-Taupō bus service gets bigger bus, but schedule still excludes commuters

New Zealand Herald October 18, 2026

The brand new upgraded Tūrangi-Taupō bus. Photo / Bronson Perich

The Tūrangi-Taupō bus service has grown, literally.

The 11-seater shuttle that formerly serviced the route has been upgraded to a full-sized passenger bus.﻿

The initially two-day-a-week service also now operates on three days: Mondays, Thursdays and Fridays.

However, Tūrangi-Tongariro Ward councillor Sandra Greenslade, who has been fighting for a bigger bus and a commuter service, said while it was wonderful that the regional council listened to her request for a bigger bus, the schedule still prohibits commuters from using it.﻿

“We’ve got three days a week in a very very limited service,” she said.

She said Tūrangi’s service is still lacking, especially when compared to services in other towns.

Waikato Regional Council, which is responsible for public transport across Waikato, has funded a seven-day-a-week service in Raglan, a similar-sized town to Tūrangi.

“I think it’s a bit mean,” Greenslade said.

Raglan Whaingaroa is a small town on the west coast of the North Island with, as of 2025, a population of 3910. Tūrangi’s 2025 population is 3960.

Waikato Regional Council chairman Warren Maher said that decisions about new or additional commuter bus services can’t be made based on a checklist of criteria.

He said there were a range of things to consider, including funding and demand for a route.

“Co-funding from central government is necessary for public transport authorities to invest in new routes, increased services or additional capacity.”

Maher also said the Raglan and Hamilton route was “consistently popular” and had a long-standing demand from commuters, students and visitors.

“This established... demand has warranted the investment in public transport services.

“The point at which these conditions apply to different towns to secure funded daily public transport services depends on the attributes of both the town and the centre between which the trips would be taken.

“For example, Hamilton as a metro centre will generate more demand for trips to its tertiary level hospital and education facilities, as well as its diverse employment market.”

Some Taupō District residents often travel long distances to get to work: One example is the Te Rāhui Solar Farm on the Napier-Taupō Highway, which is an 86km return trip from the Taupō CBD.

While building the solar farm has brought employment to locals, the cost of fuel makes travelling 86km a day expensive.

So Bam Bam Pile Driving, the company building the solar farm, operates a bus service from its Rakaunui Rd depot to the Rangitaiki worksite.

Greenslade told Local Democracy Reporting that she also knew of other companies that provide transport options for their workers as well – a move she called “sensible”.

“People can’t afford to drive to Taupō [from Tūrangi] for jobs any longer.

“$30 or $40 a day in gas; it’s completely unsustainable.”﻿

She said a commuter service timed in line with regular working hours will increase employment opportunities for her constituents and help them meet the increasing costs of living.

Greenslade said limited public transport options reduce the ability of smaller communities to travel, leaving them cut off.

“To isolate a community is a very, very bad thing.”

Taupō Ward councillor Duncan Campbell, as the council’s infrastructure lead, has championed the Tūrangi commuter bus and said he made a submission to the regional council transport committee on Greenslade’s behalf.

To help towns like Tūrangi get the services they need, Campbell is also proposing a “regional-town accessibility standard”.

Under his proposal, residents of regional towns like Tūrangi and Raglan would have “reasonable public transport access” to their nearest “major service and employment centre”, which in this case would be towns like Taupō and Hamilton respectively.

Reasonable access would include services such as a five-day-a-week commuter service and same-day return access to healthcare, government services, shopping and education.﻿

Maher said Campbell emailed regional council public transport subcommittee chairwoman Liz Stolwyk, with regional council staff cc’d, regarding his idea of developing a regional-town accessibility standard.

However, Maher said the regional transport committee had not “formally received information” on the matter.

Maher said for Turangi and the surrounding villages to receive a commuter bus, the regional council needs a business case to assess the appropriate level of service (routes/stops/times/service span) versus the operational cost of running those services for the community.

“Endorsement of the business case by the NZ Transport Agency Waka Kotahi is the pathway for securing co-funding.

“Another way in which the regional council can build a case for new or improved services is to test the level of demand by running trial services.

“Trial services need to run successfully for a minimum of three years before the NZTA can make a decision to co-fund it on an ongoing basis.”

The length of the trial service is timed to coincide with the three-yearly Regional Land Transport Plan (RLTP) and National Land Transport Programme (NLTP) funding cycle, Maher said.

“Subject to co-funding being approved ..., the regional council could look to then develop a business case for further improvement to those co-funded services.”

He said the council would typically do this when the contract for the services is coming up for renewal.

“The Tūrangi-Taūpo service is currently a trial.”

Bronson Perich is a Local Democracy Reporting journalist for Taupō and South Waikato based at the Waikato Herald.

Cyclone Gabrielle debris: Gisborne council wins award for AI mapping project

New Zealand Herald October 18, 2026

Gisborne District councillor Alexander Boros (left), Mayor Rehette Stoltz, chief executive Nedine Thatcher Swann and councillor Jeremy Muir received the SuperIdea award on behalf of the Gisborne District Council on Thursday night. Photo / Local Government New Zealand

Gisborne District Council’s use of an AI mapping tool to tackle the region’s woody debris was recognised for innovation at a national local government conference.

Local Government New Zealand’s (LGNZ) SuperLocal conference, held in Rotorua last week, brought together more than 600 local government and industry leaders from across the country.

On Thursday, four awards were presented, including the SuperIdea award, which went to Gisborne District Council for its Turning the Tide: Large Woody Debris AI-assisted Removal project.

The award recognised innovation in problem-solving, including new approaches and significant cost savings.

The winning idea had to address community needs, deliver long-term value and have the potential to be adopted by other councils.

The council worked with forest consultancy service Interpine to develop an AI-assisted system to map the large volumes of woody debris left along rivers and coastlines by Cyclone Gabrielle.

The technology enabled teams to move away from clearing sites one by one and instead assess and prioritise removal based on actual risk.

The project also received the Association of Local Government Information Management’s Data and Insights Project of the Year award, the 2026 Taituarā Members’ Choice award and the Datascape Award for Digital Local Government.

Mayor Rehette Stoltz said the latest award recognised the people behind the region’s recovery.

“Cyclone Gabrielle left us facing challenges on an enormous scale. Our teams had to find new and smarter ways of working, and this project is a great example of that.

“What makes me particularly proud is that this innovation was developed to solve a very real problem for our communities – helping us make better decisions, use recovery funding wisely and focus our efforts where they would make the biggest difference.”

Chief executive Nedine Thatcher Swann said the tool combined local expertise with technology to make recovery work more efficient and effective.

“While it was developed out of a difficult situation, what we have learned has real potential to help other councils prepare for and respond to future events.”

Council woody debris programme manager Rod Sheridan last year said the technology had been a “game-changer”, providing a smarter and more cost-effective way to identify the location of woody debris and estimate volumes quickly.

It allowed entire catchments to be efficiently cleared and improved planning, he said.

The approach supported $50 million in recovery work and saved more than $1m by helping the council prioritise areas of greatest risk.

LGNZ said the council had shown how technology and local knowledge could strengthen recovery and help prepare for future events.

Waikato Regional Council won the SuperSteward Award for its infrastructure supporting fish passage through fish stations, while Taupō District Council won the SuperCollab Award for its Oroko Rise housing development, which targets smaller homes for moderate-income households.

Manawatū District councillor Alison Short won the SuperHuman Award.

Country Life: The evolution of the country pub

New Zealand Herald October 18, 2026

Darfield Hotel owner Pravesh Kumar inside his country pub. Photo / RNZ, Anisha Satya

By Anisha Satya of RNZ

What does it take to run a pub in New Zealand’s rural towns?

“You have to be a people person,” Pravesh Kumar says.

He and his wife Monika took over the Darfield Hotel three years ago, after moving from Hawke’s Bay.

Moving to a small town with no connections was a gamble.

Originally from Haryana in India, Kumar recalls being nervous about how locals would react to him acquiring the pub.

“I was scared, to be honest. But once the ice broke, I found out it’s a different language, different culture, but all the values are the same.”

He and Monika are investing back into the hotel building, which comprises a pub, restaurant and accommodation.

It’s a hospo success story at a time when thousands of businesses are closing up shop.

He attributed that success to his “grandma’s house” approach as a publican, providing hearty meals over bar snacks and getting to know his patrons.

“You look after your people, your people look after you,” he said.

The Kumars’ story mirrors those of rural publicans across Aotearoa, according to Peter Janssen, who authored New Zealand Pubs.

The book recounts his journey through 170 classic New Zealand pubs.

“I like the story of the pubs, and I like what they’ve meant to New Zealand over the last 150 years,” he told RNZ’s Country Life.

At the heart of pubs that had survived over the decades were social, outgoing publicans, he said.

“You’ve got to have a sit and have a chat to that boring man sitting there on his own having a beer; you’re the heart of the community.”

While such pubs have always been watering holes for rural communities, the clientele have changed in the past few decades – as have their demands.

“The traditional image of the pub is, you know, a couple of old blokes sitting around a jug of beer,” he said.

“Now, young people don’t want to do that. And actually, most people, older people don’t want to do that anyway.

“And the pubs that were surviving on that sort of trend and tradition have not survived.”

The pubs that have survived have broadened their drink and food offerings – like the Rotherham Hotel in North Canterbury.

Owner Keith Fenwick, locally “Kiwi Keith”, said food makes up about half of its business these days.

“Years ago it was beer; it was about 90% ... it was beer for breakfast, dinner, and tea.

“Beer consumption has just dropped right away, especially during the day.”

The hotel now operates as a cafe during the daytime, with offerings like burgers, coffee, ice cream and homemade soup.

For more than 40 years, Fenwick has lived and worked in the hotel with the help of his wife, Moira.

Between cleaning rooms and serving patrons, he finds time to get out among the plants – he’s a market gardener by trade.

He’d hoped to find more time for the garden in 2017, when he first put the hotel up for sale – but 10 years on, it’s still on the market.

There are peak busy periods – like the Amuri A&P show in March, and the North Canterbury Hunting Competition in July – but managing quiet periods and increased costs is a juggling act.

It’s not easy, Fenwick said, but it was a rewarding job for those suited to the role of a publican.

“It is a good business; we’ll hang in there ’til something happens.”

Janssen said it’s often the publican who makes or breaks a country pub’s success.

“You’ve got to be calm, you’ve got to be organised, and you’ve got to like people; It’s a great lifestyle if you’re really keen.

“There’s one called the Silver Stream Hotel in Kimbell, near Fairlie, where a young couple took it over and just turned it around.

“It’s a fantastic pub, but that was a deliberate choice about a lifestyle they wanted to lead.”

Donna Hall and Jim McDougall, of the Strath Taieri Hotel, made that same choice last year, taking on a pub for the sake of its community.

After sitting on the market for a while and failing to renew its liquor licence, the pub closed for five weeks in 2025.

Locals approached McDougall, who’d run pubs in his past and was “born and bred in Middlemarch”, to give it a second life.

“It was important to him for the community ... if the pub closed there was not much chance of something opening anytime soon, if at all, that could replace the [hotel],” Hall told Country Life.

“A commitment that Jim and I made when we bought the pub [was] that we’d be open every day, and that we would have longer hours and we’d be consistent.

“Which often means the staff don’t have a lot to do, but we want to make it a place that people know they can come and get a meal any time of the day.”

Situated in hill country an hour from Dunedin, the hotel is a gathering spot for remote farming families, contract shearers and the local Young Farmers club.

“We try and support as many community groups as we can through the pub, through sponsorship, you know, and that’s pretty special,” Hall said.

What comes around goes around – when rural publicans support their community, that community will support them back, Janssen said.

“If you’ve got people who are outgoing and have a sense of community, they will attract people to the pub.”

Janssen said while the nature of country pubs may have changed – food over beer and families alongside mates – their role in uniting communities remains the same.

“They are much more community-minded; they’re serving a better range of drinks, they’re serving a good range of food.

“They’re just much nicer places to be.

“If you’ve got a good country pub and you live in the countryside, support it, because you don’t know what you’ve lost ‘til it’s gone.”

Brian Tamaki pleads not guilty to inciting racial disharmony

New Zealand Herald October 18, 2026

Brian Tamaki appearing in the Manukau District Court today. Photo / Michael Craig

Brian Tamaki’s first appearance on inciting racial disharmony charges coincided with the court’s cultural day.

Tamaki headed into the Manukau District Court this morning flanked by his many supporters, whānau and livestreaming team.

His backers were standing by the court doors holding signs advocating for “free speech” and asking if New Zealand is now a “police state”.

What was also underway was the court’s cultural celebration day, including stalls of Pasifika crafts and other items.

Before going inside, Tamaki addressed his support and livestream, saying this was a “landmark case” and “we’ll see what happens in there”.

“We know that this country now is facing the possibility of a dangerous swing in its democracy, and that is the attack on every day kiwis’ ability to talk to freely disagree and challenge,” he said.

In court he pleaded not guilty to three counts of inciting racial disharmony, under section 131 of the Human Rights Act.

Tamaki’s lawyer Ron Mansfield, KC, entered the pleas for his client in the Manukau District Court this morning.

The charges, under section 131 of the Human Rights Act, relate to alleged offending in June of this year.

The charge sheets say it included “abusive” and “insulting” posting on Facebook likely to excite “ill will”.

Tamaki’s supporters gathered outside court, some holding signs, while he gave a brief speech.

Mansfield told the court that there would be a number of Official Information Act and Privacy Act requests in relation to this case.

Tamaki livestreamed himself being summonsed to court last week.

Speaking to NZME then, Tamaki denied the allegations.

“I have not at all violated or crossed the line of that side of racial disharmony; that’s absolutely stupid and really rubbish, it’s just rubbish.

“All of my statements have been religious ... and I’ve been very consistent about that.”

He believed the prosecution was “politically motivated”.

“I intend to challenge these charges and defend my right to speak freely, preach my faith and hold foreign political leaders accountable.”

Tamaki said that while police haven’t confirmed to him what event the charges are in relation to, he believed it was over comments made about Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

Tamaki alleged police came to his door without any warning.

“It’s an interesting charge. I don’t know if I’ve seen any racial charge.”

He said when he was summoned to attend court the charges “won’t stick”.

“It was about that statement basically there. So you’re talking about something that was already clear that I made statements from somebody that was a human rights abuser. I exposed that big time what he was doing in India with the persecution of Christians.”

Earlier, Detective Senior Sergeant Natalie Nelson said because the charges were laid under the Human Rights Act, consent was required from the Attorney-General for police to prosecute.

However, Attorney-General Chris Bishop told the Herald he was not involved in the decision-making, and that consent to prosecute an offence under the Act was delegated to the Solicitor-General.

“This reflects the fact that it is not appropriate for the Attorney-General to be involved in individual prosecutions, which must be carried out without any appearance of political interference,” Bishop said.

Police amended their statement a couple of hours later to confirm it was the Solicitor-General who has the authority to provide consent to prosecute, not the Attorney-General.

In June this year, Tamaki made remarks on his podcast accusing Modi of persecuting Christians in India and said if churches were being burned down in India, “why don’t we burn mosques and their temples down? Tit for tat”.

He later told Ryan Bridge TODAY he didn’t mean what he said when he called for mosques and temples to be burned down.

Tamaki acknowledged he had not been threatened by any Hindu people and no churches had been burned down in New Zealand.

An anti-immigration protest has been planned by Destiny Church for later this month in downtown Auckland.

The University of Canterbury Students Association has apologised to a renowned West Auckland twin-sister DJ duo, who were booed during their set when technical issues disrupted the university’s Tea Party event on Saturday.

The Katayanagi Twins, Rain and China Katayanagi, said the crowd didn’t understand that the technical issues “wasn’t our fault” and began throwing items at them.

Email us

In a video posted to social media, one of the sisters said they were supposed to play for an hour but only performed two songs in full before the music cut out.

The University of Canterbury Students Association (UCSA) has since apologised for the issues and clarified it was the event’s fault and “not a reflection on the Katayanagi Twins”.

“We apologise to the Katayanagi Twins for the technical issues (which were entirely on us and are not a reflection on the Katayanagi Twins).”

It apologised to the sisters for not removing them from the stage sooner while working to resolve the issues.

The Katayanagi Twins had tried to switch a mixer they were using because it was overheating and the music kept cutting out.

“They didn’t understand that’s not our fault. They started throwing stuff at us,” one sister said.

“Some guy said it was the worst set that he’s ever seen.”

UCSA also said it was “disappointing to have seen the booing and throwing of items from people in the crowd” in response to the issue.

“We don’t condone this behaviour towards artists,” it said.

“We want our artists to feel safe and have a great on-stage experience, especially when issues are not within their control.

“We apologise to the Katayanagi Twins for not protecting them during their set.”

They also confirmed there would be “follow-up on crowd behaviour from the event”.

The twins described the experience as “rough” and “brutal”.

“They started chanting ‘DJ f*** off’.”

Katayanagi Twins added that they expect better behaviour from a crowd towards performers.

“Because it’s not our fault. We want you guys to have a good time, we want to have a good time.

“We also feel bad we didn’t get to play ... we need a redemption gig.”

A defence lawyer has told Mike Hosking Breakfast National’s plan to remove the right to silence in a child homicide death case is a tricky one.

Former Crown prosecutor John Munro has labelled it a “pretty drastic move”.

“They’d have to go through the Attorney-General to get advice on it first, Solicitor-General as well and Crown Law would probably advise them on it as well.

“Then it would obviously have to go through select committee and the parliamentary processes as well.”

Law and order bodies would also submit their feedback.

He said he’d pick the Criminal Bar and Law and Order Society would “probably say it’s a mistake”.

“Our legal history is littered with situations where a person has a low IQ and is under duress to say things or being forced to say things that aren’t true.”

The General Practice Owners Association is welcoming the Act Party's policy to commit $400 million over four years to retain more doctors in New Zealand, attract them from overseas and incentivise offering more appointments.

Chair Dr Angus Chambers told Ryan Bridge TODAY with Nadine Higgins that "quite a bit more" needs to be done, but the policy was "a start".

Act leader David Seymour pointed out yesterday that 35% of GPs intend to retire within the next five years.

Asked if better pay would help combat that, Chambers said it was possible that increased funding and better terms and conditions would help.

"But the other side of it is we've got to attract people into the system. And general practice has become a less preferred option.

"We're competing for our workforce with multiple other providers now. We've got cannabis clinics and telehealth clinics and ADHD clinics sucking out our workforce. The hospitals [are] always there with substantially increased salaries. And then of course we have our friends across in Australia who will pay us princely sums to go and work there."

Act leader Davis Seymour says Christopher Luxon might work with the Opportunity Party even after the National leader has repeatedly ruled out the likely kingmaker.

In an interview with TVNZ's Breakfast, Seymour was asked if Luxon would take the same approach as his party, which is open to working with them if it wins the election.

He said, "Yeah, I think he might", before explaining that he believed Luxon was trying to figure Opportunity out, as the party "tend[s] to change their views".

Recent polling has the Opportunity Party in the kingmaker position, with both blocs needing them to gain a majority in Parliament.

National leader Christopher Luxon believes the Attorney-General, and most New Zealanders, would agree with taking away the right to silence in child homicide cases.

If re-elected, National has vowed to amend the Crimes Act to make it an offence for a person to withhold information from police when they’ve been present at a location where a child aged 12 and under has been killed.

He told Mike Hosking Breakfast it’s a “common sense reaction”.

“I think New Zealanders have seen these cases for a number of years now where you’ve got three adults in a house where an event went down."

"They’ve got responsibilities just as much as rights," he added.

He said he “fully expects” to have to fight the change under the Bill of Rights and compared it to when National banned gang patches which was “against their rights”.

“Quite normal. The Attorney-General will look at the Bill, may decide it’s inconsistent with rights which has happened.

“But in this case it’s one I think most New Zealanders will sit there and go ‘yeah that doesn’t feel right and actually there are responsibilities and not just rights’.”

Chris Bishop has admitted he is "anxious" about potentially not getting back into Parliament.

The National MP told a Stuff podcast he would be lying if he said he had no thought about the possibility of not retaining his seat.

Bishop's Hutt South electorate has swung between National and Labour in recent elections, while National's low polling suggests only the party's electorate MPs could make it back to the Beehive.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon says he doesn’t remember why he chose November 7 as the date for this year’s general election over two other "easier" dates recommended by the Electoral Commission.

The commission had advised November 7 was “challenging, but manageable” partly because advance voting would begin on a public holiday. Labour has accused the National Party leader of deliberately choosing a date that would lower voter turnout.

Luxon told Newstalk ZB’s Mike Hosking Breakfast he couldn't recall why he turned down the commission's recommended dates, saying “I get a lot of advice”.

“I would have taken it from my own advisers, I would have looked at what they've said as well, but I was pretty comfortable with the date we went with,” he said.

“That's the reasons why back in January, [we] tried to give everyone advance notice, it's not a surprise it's coming."

The commission’s website shows enrolment is close to 91%, which is higher than the same time ahead of the 2023 election.

“The Electoral Commission's going bananas in terms of advertising and promoting it, making clear to everybody what they've got to do,” Luxon said.

“It's a really simple, easy thing to do. It's the least you can do, frankly, in the context of a democracy. So just get out and get registered.”

Paul Goldsmith says National will "engage fully" before putting policy to take away the right to silence in child murder cases into law.

The party's justice spokesman said yesterday that, if elected, the party would amend the Crimes Act to make it an offence for a person to withhold information from police when they’ve been present at a location where a child aged 12 and under has been killed.

He told Ryan Bridge TODAY with Nadine Higgins that the area of law was "very complex".

"Before we introduce a piece of legislation, as we always do, is we say, let's get the full legal advice from the Ministry of Justice, from Crown Law, from experts to get the precise wording right and then of course we go through a select committee process."

National had not taken advice on the policy yet as during a campaign parties are prevented from taking official advice, Goldsmith said.

Questioned if the policy would be effective, as you can compel people to talk but not tell the truth, Goldsmith said, "no law is ever perfect", but it will give authorities an extra tool to help investigations.

"The counterfactual is we carry on, and people literally get away with murder, and that to my mind is not justice."

A Constitutional law expert says National's proposal to take away the right to silence in child murder cases could work, but the details need to be right.

Graeme Edgeler told Ryan Bridge TODAY, with Nadine Higgins, that people who have the right to silence under the Bill of Rights are suspects, people who are arrested, and people who are charged.

"If you're being prosecuted, you do not have to give evidence in court."

Edgeler said the policy should apply to witnesses so their evidence could be used to prove a case against someone.

"If a person is suspected of committing the murder, or particularly if a person is going to be charged... We're trying to work out did that person do it and how do we prove that person did it.

"So this rule should never apply to someone who is going to incriminate themselves in a murder."

Similar powers exist in other areas of the law and could be applied in a similar way, Edgeler said.

Labour and National's health spokespeople have outlined plans to hire more general practitioners (GPs).

Simeon Brown and Ayesha Verrall went head-to-head in Newstalk ZB's mini health debate this morning.

Brown said the new Waikato medical school will have a focus on training GPs, particularly for rural and regional areas.

National's "primary care tactical action plan" also includes helping overseas-trained doctors get their qualifications recognised and training 120 nurses to become nurse practitioners annually, Brown said.

Verrall said she wants to make sure becoming a GP will be the most attractive career path for doctors entering the workforce.

Medical schools need to be scaled up, and Labour also supports a third school, she said.

The Chief Victims Advisor is welcoming the National Party's proposal to take away the right to silence in child murder cases.

Paul Goldsmith, National’s justice spokesman, yesterday said the party would amend the Crimes Act to make it an offence for a person to withhold information from police when they’ve been present at a location where a child aged 12 and under has been killed.

Ruth Money told Newstalk ZB's Early Edition that the right to silence is enshrined in the Bill of Rights, so authorities cannot compel people to talk.

Although details in yesterday's announcement were few, Money said New Zealand could change to a system like the United Kingdom's, where people are advised by police that they do not have to talk, but it may harm their legal defence down the line.

"If New Zealand was to introduce something similar to that... We're kind of reversing the evidential burden of proof. So we're saying that each person present will be required to explain what they were doing when the child was murdered."

Money said the policy should go beyond children 12 and under to cases of significant child abuse and "certainly child homicide".

Questioned on the legal implications of the proposal, Money said the Bill of Rights is important, "however, the death of a child is more important".

"We need to privilege the rights of these people, and certainly these children who are being assaulted and killed.

"Literally, people are getting away with murder."

New Zealand dog events ‘skyrocketing’ as owners spend more on pets

New Zealand Herald October 18, 2026

The NZ Wiener Derby moved to the bigger Rosebank Speedway. Photo / Dean Purcell

Despite the rising cost of living, New Zealanders are increasingly forking out top dollar for their pets, with breed-specific events “skyrocketing”.

Globally, the pet care market is worth almost $300 billion and is predicted to rise to $500 billion by 2034.

Meanwhile, in New Zealand, the trend is reflected in increased spending on pet insurance, specialised food and pet events like today’s Wiener Derby in Auckland.

Many Kiwis say they are going without treating themselves to provide for their pets as the cost of keeping animals grows.

The latest PD Insurance Pet Trends Survey shows 58.8% of respondents have reduced spending on luxuries, gifts and nice-to-haves for themselves.

Only 26.4% have made similar cutbacks to luxuries for their pets.

Contact the New Zealand Herald newsroom

The annual Official NZ Wiener Derby clearly showed how passionate Kiwis were about their four-legged family members.

The event, which began in 2016 with only 24 dachshunds competing, grew to well over 100 short-legged racers this year.

Miniature and standard dachshunds, as well as elderly dogs and groups of other breeds, took to the course.

Hundreds of spectators also filled the Rosebank Speedway on Sunday afternoon after the event outgrew its previous location and moved, with no signs of slowing down.

Long traffic queues caused significant delays, forcing kickoff back by an hour.

Boutique-style stalls lined the venue, including a doggy beauty and wellness brand and specialist pet nutrition companies.

Kin Marketing director Alice McKinley told the Herald that breed-specific events were becoming increasingly popular and already “skyrocketing” in the US.

“I’ve got an event called Wine Dogs down in Martinborough and Hawke’s Bay, and when I speak to other people in events, they’re always quite surprised that people are happy to pay $65 to come to a dog event,” McKinley said.

Earlier this month, the first New Zealand Golden Retriever Gathering took place in Taupō, where hundreds of the breed attended.

McKinley said the rise in popularity was driven by people being “sick of” the world becoming increasingly digitalised.

“They [owners] miss that connection ... and I think it’s just like being part of something.”

She said people also wanted to socialise with like-minded people who appreciate a specific breed.

McKinley said owners were also spending more time with their pets, who become like “best friends”.

She said for people who choose not to or can’t have children, a pet can fill a void they might have.

McKinley said other areas of the pet industry were “booming” as owners splurged on “sensible” purchases like insurance and premium food.

In particular, she said raw and real-meat diets were doing well, mirroring the high-protein trend in human food.

Meanwhile, Southern Cross Pet Insurance chief executive Anthony McPhail said he noticed pets were becoming more deeply embedded in family life than ever before.

“As is the case overseas, we’re increasingly seeing that reflected in the way people care for them,” McPhail said.

The company, which supports more than 66,000 pets across the country, had its highest annual claims cost to date following growth in the number of pets insured.

He said part of that growth reflected the broader trend of New Zealanders prioritising their pets’ health and wellbeing.

It also reflects significant advances in veterinary medicine, with some claims reaching up to $15,000.

“New Zealanders are investing more time, care and resources into helping their pets live long, healthy and happy lives, and pet insurance is increasingly becoming part of that.”

Selwyn building consents hit record as schools and health services face pressure

New Zealand Herald October 18, 2026

Selwyn’s population is booming, raising questions about infrastructure costs and capacity from Selwyn Mayor Lydia Gliddon (top) and Rolleston Residents Association chairman Mark Alexander. Photos / Frank Film / Rafaella Melo

Selwyn is the fastest-growing district, but can its infrastructure keep pace? Rafaella Melo reports.

More than half of Selwyn’s schools are using or set to receive relocatable classrooms, demand for a new after-hours health service has attracted more than double the expected uptake, and $222 million is projected to be invested in water infrastructure as the district experiences record residential growth.

New figures show 645 residential building consents were recorded in Selwyn in the June 2026 quarter, an average of about seven a day.

The Infometrics figures represent a 61.7% increase on the same period last year and surpass the previous record of 636 consents set three months earlier.

The boom raises questions about whether schools, healthcare, roads and other essential services can keep pace.

Selwyn’s estimated population reached 87,600 in June 2025, according to Stats NZ, and the council expects about 3200 additional residents annually over the next few years.

Supporting that growth would require significant investment.

Selwyn Water expects to spend about $222m in growth-related drinking water and wastewater infrastructure over the next five years, including upgrades in Rolleston, Lincoln, Prebbleton, Darfield, Malvern and Southbridge, alongside wastewater network improvements and work at the Pines Wastewater Treatment Plant.

The plant was serving a population equivalent of about 65,000 and operating within its designed limits, according to Selwyn Water.

However, the organisation said continued growth meant new connections were being carefully managed, with some developments requiring further infrastructure assessment or investment.

Meanwhile, drinking water and wastewater charges have risen 18% for 2026/27, adding about $280 to an average urban household’s annual bill.

That brings the estimated annual cost to $1831 for drinking water and wastewater services.

The increase was initially projected at 24% but was reduced after a review of charging and costs.

Selwyn Mayor Lydia Gliddon warned there was an increasing risk existing ratepayers could end up carrying more of the costs of infrastructure needed to accommodate growth.

“Councils are simultaneously being asked to constrain rates and fund more infrastructure,” she said.

“Growth should pay for growth, and councils need the tools to recover the cost of infrastructure required rather than relying on existing ratepayers to pick up the bill.”

Gliddon said the Government’s Incentives for Growth Fund was a step in the right direction, but councils needed more sustainable funding options.

Transport is another challenge, with council figures showing 70% of the district’s vehicle population uses 30% of its roads, mostly in eastern Selwyn.

Selwyn District Council acting executive director of infrastructure and property Keith Beal said some infrastructure was experiencing higher demand, with projects reviewed as growth patterns changed.

He said fast-track developments could create additional challenges when their timing, scale or location differed from existing infrastructure plans.

“The greatest challenge that we’re seeing is for infrastructure that requires long lead times and significant capital investment, such as transport, water services and community facilities,” Beal said.

“The key issue is maintaining alignment between where growth occurs and when supporting infrastructure can realistically be funded and delivered.”

Contact our Christchurch newsroom.

Healthcare services were also facing growing pressure.

Rolleston’s new after-hours health service dealt with 750 patients in September, two and a half times the 300 initially forecast per month.

The service, which opened on August 8 in response to population growth, also treated 765 patients in its first 23 days.

Health New Zealand regional planning, funding and outcomes director Chiquita Hansen said the organisation and Phoenix Health were working together to ensure sufficient capacity was available.

She said primary care capacity had also expanded in recent years, with satellite clinics established in Rolleston, Lincoln and Prebbleton, and a new general practice at the Rolleston Health Hub.

“While some areas continue to experience pressure, primary care is increasingly being delivered through team-based models that are not solely reliant on GP numbers.”

Health NZ figures show patient enrolments across seven medical practices serving Selwyn increased from 51,049 to 70,297 over five years.

However, the figures are indicative only, as some practices also serve Christchurch residents, while Selwyn residents may be enrolled with Christchurch GPs.

Meanwhile, Rolleston Medical Centre has paused its waiting list for new patient enrolments.

Hansen said Health NZ was working with the council and primary care providers to strengthen workforce capacity as the district continued to grow.

The scale of growth was also reflected in the district’s schools.

Ministry of Education figures show 13,241 students were enrolled in Selwyn state schools as of July 2025, a 26% increase since 2020.

Lemonwood Grove School in Rolleston is nearing capacity for students living within its enrolment zone.

The ministry expects the opening of Te Rau Horopito School earlier this year to help ease pressure on Lemonwood Grove over time.

Of Selwyn’s 36 schools, 22 are either using or set to receive relocatable-type classrooms, according to the New Zealand School Property Agency.

The prefabricated teaching spaces can be moved between school sites to meet changing educational needs.

New schools in Prebbleton and Lincoln are in development, while teaching facilities at Rolleston College’s second campus are nearing completion, with further expansion funded through Budget 2026.

The ministry’s Canterbury and Chatham Islands director of education Coralanne Child said school rolls, population projections and residential development trends were being monitored to identify where additional capacity might be needed.

Rolleston Residents Association chairman Mark Alexander has watched the town grow from about 1000 people to an estimated 34,000 over the past 32 years.

A former Selwyn district councillor who served from 2010 to 2022, Alexander said the growth had been mostly positive, bringing new shopping, recreational and community facilities.

But he believed central government had been slower to respond, particularly in education and healthcare.

Alexander said planning for such rapid growth was difficult, with population increases repeatedly exceeding even the council’s highest forecasts.

“Councils are often in a no-win situation. If you guess low, you’re wrong. You guess high, you’re wrong.”

Despite the challenges and missing a once-upon-a-time close-knit community, he said he would still choose to live in Rolleston, where he could now meet most of his shopping and recreational needs without travelling to Christchurch.

For Andreza Gama’s family, their recent move to Rolleston has been a positive experience.

She and her husband, Jasse, 38, moved from Halswell to a rental property in Faringdon in April, with their son Nicolas, now 1 year and 11 months old.

The family wanted to experience life in Rolleston before potentially buying a home there, attracted by affordable housing and family-friendly amenities.

Gama said having shops, playgrounds, schools and other facilities nearby meant they could walk and cycle more often.

She had also easily secured a place at a local preschool for Nicolas.

But she believed housing development was moving faster than infrastructure improvements, particularly road access.

She said traffic leaving Rolleston could be slow, especially for people commuting to Christchurch.

One unexpected difference from Christchurch was having to pay a separate water bill.

“I wasn’t used to it,” she said.

Despite that, Gama said the family was enjoying the move and could see improvements being made as the town expanded.

Rafaella Melo is a multimedia journalist with more than 10 years’ experience in Brazil. She spent two years reporting for Hawke’s Bay Today before joining the NZ Herald’s Christchurch team in 2026.

Aitutaki braces for Tropical Cyclone Wati

New Zealand Herald October 18, 2026

Tropical Cyclone Wati is heading towards the Southern Cook Islands. Photo / Cook Islands Meteorological Service

By RNZ Pacific reporters

The Aitutaki Island Council has activated its emergency operations centre as Tropical Cyclone Wati approaches.

Wati, a category 2 system, is moving southeast towards the Southern Cook Islands, with conditions expected to deteriorate over the coming days.

The Cook Islands Meteorological Service said Wati was gradually moving south to southeast at about 16km/h and was about 290km north of Palmerston at 2pm Saturday local time, with max sustained winds of up to 91km/h close to its centre, with gusts reaching 130km/h.

Its forecast for Aitutaki and Ngaputoru (Mauke, Mitiaro and Atiu) is:

For the Northern Cook Islands, the Meteorological Service has issued its final special weather bulletin for the group.

Emergency Management Cook Islands director, John Strickland told RNZ Pacific it was monitoring Wati as it moved towards Aitutaki.

He said Aitutaki island was very much set and prepared.

“Aitutaki is under the management of the island council which is the mayor, his council, and an executive officer for the Government.

“They have now activated their own emergency operation centre and are ready for anything that might hit them probably tomorrow morning or maybe tonight,” he said.

Schools have been organised on the island, and a maintenance team, police, the water authority, Red Cross and other supporting agencies are on standby for Wati.

Strickland said it was predicted that Wati would go between the islands of Mauke, Mitiaro and Atiu.

The Cook Islands Meteorological Service’s Nathan Tism said it was fortunate that they spotted the tropical depression before it turned into a tropical cyclone.

“A lot of warnings were sent out to everyone before the system intensified, and because it was up in the north tracking towards the south where no islands in its pathway, we were quite fortunate with that,” he said.

The system is forecast to leave the Exclusive Economic Zone of the Cook Islands in the next three days.

“So probably by Monday local time, it will weaken and develop into a low pressure,” Tism said.

Elite-level incompetence is Manchester United’s problem – not Michael Carrick

The Guardian Sun, 18 Oct 2026 19:56:30 GMT

Getting rid of head coach is not going to solve the problems that led to his appointment. Perhaps it’s worth, for once, doing something different

At the final whistle at Elland Road the TV cameras cut to a lingering shot of Manchester United chief executive Omar Berrada, looking down pensively from the stands, deciding, it is to be hoped, on a little clemency, a re-sheathing of the managerial shotgun.

Here we have the man who hired the man. The man who fires the man. The man who also hired or rehired the previous two men he had to fire. Berrada was poached from Manchester City on the basis of his ability to grow commercial revenue (yes, OK, stop laughing), and appears, like everyone else with any actual reach around here, to exist in a strangely consequence-free bubble.

How do you solve what is, on revenue versus results, the worst-run club in world football? By changing the name of the latest patsy on the touchline, of course. For now a hard-fought point is perhaps enough to stave off that pre-programmed emergency response.

Stand down the cowboy cops. Call off the blue and white saloons. Although with a run of Bournemouth, Chelsea, Aston Villa and Liverpool next up in the league it will no doubt soon be time to go out there and arrest Lee Harvey Oswald again. What’s that you say? OK, well, dig him up again. Re-arrest him. Whatever it takes. Someone has to stop these lone gunmen, these managerial magic bullet merchants from derailing the Manchester United supremacy.

This was a dual-track football match between Leeds United and Manchester United, on the face of it a good, even game between two teams of well-matched players. A 1-1 draw was fair in the end, although Leeds played well and probably should have won. But of course they won’t be the story.

Instead this game had already been billed as that familiar thing, a referendum on the future of Michael Carrick. A stay of execution for a week or two. Or another livestreamed firing squad for the Super Sunday cameras.

There has been a predictable sense of low comedy about Carrick’s own transformation in the United dugout this season. It was always going to be the case that his widely praised qualities in victory, blazer, T-shirt, jawline, inscrutable sense of calm, would become his fatal flaws in defeat.

Where’s the passion, the whirling arms, the range of tailored collars? At Elland Road Carrick simply looked drained in the second half as United were pegged back and overrun at times, the beard a little more ragged, the hair unkempt but still sweeping, the look of a brave, doomed tugboat captain resigned now to the approaching tsunami wave on the horizon.

A point leaves United 13th in the league and still struggling to reverse a dreadful start to the season. But it was a good game for two people. First for Carrick, who remains a million miles away from creating the problems afflicting this club, even if you accept that his presence as head coach is one of them.

Michael Carrick did not hire Michael Carrick. Getting rid of Michael Carrick is, by definition, not going to solve the problems that led to his appointment. But it might just help to prolong them. Whatever his ultimate ceiling, it is surely worth keeping him just to try, for once, to do something different.

This was also a good game for Lisandro Martínez, who went off injured at half-time with United 1-0 up, and who was also vindicated in his allegedly controversial (translation: entirely correct) comments on the club hierarchy in midweek.

United’s energetic first-half performance clarified one half of this. The players are committed in support of the manager, at least to the best of their ability. The second half made the other half of the argument, that this remains a mismatched, lopsided, cut-and-paste squad, always likely to be pulled apart by opponents as urgent as this Leeds team, which fully deserves its current seventh place in the table.

The problems are so obvious it is barely worth repeating them. But here goes. The third-richest club in the world played a second half with three of its back four out of position. Harry Maguire, signed under José Mourinho, remains the best straight defender. But Maguire is also essentially a man-shaped solid wood armoire in a pair of shorts at this stage in his career, always the slowest person on any pitch, which means you will not be able to cover space, play a high line or counterattack without leaving yourself exposed to the counter-counter.

So good luck, guys. And remember Omar, who gave you this whisky bottle and loaded pistol of a squad, will be watching.

This was made painfully clear after half-time as Martínez went off and Noussair Mazraoui came on. Leeds scored an equaliser that felt structurally inevitable. They found space down their right side repeatedly. At times they seemed to be constantly peppering the seats behind the United goal, like a group of kids hammering a ball against a garage door. By the end Leeds had more possession, more shots on target and just looked a happier, better structured entity than the travelling heritage exhibit at the other end.

Sign up to Football Daily

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

after newsletter promotion

The key point here is to accept that all of this is entirely logical. This is not a mystery, a haunted house, a place of bad voodoo. Why do we talk about Manchester United so much? For obvious reasons. It’s a massive part of the English football landscape. Mainly, though, because this is a story of mind-bending waste, real-time elite-level incompetence played out on a weekly basis.

Yes, you could sack Michael Carrick. It won’t change much. Let’s destroy Eddie Howe for a bit instead. But the available evidence suggests every single person making executive decisions here is outmatched and outmanoeuvred.

There is a reason Manchester United feels like one of those high street legacy chain shops just before it collapses, piles of Quality Street by the door, a rat in the lingerie department, destined to become a pop-up vape shop run by Albanian money launderers. There’s a reason it feels so badly run. This is because: it is.

We know the Glazer ownership has zero interest in minding the details, that this has been a wonderful acquisition whatever the performance on the pitch, an asset supremely sweated. We know also that Sir Jim Ratcliffe is pub-level incoherent on the details he promised to fix. Remember when he was going to sit down and decide what the “style of football” would be? How’s that working out?

Instead Carrick is left shuffling a first XI acquired by endlessly revolving administrations. Here United had four defenders signed under Erik ten Hag, two Ruben Amorim recruits, two from the mist-shrouded age of Ole Gunnar Solskjær. No players were recruited under Ralf Rangnick, of course. But then Rangnick wanted to sign Erling Haaland, Luis Díaz, and Julian Álvarez, which all sounds far too sensible.

An organisation can be built with many hands. But not when so many of those hands appear to be so far from best in class it’s hard to work out which class they’re supposed to be attending. John Murtough, the former Manchester United football director, is currently director of global development at Atalanta, who have a 24,000-seat stadium and almost zero global presence. Meanwhile Berrada, the axeman, seems entirely invulnerable from the axe himself, despite the fact his job seems to orbit around resolving the consequences of his own mistakes.

United probably will sack their current manager before the year is out. This is the way this machine has to operate, always looking to buy itself, and those in the executive seats, a little more time on the payroll, an entity that has been hollowed out and allowed to rust, run on buzzwords and brown paper and string. Meanwhile, over to you Michael. We’ll see you next week, and maybe even the week after that, for more of exactly the same.

The Guardian Sun, 18 Oct 2026 18:57:48 GMT

Ministers, officials and police under pressure over response to protests as government holds crisis talks amid ‘colossal failure of the state’

The French president, Emmanuel Macron, has criticised “unbridled violence” after one of the most violent days of unrest in years left public buildings burned, hundreds of shops destroyed and looted and more than 2,000 people arrested in cities across the country.

“Watching these images, we have all asked ourselves how could French people do this to France?” he said in a televised address.

Macron said “nothing justifies” violence and that local state officials would be able to ban certain street gatherings if they deemed it necessary.

He said a distinction must be drawn between what he called genuine, peaceful demonstrators making demands over the cost of living and the education system, and others who “destroy, ransack and loot”. He criticised what he called “factious groups from the ultra-left, joined by numerous delinquents”.

Politicians on the left and right called for the resignation of the interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, after the government appeared to have been caught by surprise by the scale of violence on Saturday as state buildings were stormed and torched, bus stops smashed, roads barricaded and shops broken into and destroyed. Protests also took place in Spain, Italy and Portugal.

Crowds clashed with police at Place de la République in central Paris on Sunday afternoon as violence flared for a second day. Electric bikes were piled in some streets and set alight. Bottles and rocks were thrown and thick plumes of smoke rose from burning bins. Police responded with teargas and stun grenades.

Police and officials faced challenges of different types on Saturday. First, tens of thousands of peaceful protesters attended calm marches through major cities including Paris, supporting schoolchildren’s demands for more teachers and repairs to decrepit schools. Those marches, which came after four weeks of street marches and barricades of schools, were attended by parents, teachers and grandparents as well as students and workers protesting over the high cost of living. The demonstrators carried banners saying the government was not listening to them and calling for more money for public services.

But separately to those peaceful demonstrations, different groups caught police and officials by surprise with moving gatherings, sporadic burning, the barricading of streets and clashes with police in cities including Paris, Bordeaux, Nice and Marseille.

Finally, masked looters took advantage of what French media called the “chaos” on the streets to smash shopfronts and grab goods. In Paris, groups of looters, some of whom appeared to be children, were seen running through the night with clothes and shoeboxes after masked adult men smashed shopfronts.

In Paris, where police said a record 855 people had been arrested, the burnt-out remains of barricades built using bikes, bins and other materials littered streets on Sunday. Several streets had smashed shop windows and the remains of torched cars. The capital had experienced “a level of violence that we have never seen before, I believe”, said the Socialist deputy mayor, Lamia El Aaraje.

In Limoges in central France, where the 19th-century town hall was burned down, the mayor, Guillaume Guérin, said the people who stormed his building “were not demonstrators that defend causes” but “people organised for war”. He said those who stormed and torched the town hall had told a building caretaker he would be killed, and told elected officials they would “burn”. He said there had been a failure of the state to deal with the crisis.

“Around 3.30pm our municipal police, although present in number, found themselves no longer able to fight against the violence of rioters because they had run out of ammunition,” Guérin said. He called this “a colossal failure of the state”.

Guardian reporter filmed masked militants seconds before West Bank attack on French mayor

The Guardian Sun, 18 Oct 2026 18:39:23 GMT

New video footage of Israeli settler assault on European delegation as Netanyahu attempts to raise doubt

Hours after Israeli militants attacked a delegation of European diplomats, French clerics and a visiting mayor in the occupied West Bank, Israel’s leader, Benjamin Netanyahu, responded by questioning the delegation’s account of the assault.

“Serious accusations require serious evidence” was the all-caps headline of a social media post from the office of the prime minister. As news of the attack spread globally there was no pledge to find those accountable and bring them to justice.

Instead Netanyahu’s team dismissed video of Bernard Baudoux, the mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries in northern France, on the ground grimacing in pain and shock, photos of the smashed window of a diplomatic car, and footage of masked men threatening diplomats and activists with sticks.

“These images alone do not establish the complete sequence of events or individual responsibility,” the statement said, warning of “concerns about a coordinated campaign to smear Israel”.

The prime minister’s office went on to cast doubt on the integrity of senior French, Belgian and Polish diplomats in Jerusalem and clergy from the Catholic church who witnessed and reported the attack.

“We call on the public and responsible journalists to demand verifiable evidence, reject hearsay and refuse to turn unproven allegations into a collective indictment of the Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria [the occupied West Bank],” it said.

Footage below filmed by the Guardian (no audio) shows the moments before Israeli settlers attacked the French mayor Bernard Baudoux, who was in the Palestinian town of Taybeh with a delegation of European diplomats. A second clip shows the immediate aftermath of the attack. The final section shows one group of settlers attacking the car carrying Baudoux and others.

Verifying the details of attacks can be painstaking journalistic work, seeking out eyewitness accounts, photos and videos for confirmation.

But this weekend the Guardian was in Taybeh, and witnessed the masked militants speeding up a hill in order to attack diplomats and French visitors who had spent a morning peacefully harvesting olives with Palestinians who own the groves.

Shortly after 1pm, they were warned that settlers had attacked Palestinians harvesting olives nearby. Keen to avoid confrontation, the group decided to leave and were approaching their vehicles as the militants closed in, masked, menacing and brandishing sticks.

The Guardian filmed the moments before Baudoux was assaulted, showing him approaching an SUV with his wife and Vincent Dollmann, the archbishop of Cambrai, escorted by diplomatic security. Our vehicle pulled away, making room for the two parked by the road to follow.

Moments later the settlers attacked, apparently determined not only to force the foreigners to flee but to extract a price for joining Palestinians on their land.

It was clear the group contained foreign dignitaries because the cars had diplomatic plates, and Baudoux was apparently targeted for his nationality, because he was wearing his mayor’s sash of office. One of the attackers aggressively shouted “France, France” before pushing him to the ground, eyewitnesses said.

Metadata from that video shows there were just 22 seconds between the last shot of Baudoux remonstrating with his attackers and footage of him slumped on the ground taken by activists in the second car.

The embassy security team then helped him into the vehicle but the attack continued as they drove off. Footage filmed from the hillside opposite shows the settlers attacking the SUV as pulls away.

The force of their blows smashed one of the reinforced windows at the back of the car, which can be seen intact in the first video. A photo of the crumpled pane taken minutes later in the relative safety of Taybeh shows the force of the impact.

If the militant settlers had broken one of the windows next to the passengers, it is unlikely those inside would have escaped injuries.

Israeli authorities have repeatedly attempted to obfuscate details of attacks on Palestinians and undermine survivor or witness accounts.

For the prime minister to deploy the same tactics on senior diplomats from European allies – however strained their current relationship – marks a new embrace of isolationist extremism.

A day earlier the American photojournalist Heidi Levine was hospitalised after a brutal attack by Israeli militants blocking the Palestinian olive harvest in another village. Netanyahu’s office described it as an “alleged assault” and a “disputed incident” adding “the facts … remain unclear and are under investigation”.

The message from the very top of Israel’s government, that the state was reluctant to impose consequences or seek justice for that attack, may have emboldened the attackers on Saturday.

There was one unprecedented response in Jerusalem, however. On Sunday, more than a dozen of Israel’s top former diplomats gathered outside the foreign ministry where they had all worked for decades for an unprecedented protest.

Two former directors general, one deputy director general and a host of ambassadors held up signs calling for action on the campaign of terror by Israelis against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.

“Bibi [Netanyahu], foreign minister [Gideon] Sa’ar. Stop Jewish Terrorism. It’s in your hands,” read one banner.

At 7.16pm, just around the time those Sunday night blues kick in, England’s Champions Cup cohort finally had something to cheer about. It was not pretty but after seven of their Prem rivals had failed to claim victory in the opening round of the competition, Saints survived a sizeable scare from Cardiff to put one on the board for the Prem, thanks in no small part to the excellent George Hendy.

It might be harsh on some of the performances this weekend – Gloucester were immense in drawing with Bordeaux, Exeter mightily unlucky to be beaten in Toulouse – but zero wins would have been a crushing embarrassment for a league that has been feted for its attacking exploits so far this season. Hendy also made the first try, stopped a certain Cardiff score and enhanced his reputation as a player who can make things happen for the Prem champions. “That has always been his forte, his super strength, George can break the game open, he can make breaks other people can’t,” said Northampton’s director of rugby, Phil Dowson.

Credit to the visitors, however, who were less than impressed with the scheduling of this fixture given they run out again just five days later and felt forced to heavily rotate as a result. They scored two impressive tries and midway through the second half had Northampton fans fearing an upset.

Northampton opted to chop and change too with Tommy Freeman, Henry Pollock, Alex Coles and Emmanuel Iyogun left out of the matchday 23.

Sideways rain will always be a leveller and the opening 10 minutes here left you longing for the sugar rush of last weekend’s 119-point try fest. Hendy swerved his way through the Cardiff defence and charged clear, feeding the supporting Alex Mitchell, whose floated inside pass found Pater. Saints’ second try came after Rory Hutchinson’s inventive diagonal kick forced a Northampton scrum five metres out. The referee, Jérémy Rozier, at the suggestion of the TMO, disallowed the score, however, insisting the ball had been dislodged in the tackle.

They extended their advantage soon after the restart when Will Butt grounded and Slade converted, but they continued to be tested by Toulouse, who squeezed ahead as Matias Remue and Ntamack both scored in quick succession, with the fly-half converting both. Wimbush completed his hat-trick and Slade’s conversion put Exeter in front again, but Ben Hammersley was then shown yellow and Toulouse struck through Remue’s try to edge ahead.

Slade sent a penalty wide in the final moments as Toulouse snatched a narrow victory.

Pau secured their bonus point in the dying stages when Searle’s attempted pass was intercepted and Fabien Brau-Boirie blazed home to confirm the win. Press Association
