‘This is horrifying. This is madness’: the row over competitive yoga

The Guardian Sun, 18 Oct 2026 13:00:00 GMT

Some yogis welcome the idea of competition – for others, it is anathema. Will those keen for yoga to become an Olympic sport win the argument?

Vaishnavi Saravanakumar describes herself on Instagram as “India’s rubber band girl”. In a typical video post, dressed in a rhinestone-studded crimson catsuit and accompanied by a Bollywood-rap anthem, she demonstrates an improbable feat. From standing, she snakes into a deep back bend, curls her head and shoulders up under her tiger-striped calves, and finishes beaming to camera with ankles crossed under her chin. This is yoga as we have seldom seen it before.

Earlier this year, the Indian government announced that it will push for yogasana’s inclusion in the Olympics, ahead of the country’s bid to host the 2036 Games. The news came the week before the inaugural World Yogasana Championship, held in Ahmedabad in June, at which Saravanakumar, a gold medallist, was one of 522 yogis competing.

Olympics? World championships? It’s enough to make some of us choke on our Yogi tea. How can a 5,000-year-old practice that values self-awareness and letting go of external validation be a suitable forum for judging, point-scoring and, not to put too fine a point on it, showing off?

In fact, in India, yoga competitions are nothing new. The first formal asana competition took place in 1973 in Calcutta (now Kolkata). Only recently, however, has it been pitched as entertainment for a global audience. At the championships in Ahmedabad, which ran over five days, 79 countries were represented, at a stadium with 2,000 spectators. The event was broadcast live on national TV. Perusing the 269-page rulebook, there is even an anti-doping policy. For yoga.

Udit Sheth, president of Yogasana Bharat (Bharat being the traditional name for India), has spent years working to turn yoga into a global competitive sport. An entrepreneur involved in building and operating sports stadiums, it was his vision that brought the world championships to life. “My work in sport, and my own yoga practice, really made me interested in how we can package an ancient heritage in the right manner to take it to the Olympics,” he tells me over Zoom from his office in Mumbai. “But to be clear, we’ve coined the word ‘yogasana’ to describe it, not yoga. Yoga is a very wide practice that includes meditation and concentration. Asana [the physical postures] is only one part of the eight petals of yoga.” The other petals, or “limbs” as they are also known, include moral vows, breathing techniques, meditation and enlightenment.

While competitive yoga might make sense for limelight-seeking contestants, I’m sceptical about whether it will engage spectators. Might it not be a teensy bit boring? If Sheth is offended by the question, he doesn’t show it. “These talented athletes have remarkable strength, posture, balance and discipline. If America’s Got Talent and Britain’s Got Talent can be on television and get such great ratings, these yogasana athletes can also do wonders.”

Would a fair comparison be gymnastics? “It’s a useful starting point,” he says. “Both practices demand strength, flexibility and coordination. Both involve assessment by judges. But the difference is that yogasana has a traditional solo event, a group event and a pair event. Unlike gymnastics, it is static. The challenge is to remain composed and controlled when you are in that posture. It’s not merely about reaching a difficult position, it’s about staying in it. It’s about how to excel while being still.”

Some categories require athletes to maintain the full extent of the posture for 60 seconds. Maybe the thrill for the viewer comes from waiting for someone to fall over, I suggest. But Sheth believes the drama comes from watching people striving to excel. “The crowd becomes the judge. That’s where it becomes interesting. One routine of three minutes would have maybe seven or eight difficult postures. Asanas are categorised by difficulty and an objective code of points.”

Further nods to the entertainment industry come from the event’s hectic theme music with its driving bhangra beats and shouty vocals. Then there are the flamboyant costumes. “When you see the contestants, it’s almost like you’re on the ramp for a fashion show,” says Sheth. “There are sequins, and the female athletes take their makeup to the next level. People want to look great on Instagram. But we are careful to preserve cultural sensitivity; revealing clothing is not permitted. We can’t have women competing in bikinis.”

Perhaps unsurprisingly, not all yogis approve. “It’s not even that I have an issue with people performing with their bodies and then calling it yoga for individual recognition and gain, or for cultural nationalism,” says longstanding UK-based yoga teacher Divya Kohli. “My problem is that the abiding foundations of yoga require that you are no longer a servant to your ego. That means you do not seek external approval. Measuring how someone does a posture on physical difficulty and awarding points for it? This is horrifying. This is madness.”

Sheth suggests that turning yoga into a sport might encourage more young people to find their way back to traditional yogic principles. “The only way to get the youth of the world to understand the yogic way of life is to give them something exciting, to take it out of spirituality and into excitement, into sport.”

How does he respond to charges that, by its very nature, yoga should not involve competition? “It’s a fair question that deserves a thoughtful answer,” he says. “Many people practise yoga because it gives them the space away from comparison and external judgment. What we are offering is a competitive pathway for people who want it. We are not forcing anyone to do it and we are not claiming to assess the whole of yoga, only the asanas, and only those that are agreed on. Also, if any sport is done right, the competition is within. It’s me versus me, it’s not me versus you. It’s how good I am today against how good I was two weeks ago.”

Not everyone in India is happy with the direction of travel, though. In 2020, Yogasana Bharat became India’s national yoga federation. But after a legal challenge brought by the Yoga Federation of India (founded in 1974), in July this year the Delhi high court quashed Yogasana Bharat’s recognition on the grounds that its status was granted by the Indian Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports when it had been in existence for just three months. It held that this violated the national sports development code. The court ordered a fresh selection process of all eligible bodies, including the incumbent, which is continuing.

There are further hoops to jump through before Olympic yoga can happen. World Yogasana has 40 affiliates globally, including in Canada and various African nations, but it needs at least 50 across three continents to meet the International Olympic Committee’s recognition criteria. There is no affiliate yet in the UK and only a few in the rest of Europe (so far, Spain, Bulgaria, the Netherlands and Romania).

Yoga competitions in the UK have largely emerged from London-based Bikram (hot) yoga studios. Sam Cruickshank, president of the Great Britain Yoga Sports Federation, says that at competition level, UK yoga sport is still in its infancy. “It is quite niche. At the national championships, we only get about 20 people competing.”

He stresses that to compete in the UK, you don’t need to be an elite athlete and it is open to any style of yoga. “What makes it inspirational is you can be stiff, you can be injured. It doesn’t matter. You can do simpler postures in accessible versions. You can still enjoy being up on the podium. I tell people to think of it more as a demonstration than a contest.”

Inevitably, Cruickshank finds himself having defensive conversations about competition with fellow yogis. “What I often say is that it’s not about making yoga competitive, it’s about taking our innately competitive nature and making it more yogic. I like to compare it to some of the martial arts that have a deep kind of spiritual, ethical background and tradition, but no one says, you can’t do judo or karate at a competition.”

Now 54, Cruickshank took up yoga relatively late in life. “I’m not particularly flexible or fit,” he says. “I only started in my late 30s to address midlife issues, you know when the body starts to creak a bit and you don’t have so much energy.” He attended classes at a hot yoga studio in London where many of the leading lights of the competition world were teaching. It was only when he watched an event (performed at room temperature, usually after a hot yoga warm-up session) that he understood the appeal. “It was really inspiring. I couldn’t initially see myself competing but I got so much encouragement from my teachers who made me believe that this was something I could do and was worth doing.”

He began competing in 2018 in the UK and has since done so in China and France, as well as acting as MC at the European Championships in Malmö, Sweden. “Being up on that stage in Beijing in 2018 was one of the most terrifying experiences of my life,” he says. “You weren’t allowed music back then, so it was total silence apart from the clicking of cameras.”

Despite that, he stresses that one of the best things about competitive yoga is enjoyment. “It does have massive social benefits. The competitions are really good fun. You meet all sorts of people. When you get to international level, you have an excuse to travel around the world with a bunch of like-minded people.”

For some people, he says, treating yoga as a sport can help to maintain motivation. “What happens, especially with hot yoga, is there is rapid, astonishing progress at the beginning. Then you plateau because your body isn’t going to exponentially get stronger and more flexible. Competing gives you a way of measuring progress in your practice. Maybe this year you’re focusing on doing a three-minute sequence for competition. And then the next you might attempt slightly more difficult postures.”

Almania Colombo, 41, is a former dancer with the American Repertory Ballet. Like Cruickshank, she fell into competing almost by accident. A three-time European competition winner, she also won international championships in 2016 and 2018. She is now on the technical committee for the International Yoga Sport Federation – which is not affiliated with World Yogasana – and teaches hot yoga in London. “I was doing my yoga teacher training in Los Angeles in 2011 and one of my friends wanted to compete, and asked me to join her,” she says. “For me it represented a new challenge, and something that intimidated me a little. I believe that in life it’s good to do things that scare you, especially if the fear is in our minds and not a real threat.”

Although she was used to performing in her former career, doing yoga before an audience presented unique challenges. “Competing in yoga feels very different,” she says. “As a dancer you are constantly moving, and in a yoga competition you have to find the stillness. You can’t hide anything, time seems to slow down and you feel everything around you so much more.”

Her first European championship took place in the incongruous setting of a Prague shopping mall. “We had a stage set up in the middle, with escalators all around, and people watched from the balconies above. It was November, people were wearing coats and shopping while we were in leotards. The environment was loud, busy and colourful, and weirdly enough that helped me find the total stillness in me, not allowing my own inner voice to be too loud.”

A key issue facing yoga’s chances of reaching the Olympics, she says, “is that there are many organisations running their own competitions and not joining the same umbrella. Although yoga means union, and it’s what we are trying to achieve, there is still a lot of unnecessary ego.”

Nevertheless, a pathway has been started. Yogasana is likely to feature as an Indigenous sport at the 2030 Commonwealth Games hosted by India. Although still subject to approval, the other contenders are games rooted in Indian playgrounds – kabaddi and kho kho – which are widely considered to be less likely to attract the necessary level of interest from other Commonwealth nations. If yoga does feature in 2030, the next step would be for it to be introduced as a demonstration sport at the 2032 Olympics in Brisbane.

Sheth remains hopeful. “I think there is an opportunity to create a system for yoga like Fifa, where every country has its own federation.” Sustainability for the long-term is key. “It’s not only about getting to the Olympics, it’s about staying there. We don’t want to end up like breakdancing. It got to the 2024 games in Paris. But that was the end of it.”

Forty years on from the tragic killing of Ahmed Iqbal Ullah, activists call for renewed fight against the far right

The Guardian Sun, 18 Oct 2026 12:00:01 GMT

The racist murder of a British Bengali schoolboy was a landmark moment. Now campaigners seek to build a multiracial alliance to combat the challenges of today

“For my brother Ahmed, British values meant standing up for others. It was doing right. It was supporting and looking after the underdog, whoever that may be, regardless of their colour or background,” Selina Ullah says, of the brother she lost to a senseless act of violence 40 years ago.

Ahmed Iqbal Ullah, a British Bengali schoolboy, was 13 when he was murdered in a racist attack in the playground of Burnage high school, in south Manchester, in 1986, after defending young pupils from bullying.

Ahmed’s murder – by a 13-year-old white British pupil who was sentenced to the youth equivalent of life, was a landmark moment. The Macdonald inquiry into the racism and racial violence in Manchester schools that surrounded Ahmed’s death sparked a national debate about antiracism in education.

Forty years on, Ahmed’s memory is at the heart of the Ahmed Iqbal Ullah RACE Centre (AIU), which houses archives on Black figures in Manchester, community history on events such as Manchester carnival, and pan-African activism in the city and beyond.

The 1970s concept of “political Blackness” – the idea of a strategic multiracial alliance across groups affected by racism – fell out of favour in the 1990s, as it became seen as an inadequate reflection of differing experiences.

But the story of AIU speaks to the power of solidarity across communities. Since it was founded in 1987 in Ahmed’s memory by Lou Kushnick, a Jewish-American professor at theUniversity of Manchester – with teacher Jackie Ould as its education co-ordinator – it has provided archivists, teachers and campaigners with the inspiration and resources to document under-recorded Black, antiracist and migration histories, fight social injustice and push for greater representation in education.

A memorial event, The Legacy of Ahmed: 40 years on, was held last month. It was attended by Ahmed’s family, AIU’s head, Maya Sharma, justice campaigners from 1986, including lawyer Robert Lizar, and a new generation of antiracism activists.

At the event it was argued that “political Blackness” – the framework in which AIU was founded – had a new relevance in the face of a resurgent far right.

Zara Manoehoetoe, a youth worker with Manchester antiracism organisation Kids of Colour, said: “Politically black is the note that we have to ground ourselves in, because anti-blackness manifests for all of us.

“We are working with young people from across Greater Manchester … The international context lives in their DNA, it lives in their homes, it lives at the kitchen table, it lives in the food that their mothers and their nanas are putting on their plates.”

The writer and film-maker Tariq Mehmood was a speaker on the panel alongside Manoehoetoe.

In 1986 Mehmood joined the justice campaign, spearheaded by Selina Ullah, which preceded the Macdonald inquiry.

Mehmood urged activists today to move offline and into grassroots organising across communities, amid a “continuing struggle” against racism in the UK and genocide in Gaza.

He added: “We were not victims [in the 1980s]. We educated ourselves. We organised youth movements. We organised workers’ organisations. That’s Indians, that’s Pakistanis, that’s Bangladeshis, that’s Africans, a whole plethora of anti-imperialist organisations … and in that context, we were Black.”

Prof Gus John, who served on the panel for the Macdonald inquiry and co-authored the book of the report, Murder in the Playground, was among speakers at the memorial event.

John said of the inquiry and the book: “What we were saying was it was important that schools have a responsibility to teach children and enable them to understand racism, how it operates in society and how they could be implicated in perpetuating it.

“Kenneth Baker [then education secretary] refused to accept the report, refused to raise the matter in parliament, and refused to put this book in the House of Commons library. Roll on 40 years … and every day, we hear more and more stories of racist incidents.”

Nika Muthra-Shah, the director of educational innovation at the Rekindle Collective, the Black-led supplementary schools programme, spoke of how young people are “feeling a lot of anger and a lot of fear about the rise of the far right”, and how the collective was countering it through youth empowerment, education in critical thinking and encouraging dialogue.

The memories of speakers who were at school with Ahmed highlighted how racism – and the fight against it – shape young lives.

From the audience at the memorial event Naeem, who was in the playground the day Ahmed was stabbed, said: “Ahmed was a very good friend. I was sometimes jealous of him because he used to wear the best clobber – Adidas tracksuits, like Run DMC!

“[When Ahmed was killed] we didn’t get any help or support from nobody, and we just got on with our life. After then, my life just deteriorated, I wasn’t bothered with school, I was fighting, I was suspended, I became racially abusive towards people. I turned my life around, [but] it’s always in my heart.”

Pervez Iqbal, who was a year older than Ahmed at Burnage High and part of the original justice campaign, was inspired by the tragedy to pursue a career in education.

He said: “We grew up very quickly when in reality we were still children who needed some guidance. Those experiences eventually gave me the determination to do something positive in my life. I studied, became a teacher and eventually I returned back to Burnage where I worked for 23 years.

“Schools and communities can change, education can change attitudes, and people working together can create something better for the next generation. My message for today is simple. Never forget Ahmed [or] our responsibility to educate, guide, and protect people.”

In October, Home Office figures revealed racially and religiously motivated offences have reached record highs in the UK. Police recorded 146,825 hate crimes in the year ending March 2026 – a rise of 7% in the past year. Offences targeting Muslims increased the most – up 15%, from 4,479 to 5,132.

World leaders must wise up to threat of cyber-attacks or rogue fridges will be least of their worries

The Guardian Sun, 18 Oct 2026 11:46:50 GMT

Global cooperation seems unlikely despite AI increasing the risk of digital fraud and the need to protect the financial system

Rogue French fridges were an unlikely talking point for the world’s leading economists, central bankers and finance chiefs meeting in a sultry Bangkok last week – helping to underline the spiralling cost of cyber-attacks.

Kristalina Georgieva, the managing director of the International Monetary Fund, seized on news that supermarket chains across France had to chuck out piles of spoiled food after hackers accessed their fridge controls and turned up the temperature to 50C.

Speaking at the fund’s annual meetings in the Thai capital, she was keen to hammer home the importance of guarding against “bad actors” in a rapidly changing, interconnected world – especially now that AI was “putting the potential of digital fraud on steroids”.

Policymakers have been warning for some time that the AI boom could at some point threaten financial stability via a share price crash – a “correction”, as it is euphemistically called.

But a different, related threat came into sharp focus in Bangkok. Georgieva said she was concerned that cybercrime, turbocharged by AI, could undermine trust in the financial system altogether.

Social media feeds are rife with adverts using celebrity fakes to punt cryptocurrencies or gold, and even the old-school email-style scams can be generated far more prolifically.

Just as a sea of AI slop has the potential to undermine trust in fact-based reporting and send people down political rabbit holes, Georgieva fretted that cyber-fraud could knock consumer confidence in mainstream banks.

Recalling her own childhood behind the iron curtain in Bulgaria, she said many people did not trust the system, and kept their cash in a shoebox under the bed. “I worry, today, that unless we figure out how to get ahead of this curve … we may end up with lots of people with shoeboxes under their beds,” she said.

It might not even take a cybercrime wave. This week the JP Morgan chief executive, Jamie Dimon, warned that the bank would not allow digital agents to operate on its customers’ behalf. “You don’t want rogue agents, and there could be thousands of them,” he said.

AI agents, including Meta’s Muse, are starting to offer their users the opportunity to hand over their financial details. The agents will then scout for the highest savings rates and shift the user’s money accordingly.

Financial regulators fret about this for a number of reasons. One is that if such services become widely used, they could have destabilising herding effects. With deposits able to be moved around the financial system at a moment’s notice, it could accelerate a bank run in times of uncertainty.

A second worry is that highlighted by Dimon: who is responsible if your AI agent makes a financial decision on your behalf that turns out to be disastrous – or even criminal?

The answer is probably that we will need case law to find out, which will only come when something goes badly awry.

That is alarming because legal ambiguity about who owes what to whom when things go wrong can be an accelerant to financial instability.

We learned that lesson back in the 2008 financial crisis, when it turned out that some banks had built financial products with such fiendishly complex liability structures that they were effectively impossible to value – unleashing panic.

Speaking alongside Georgieva, the Bank of England governor, Andrew Bailey, who chairs the Financial Stability Board of global central bankers, pointed to another arresting news story from this week – that Anthropic had warned AI models might soon be able to “self-replicate” in domestic devices. Who should bear the responsibility – and the costs – if your internet-enabled oven, or telly, blows up as a result?

One entirely prudent response might be for consumers to reject internet-enabled devices and stick to “dumb” appliances instead that can’t be hijacked by self-replicating bots. This month, some of those French supermarkets rushed to take their fridges offline to avoid the hack.

While it may not be much of a loss to society if internet-enabled kettles and fridges do not take off, the financial analogue to a dumb appliance would be Georgieva’s shoeboxes – and that would have costs for those consumers, and the smooth running of the economy as a whole.

As Bailey somewhat apocalyptically put it: “If we don’t have trust in money, we don’t operate as a society.”

Senior financial policymakers are genuinely disturbed at the collision between rapidly developing AI and the global financial system – which now extends well beyond heavily regulated banks – to embrace social media platforms, payments apps and other financial tools.

It is unfortunate this moment comes as the US – the crucible of the AI boom – is governed by a man whose main contribution to the debate has been to seek to rename AI “superintelligence”.

At the Bangkok meetings this week, Kevin Warsh, the chair of the US Federal Reserve, obediently used Donald Trump’s phrase on stage – as all US government agencies have been ordered to.

There has been some progress in acknowledging the risks. Trump’s superintelligence taskforce, chaired by the director of national intelligence, Jay Clayton, is setting up mechanisms for AI labs to report “breaches, hacks, jailbreaks, and other ​issues” – although not, it seems, to submit their models for pre-launch testing.

The UK has pledged to take up the issue of AI safety as part of its agenda for the G20 presidency next year, and G7 finance ministers announced in Bangkok that they would carry out simulations to test the resilience of the global financial system to cyber-attacks.

That could help to highlight vulnerabilities, but the questions at stake are much wider and more complex than whether criminals can hack the banks – and are urgent now, just as the prospects for international cooperation seem bleak. Superintelligence will seem anything but super if its misuse becomes a trigger for financial chaos.

‘Damp squib’: Ed Davey can breathe easy as Lib Dem leadership challenge fails to materialise

The Guardian Sun, 18 Oct 2026 11:00:03 GMT

Lengthy meeting heard grumbles about ‘blue wall’ policies and ‘Ming vase’ tactics but no real rancour

As political showdowns go, this week’s gathering of Liberal Democrat MPs, billed by some as a crunch moment for Ed Davey, was a touch underwhelming. “I had expected a damp squib,” one attender put it. “It was damper than I thought.”

Far from generating a mass of opposition to Davey’s leadership, let alone a formal challenge to his position, the lengthy gathering in a Commons committee room on Tuesday evening brought a few minor grumbles, but little else.

“My main feeling was a sort of irritation that we were forced to sit through this very long meeting, one where in the main we all aggressively agreed with each other,” another MP put it.

This is not, however, the entire story. There is disquiet with Davey’s patient and sometimes cautious leadership style, as shown most dramatically by the sudden resignation a week ago of Charlie Maynard, the number two in the party’s Treasury team, over concerns the Lib Dems were failing to cut through with voters.

If Maynard hoped to spark a wider revolt, it did not happen. “It felt like he was trying to light the touchpaper, but it fizzled out instead of exploding,” one MP said. Another was more blunt: “Charlie really has fucked it up. He has zero political nous.”

The situation nonetheless remains tricky. Davey led the Lib Dems to a century-best performance in the 2024 election, winning 72 MPs, and is safe for the foreseeable future. That said, frustrations that were already bubbling up before September’s party conference have arguably become more acute since.

This is largely the result of the two policy decisions set out by Davey at the conference: a promise of £17bn in income tax cuts if the party is elected, and support for the pensions triple lock, just as Andy Burnham pledged to change it.

Both chimed explicitly with Lib Dem efforts to build momentum in the so-called blue wall of affluent home counties constituencies where the party made big gains from the Conservatives in 2024.

While just about every Lib Dem MP agrees that protecting these seats and potentially winning more is vital, some worry that Davey is being so careful to not alienate former Tory voters that any distinctively liberal message has been lost.

“Making us the party of tax cuts just jarred with activists,” one MP said. “It’s not that we don’t want taxes cut, it’s just that the overt positioning felt incredibly blue wall-y. It’s like we are aping the Conservatives, while they are aping Reform.”

They added: “There are levels of nuance here. Ed will be given time to make changes. But there are a lot of unhappy people in the party at the moment, and not just MPs.

“Charlie Maynard didn’t help. Now we have to rally around the leader, do all the Operation Big Dog stuff, and we haven’t addressed the issues about who we actually are.”

Supporters of Davey argue that he is listening, but also point to the lessons of the 2019 election, when the party had a very clear national message – stop Brexit – but won just 12 seats, with a vote total higher than 2024’s but spread too thinly.

“Ed was very clear in the meeting that he understands people’s frustrations,” an MP said. “There are some legitimate grievances. But he has enormous credit built up, and people are prepared to give him the time he needs to make the changes he needs to make.”

Thus far, public opposition has come from only a handful of people, also including another MP, Tom Gordon, who called Davey’s argument that the triple lock needed to be saved to protect the pensions of people currently in their 40s “downright insulting”.

Some MPs are privately unimpressed by what they view as performative complaints from, as one put it, a “small minority who feel the world fails to recognise their staggering genius”. Another said: “The plea, particularly among colleagues with small majorities, is: please think when you do these things, as it undermines us.”

Another factor protecting Davey is the absence of a plan for what would come next. There are ambitious and capable MPs in the 2024 intake, but they lack experience. If Davey was ousted, a leading contender would be Daisy Cooper, his deputy and Treasury spokesperson – who some Lib Dems feel shares the same cautious approach.

One MP said: “A lot of people are terrified of a Daisy leadership – it’s the main reason why Ed is still in place. It is politely phrased as a ‘lack of a viable alternative’.”

For now, it seems, the party will maintain its own version of Labour’s “Ming vase” tactic – trying to remain sufficiently benign and unobjectionable to hoover up enough tactical votes to gain more MPs, and then perhaps support a Labour government on the condition it introduces the Lib Dem holy grail of a proportional election system.

“That’s the big plan: win the seats to deliver PR and then we can be liberals,” one MP said. “But that relies on a lot of things going right.”

There is worry, and some disagreement. But as yet, no real rancour. “Some of this is just the usual mid-parliament blues, which the 2024 intake have never experienced,” one senior party figure said.

“We are still small enough that we can have individual conversations to sort things out. And we don’t do drama. So there will be no implosion. Just some soul searching.”

Dining across the divide: ‘He thought extra spending on defence would be wasted. He’s probably got a point’

One works in construction, the other finance – would they see eye to eye on Britain’s security, the royals and net zero?

Occupation Logistics manager on a construction site

Amuse bouche He was homeless as a teenager but later got BA and master’s degrees, and has since worked for charities, the oil industry and he was even a bingo caller for three years

Occupation Works for a bank in a risk-and-control role

Amuse bouche He’s trying to visit all 92 professional football league grounds in the UK. He’s done just under 50

Carey I wasn’t nervous, I enjoy talking to people and, as my wife puts it, I’ve always got an opinion. Chris is a very amiable individual.

Chris I was a bit nervous. He’s had a radically different upbringing to me, so it was interesting to hear his life story.

Carey For starters I had monkfish skewers, then crab pasta with a glass of white wine, and for dessert I had an old fashioned with a nice cheesecake.

Chris I had tuna tartare to start, which was fantastic, then grilled monkfish and fries with a glass of white wine. For dessert I had panna cotta with an old fashioned.

Carey Chris thinks we should increase defence spending, but there is currently waste within the military spend. Before I give somebody more money, I want to see they’re looking after the money they’ve already got.

Chris Given where we are geopolitically, increasing spending on defence is something we have to do. To me, it’s not a question of buying shiny new missiles, but defence against cyber-attacks.

Carey I would argue the value of big shiny toys like nuclear submarines is slightly degraded in the modern arena – and if you’re saving billions a year on not having big flashy toys, you don’t need an increase. But I also agree we should pick up the bill for cyberwarfare.

Chris I think he generally felt that more money would probably be wasted. He’s probably got a point, to be honest.

Carey I think we should abolish the monarchy. For me, it’s about lack of transparency. There are more than 1,000 cases of the royals seeing acts of law before they were passed, with no information about what the act was like before it was given to them. We should remove the privilege of an individual to interfere in parliament. People argue that they bring in tourism, but France abolished their monarchy and the Palace of Versailles gets far more visitors than Buckingham Palace.

Chris I’m not a great lover of the monarchy, but what would you have instead? I look at the leaders of the current political parties and I’m not sure I necessarily want any of them as head of state.

Chris I think net zero as a target is completely the right thing to do, but I have no idea if the timing that we’ve set is achievable. I’m not against us using the oilfields in the North Sea – it would extend the timescale under which we could move to net zero, but that might seem more manageable for people.

Carey I agree with Chris that the likelihood of us achieving net zero as it stands is pretty low. But the big issue for me is: who pays? We have major players in this country, such as Amazon and Starbucks, that pay marginal or zero tax while paying low wages to a lot of people. Tax them and make them pay for it. Then it’s achievable.

Carey I always find it interesting to talk to people with opposing views, because it helps me build and question my own. The way that you learn is to say things to people who will challenge you.

Chris My takeaway is what a really interesting guy he was, how well-informed, and how he had turned his life around – I had absolute admiration for him. I do think mistrust of the government did underpin a lot of his views, and he’s probably right on that. He didn’t fundamentally change my opinions – but I would do it again in a heartbeat.

The problem with telling people the world is ending

The Guardian Sun, 18 Oct 2026 11:00:02 GMT

In the face of terrible crises, it can feel right to shock people into action. But what if that has the opposite effect?

These days, it’s easy to succumb to hopelessness. Whether you’re thinking about the climate crisis, the prospect of AI apocalypse, war or political turmoil, the list of challenges facing humanity can seem insurmountable.

It certainly feels unprecedented, and much of it may be. The sense of impending doom, on the other hand, is nothing new. And what we have learned from the past is that doomerism can lead to paralysis. If everyone freezes, then nothing changes – but if we want to have a chance of mitigating some of the threats I’ve mentioned then action is what’s required.

In 1947, The Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists created an infamous magazine cover with a “Doomsday Clock”. The hands move closer to midnight whenever events push humanity a little closer to catastrophe. They move back when we make the world a little safer. The original setting was seven minutes to midnight, and the hands are now a mere 85 seconds away.

The Doomsday Clock was a particularly memorable form of crisis communication. The idea was to wake people from their day-to-day routines and help them realise the grave risks facing us. As such, it stands in a long tradition of debate about how to inform, warn and inspire members of the public to take action.

On one end of the spectrum are the doomers. These are often activists and whistleblowers who feel a genuine sense of dread about imminent disaster, and want to inspire the same alarm in others. Recently, former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon made headlines by arguing that frontier AI models pose an existential risk to humanity.

At the other end are critics who tend to dismiss these calls as either overblown or self-serving. These folks argue that hyperbolic claims either lead to needless panic or distract from more important issues.

I find myself in a third camp of people who harbour sincere concerns about the problems facing humanity, but worry that feelings of dread will immobilise people. Inaction is a sensible response if you are led to believe that we are past the point of no return, or that the scope of the problem is so immense that anything you do won’t make a difference.

The problem with doomerism isn’t necessarily that the risks are exaggerated, but that it may create a self-fulfilling prophecy – by engendering helplessness, rather than galvanising people.

This aspect of human psychology has been well known for many years by experts on persuasion. When people hear messages designed to appeal to our fears, they can be moved to take action. But this only tends to work as a one-off, and only then when the messages convey a sense of efficacy – a belief that it’s still possible to make a difference. By contrast, if people are inundated with scary and overwhelming stories about the climate or AI, they tune out. Like the boy who cried wolf, those bearing these messages can quickly find themselves ignored.

A big problem for us now, then, is that the modern information ecosystem tends to reinforce negativity. For decades, a core principle in the news business has been “if it bleeds, it leads”. This came from an understanding among journalists that humans are drawn to bad news. This principle now dominates what you see online.

My colleagues and I looked at traffic to news stories on Upworthy. com. This was a website that became famous for conducting A/B tests of headlines to see which one drove clicks, and then using the most popular headline. We analysed 22,743 of these mini-experiments and found that each additional negative word in a headline increased clicks by 2.3%. Psychologists call this the negativity bias: bad is more attention-grabbing than good.

So how does consuming these stories affect our behaviour? We tested the impact of negative messaging around climate in a massive study with 59,440 participants in 63 countries. We had climate experts create 11 different messages to determine exactly which of them changed beliefs and mobilised people to take real action.

after newsletter promotion

The messages included emphasising scientific consensus (for example, noting that “99% of expert climate scientists” agree on the facts), social norms (stating that a majority of people in each nation was concerned), consequences for one’s region (emphasising the increased frequency and severity of wildfires and floods) or the effects of climate change on future generations (asking participants to imagine writing a letter about their actions regarding the climate crisis that would be read by people decades from now).

We also included a text loaded with doom and gloom that told participants: “If your anxiety about climate change is dominated by fears of starving polar bears, glaciers melting and sea levels rising, you are barely scratching the surface of what terrors are possible, even within the lifetime of a young adult today. And yet the swelling seas – and the cities they will drown – have so dominated the picture of climate change/global warming that they have blinded us to other threats, many much closer at hand and much more catastrophic …”

This terrifying passage was the one that proved most effective at getting people to spread it on the internet or social media. But like other fear appeals, it failed in inspiring real action: it was the single worst message for getting people to make the time and effort to mitigate climate effects – by planting trees, for example. It also failed to increase belief in the climate emergency or support for climate policies.

This absolutely doesn’t mean we should avoid sharing the facts about the climate crisis. The message that emphasised the overwhelming scientific consensus noted that the “Earth is warming and climate change is happening” due to human activity. It was more effective than negativity on every outcome we measured, except for sharing on the internet. It conveyed the facts in a sober manner, with the backing of 99% of climate scientists.

What this shows is that, instead of making people feel inept and miserable, we need to take the exact opposite approach. Scientific consensus isn’t the only powerfully motivating message. My PhD student Danielle Goldwert has found that telling people about the potential emotional benefits of climate action – such as increased hope and connection – makes them significantly more likely to take action, be it political participation, advocacy, donating money to climate causes or changing their lifestyle.

If we want to motivate people in the face of dire threats, we must give them a reason to hope. Without that, we are destined to doomscroll while the world burns.

Jay Van Bavel is a professor of psychology and neural science at New York University.

Not the End of the World by Hannah Ritchie (Vintage, £18.99

Hope in the Dark by Rebecca Solnit (Canongate, £10.99)

The Future We Choose by Christiana Figueres and Tom Rivett-Carnac (Vintage, £12.99)

‘Medieval romance overflowed with sexually active fairies’: the surprisingly long roots of romantasy

The Guardian Sun, 18 Oct 2026 11:00:01 GMT

Critics mock it as raunchy trash – but this enchanting genre is much older, and wilder, than you might imagine

There’s a popular genre, filled with beautiful, human-sized fairies having sex with humans (often quite violent sex, but the people reading it seem to enjoy it). Word is that it’s badly written and unashamedly escapist – all golden, glittering palaces, wild adventure and, of course, gorgeous fairies. It’s certainly popular – plenty of the stories have been translated into numerous languages, spreading across continents. Serious commentators are sure it spells bad news: at best, it’s just a load of trash; at worst, it’s actively leading people astray. Most damningly of all, women produce and consume it. Welcome to the 12th century, where fairy romance is all the rage. Sound familiar?

The romantasy that fills our shelves and bestseller lists – from Sarah J Maas’s A Court of Thorns and Roses to Callie Hart’s Quicksilver – is not a new genre, but part of a centuries-old heritage. You only need to look at the medieval predecessors of the modern romantasy novel to understand why it’s enjoyed by millions and why, even after hundreds of years, fairy romance has such power over us – and why there are still those who want to diminish and dismiss it.

Medieval romances originated in the French courts of the late 1100s and were wildly popular, quickly spreading throughout Europe, not only from country to country, but also down the social scale, so that even farm workers and impoverished nuns knew the stories. They drew on tales of fairies in earlier myths, especially within Arthurian legends, and were adapted and expanded to be as thrilling as possible, providing people with the same escapism that romantasy does today. Read either the medieval or the modern tales and you’ll find glitter and blood and adventure, not to mention crystal palaces, glorious and perilous enchanted realms, terrifyingly handsome fairy knights, and queens who live in unearthly splendour. As one author of a 13th-century romance pointed out, speaking about the real world brings “grief and torment” – so why not turn to fairies?

The wild sexual freedom of modern romantasy was there in medieval romance too, which overflowed with sexually active fairies, both male and female. There are detailed descriptions of fairy bodies, legs and breasts, and while the veil tends to be drawn over the act itself, both fairies and mortals are always “taking what they desire”, “making merry together”, “holding each other in their arms” and getting each other pregnant – even when either the mortal or fairy is married to someone else, or has only just met. And while there are fairy lovers who are kind, gentle and courteous, medieval audiences also thrilled to the idea of a brooding fairy shadow-daddy: the fairies often simmer with threat, never losing their darker edges even when the story ends with the lovers paired off happily. As with romantasy today, the medieval stories, by dint of being fictional, were a safe place to experiment with sex in a repressed society.

This was even more important as medieval romance, like modern romantasy, was often written by women (such as the 12th-century poet Marie de France), and had a large female audience (something even Chaucer commented on) – so these stories were often a place for women to explore their desires, free from the idea that they should be chaste and subservient. (For reasons too complex to get into it right now, it was generally accepted that fairy sex didn’t quite count, so women who slept with fairies were still thought of as virgins.)

Romantasy still provides this space now: although women may be more sexually liberated than they were in the middle ages, we’re often still uncomfortable with female desires. It’s certainly not a coincidence that many romantasy books today are targeted at teenage girls, who may not be able to talk openly about sex, and are popular with women from more conservative backgrounds. And while the darker, more coercive side of fairy relationships (in both modernity and the middle ages) likely reflects the common fantasy of being overwhelmed, it also helps to alleviate any lingering guilt – after all, the less consensual the encounter, the less the mortal party can be blamed for it.

These stories include a freedom from gender roles as well: in modern romantasy, women are the heroes, the drivers of the plots (the heroine of Saara El-Arifi’s Faebound is an elf military leader; in A Court of Thorns and Roses, a female hunter takes centre stage), while the male love interests, while apparently threatening, are normally intensely loving and vulnerable underneath. Medieval romances also flipped gender roles: you might think it’s a genre of knights rescuing damsels in distress, but more often than not it’s about powerful fairy queens rescuing distressed knights. Take the 12th-century narrative poem Lanval, for example, the story of a penniless and overlooked knight saved multiple times by his beloved fairy queen, that ends with her riding away to fairyland with him behind her on her horse.

While the appeal of all this to the female writers and readers is clear, men happily indulged in these fantasies, too. Lanval was written by a woman but later translated by a man. Even in recent years, it’s been reported that 18% of romantasy readers in the US are men, who enjoy the tales of male characters who love openly and unashamedly, and the strong, powerful women who love them back.

Of course, medieval courts were as familiar with the criticisms of fairy romance as we are. Chaucer even wrote a romance parody – Sir Thopas – about a knight seeking an elf queen. Today, romantasy authors are accused of cheapening popular culture by journalists who often compose articles by flipping through the books looking for the naughty bits, just as Chaucer’s parody featured dirty jokes about elf sex. As a genre, it’s easy to mock, easy to dismiss the stories as “smut” and nothing more.

But this alone can’t explain the ridicule – after all, there are plenty of modern fantasy books crammed with sex that get praised (take George RR Martin’s A Game of Thrones, for example). Instead, the vitriol seems to stem from the fact that it’s a genre enjoyed by women. In the 14th century we had Chaucer mockingly claiming that women held romances “in full great reverence” and clergymen complaining vociferously about the fact that women listen to romances “joyously and willingly”; today the genre is accused of making women stupid, with critics arguing that sexy queens shouldn’t be discussed at literary festivals.

The irony is that fairy romance gave us plenty of great literature, some still well known today (Shakespeare’s Titania and Oberon in A Midsummer Night’s Dream are straight out of romances, while Don Quixote is a romance parody, though heart­breakingly fairy-free); others have been largely forgotten (like one of my absolute favourites, the story of Guingamor). Fairy romance also gave us a huge number of long-forgotten fun romps (my secret heart belongs to the 13th-century Claris and Laris – more than 30,000 lines of pure fairy nonsense).

Medieval romance faded from fashion in the late 1500s, after four glorious, fairy-filled centuries, in part because fairies themselves were changing – becoming miniature, flittering things that were less appealing as lovers (unless you had some fairly niche tastes). But while it is depressing that criticism has not moved on since the middle ages, it’s an utter joy to see female-centred fairy fantasies returning, hundreds of years after the first medieval romances were composed. So why not read some of the medieval romances, along with modern romantasy? You’d be participating in a centuries-old genre of freedom, imagination and joy, and I’m not sure you can ask for more than that.

Perilous Enchantment: The True History of Faeries by Sarah Clegg is published by Granta. To support the Guardian order your copy at guardianbookshop. com. Delivery charges may apply.

The best toys and gifts for eight-year-olds, tested by eight-year-olds

The Guardian Sun, 18 Oct 2026 11:00:00 GMT

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

From science kits to karaoke machines, shower sets to brain-boosting games, here are the presents our mini testers loved the most

The best gifts for seven-year-olds

Eight is such a wonderful age. Kids are old enough to have their own interests and hobbies, but still young enough to get swept up in play and be absorbed for hours if you find the right toy for them.

By eight, children’s interests and skills are taking shape. They’re more confident readers, more strategic thinkers and curious about how things work. And while they think they’re extremely grown up, eight-year-olds still need plenty of time to play for their overall wellbeing.

Here’s a rundown of toys and gifts that will keep eight-year-olds occupied for months to come: a roster of creative kits, clever games, outdoor adventures and timeless toys that will keep them happy and busy (while sneakily learning).

As an experienced toy tester, I am living an eight-year-old’s dream. I have written about toys and parenting for almost 10 years and have also worked in schools and children’s publishing. As well as professionally observing children’s play, I also have three children, and in these guides I aim to balance what kids love to play with and what parents want in their house.

I also asked children’s play specialists and development experts about the best toys to support the developmental stage most eight-year-olds are at – from school skills to wellbeing – for a holistic approach.

A gang of lively eight-year-olds were enlisted to test toys and gifts on my behalf, and they weren’t shy in telling me what they thought of them. Their own gift picks can be found throughout this guide.

The toys and gifts that made the cut here balanced all these needs. Sustainability was always on my mind when compiling this list, with the guiding principle of buying well, not more. I selected toys and gifts that my testers came back to over and over and should last them well into the tween stage.

Those of a certain age may remember the TV show Penny Crayon; everything Penny drew came to life, getting her and her mates out of all kinds of strife. Well, this pen can (sort of) make the Penny Crayon dream come true for your child. The 3Doodler pen delivers a stream of BPA-free plastic, which cools as it hits the air, allowing children to create what they draw – “I made a pair of sunglasses and a very creepy-looking robot,” my tester reported with glee. The use of plastic made me hesitate to include it in this guide, but it kept my tester absorbed for hours. The filaments are made from a biodegradable material but can’t be put in household recycling.

3Doodler Start+ 3D essential pen set

Materials: plastic Suitable for: 6+

“An eight-year-old’s interests include more complex games,” says Laura Moore-Williams, an early years consultant. Around this age, many children are taught to play chess at school, and the benefits are huge. It builds focus and critical thinking, while teaching patterns, spatial awareness and sequencing. All this will build important neural pathways in the developing brains of eight-year-olds. This board is a gift for life – it’s made from walnut and sycamore, and the pieces are handcarved. It folds in the middle with the pieces stored inside. My eight-year-old tester plays chess at school (many primary schools teach it at this age to develop problem-solving skills and mathematical and numerical reasoning), so their eyes lit up when they saw this board. They loved playing with a “proper” set rather than the tiny board they had been using.

Jaques of London complete folding chess board

Materials: wood, baize base for pieces Suitable for: 6+

Eight is a great age for getting kids into a book series they can independently read and enjoy. Tom Gates was a huge hit with the eight-year-olds I spoke to. The books follow the slightly hapless but likable schoolboy Tom as he tries to wind up his annoying older sister, get his band going and eat as many caramel wafers as possible – while avoiding doing any homework. The books are filled with illustrations and aren’t too text heavy. My eight-year-old tester is a slightly reluctant reader, but they were racing through the books and begging for the next one.

Tom Gates Series 1 by Liz Pichon

Materials: paper Suitable for: 8+

“For eight-year-olds I rate advanced Lego sets,” says Moore-Williams. My eight-year-old tester loved this Mario Kart Lego set, whooping “awesome” with gusto as they clapped eyes on the box. Beyond the unboxing, it’s fun to build, with nothing that’s too repetitive, and they’re left with an amusing toy they can either display or play with (my tester definitely opted for the latter).

Lego Mario Kart Piranha Plant Power-Up Pursuit

Materials: plastic Suitable for: 8+

“We started to have a Saturday afternoon games session with friends, and they brought this over to play,” said one eight-year-old tester. “It was fun for the adults and the kids, and it was easy to get the hang of.” When I tested this game with eight-year-olds and their younger siblings, it had them all giggling. It’s easy to get playing quickly (eight-year-olds don’t want to read dissertation-length instructions) and it’s pretty rapid fire – a game is won or lost within minutes – so it’ll hold even the shortest of attention spans. It’s also small enough to slip into a bag and whip out at a restaurant or pub on a rainy afternoon to keep kids from getting fidgety.

Oh My Pigeons! party game

Materials: plastic, paper Suitable for: 8+

We all know getting kids outside is vital for their physical and mental wellbeing, but it’s often easier said than done. For this guide, I looked for gifts that would get them to break cover, and this scooter fared well.

Built for bigger kids (and adults), it’s got plenty to keep eight-year-olds excited. It has large, speedy wheels to cover longer distances – particularly handy if your kids are scooting to school. The chopper-style handlebars look cool and offer a good degree of control. Our eight-year-old tester was keen to take it to the skate park to test and had plenty of fun showing it off as well as racing it around. It is more expensive than other scooter models, but it’s also built to be easy to service and repair. Micro Scooters sells almost all the spare parts for its scooters – it even has a spares finder section on its site and a video library with how-to guides for most adjustments. Despite having a warranty of only two years, this scooter will probably last the recipient way into their teenage years and survive being handed down plenty of times.

Micro Scooters Micro Speed deluxe scooter

Materials: aluminium, metal, polyurethane Suitable for: 8+

“Outdoor toys are a worthwhile investment if you have space for them,” says Daisy Upton, play specialist and author of the Five Minute Mum book series. This football kit requires some space – but if you’re looking for an outdoor toy for eight-year-olds and have a decent-size garden, it’s a winner.

My eight-year-old testers flocked to this kit, playing together and crucially not thinking about screens or schoolwork. “Developmentally, an eight-year-old needs to build strong peer relationships through play,” says Moore-Williams. While kids may have a football goal already before they’re eight, I picked this set because it feels like a step up that’s right for around this age. The goal is big enough (8ft x 6ft) for a proper-ish game, plus there’s a rebound net and target-practice sheet. The resistance parachute was wildly entertaining on its own. The goal is built to be up in all weathers, but it comes with a storage bag if you want to pack it away.

Rebo portable PVC football goal with training kit

Materials: PVC goalposts, net, anchors, fabric bag, football, pump, plastic cones, training ladder, fabric parachute, fabric target-practice sheet, elastic toggles Suitable for: 3+

Sign up to The Filter

Get the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.

after newsletter promotion

My eight-year-old testers loved this idea: a weekly comic that comes in the post. Inside is a range of strips, which the reader becomes familiar with over time. Most issues we received included the wildly popular and zany Bunny vs Monkey by Jamie Smart, and serialised strips that depicted exciting adventures. There are also activities inside showing readers how to make their own comics, which my trio of testers loved. And, as a journalist, it is heartening to see that print is not dead for gen Alpha. You can subscribe for an initial six issues for just a quid, after which it auto-renews every 13 weeks for £36.99.

The Phoenix comic subscription

Materials: paper Suitable for: 7+

Whether you have space outside or are just heading to the park or woods for an hour, this kit is brilliant. My eight-year-old testers were obsessed with the idea of making their own “booby traps” – thanks in no small part to Home Alone’s Kevin McCallister – and it was a joy to watch them use it.

“I’ve got so many plans for how I’m going to use this, I can’t wait to tell my friends about it – they’re going to want one for themselves,” my eight-year-old tester said after one session of play. Inside the drawstring bag are a wooden plank, wooden box, rope, string, two pulleys, carabiners and some cards that suggest challenges to attempt.

The Den Kit Co pulleys kit

Materials: jute, wood, string, metal Suitable for: 6+, adult supervision required

“Everyone is obsessed with KPop Demon Hunters,” one eight-year-old told me, as if I was 1,000 years old and had been living under a rock. I generally sought to avoid potentially fleeting trends when compiling this list, but this one has real staying power beyond the Demon Hunters craze. While there are loads of karaoke machines on the market, this one feels robust – it survived being thrown about by many of my testers – and comes with two mics, a light and eight built-in games. A button on the mic adds vocal effects, and you can connect a Bluetooth device to use it as a speaker. Unfortunately for my headache, my testers went back again and again to this karaoke machine, which is why it made the cut.

VTech electronic karaoke light party

Materials: plastic, electronics, metal Suitable for: 14+ (manufacturer’s age suggestion)

Every adult I’ve mentioned Fimo to during testing has the same wistful reaction about playing with it as a child. It’s just as good as you remember it, folks. My eight-year-old testers loved making animals out of the multicoloured pack and baking them in the oven. This is relatively mess-free crafting, without any rigid rules to follow (although there’s plenty of inspiration online if you’re stuck for ideas). Fimo is single use, but the idea is you make something to play with once it’s cured – my testers loved creating their own characters.

Staedtler Fimo soft oven-hardening polymer modelling clay

Materials: polymer clay Suitable for: 8+

Moore-Williams also recommended Stem (science, technology, engineering and mathematics) kits. This particular set has 100 projects to keep eight-year-olds’ minds and fingers busy.

“As soon as I saw this set, I wanted to make a security alarm!” one eight-year-old tester said. Personally, it gave me flashbacks to school physics, but my testers loved it: “We can pick what we do from loads of options, which is sooo fun,” said one. There are plenty of projects in this Stem set to keep kids busy on rainy days.

On Bots 100 electronics kit

Materials: plastic, metal Suitable for: 8+

“I really need some beauty products,” an eight-year-old tester said to me. I glanced at their parents and could see that perhaps their hopes didn’t align.

This Lush gift set is a perfect compromise for those not-quite-tweenagers. Yes, it’s a beauty product, but still playful. Inside is a zingy Happy Hippy shower gel that’s more citrus-leaning than candy store, and Lush’s Outback Mate. This is a solid soap bar with a minty scent – a nice change from some of the cloyingly sweet scents that make up lots of products for children this age. This gender-neutral set is great for even the most determined mini soap-dodgers.

Lush Fresh As gift set

Materials: soap, shower gel; packaging: recycled board, recycled paper, recycled plastic bottles Suitable for: 3+

Every play expert I spoke to championed a “less is more” approach for children of all ages when it comes to toys. “Common mistakes adults make when choosing toys are being swayed by fads that hold children’s attention for only a few weeks,” says Moore-Williams. They’re “overloading children with too much choice instead of curating a smaller, versatile collection”.

Winning toys tend to be a bit more complex for kids this age – there’s a longer attention span for strategy games, puzzles and creative projects. At eight years old, children are more likely to be developing specific hobbies and interests that last longer than a common cold. For any gift, it’s always a good idea to tap into the recipient’s interests.

“As children get older, we should be asking, ‘What specific play does this child enjoy the most?’ ‘What are their special interests?’ ‘Can we get something to encourage this further?’” says Upton. “Really lean into what they love to do most, what lights them up, and you can’t go wrong.”

Do they love to sit and draw? Get them some open-ended craft supplies – some decent felt-tip pens, stacks of paper and notebooks never miss in my experience. If they love sport, look at what might help them enjoy playing more – kit for keen footballers, goggles for swimmers and warm-up gear for dancers would be useful and show that you know the child and support their interests.

At this age, experiential gifts are a great idea if space is tight or your recipient isn’t hugely into toys.

You can buy vouchers for a trip to Legoland for £39, and this theme park is specifically aimed at this age – there are plenty of rides suitable for many eight-year-olds. If you want something more sedate, theatre vouchers were a gift lots of eight-year-olds told me were on their wishlists. Buying vouchers from services such as Theatre Tokens will let your child have some agency and pick tickets at more than 300 theatres throughout the country.

For more, read our guides to the best toys and gifts for seven-year-olds and the best sustainable toys for kids

Zoë Phillimore is a journalist with 20 years of experience. She’s tested many things, from mattresses to makeup, and she’s slightly obsessed with finding small new businesses to spotlight. Aside from this, Zoë loves travel, being outside – especially on the beach – and finding screen-free things to keep her three active children busy. She shares her discoveries on Instagram

If Trump fells 430 trees in the middle of a golf course, do they make a sound?

The Guardian Sun, 18 Oct 2026 10:00:56 GMT

In attempting to turn a public space in DC into an enclave for elites, Trump is moving the US capital closer to Graceland

When is a tree not a tree? When it’s an obstacle to a par-3. If a tree falls in the middle of a golf course, does it make a sound? Yeah, probably. I wasn’t there, but I have to assume, based on my limited knowledge of the laws of physics.

What I do know is that Donald Trump’s crusade to clear more than 400 trees for the purposes of redeveloping East Potomac Golf Links into a championship-level course isn’t happening. For now.

The US district judge Ana Reyes shut down the project this week, though the administration claimed it had already cleared 430 of the planned 529 trees. This was after a May order from Reyes to require the White House to request approval for cutting down more than 10 trees. Reyes ordered a full stop to the tree clearing until 26 October, and threatened contempt of court if the administration doesn’t abide.

As is always the case with this president, he is attempting to assert some manner of control over a public asset. In this case, said asset is a golf course, which means he’s really invested. You might not be able to get him to stop staring at Jon Husted’s ass to sort out inflation, gas prices or the conflict in Iran, but you better believe he can put aside the senator from Ohio’s manly posterior long enough to sort out dramatic changes to a public golf course.

By seizing control of East Potomac Golf Links without any oversight or approval, the administration is essentially seizing that asset from the American people. By turning East Potomac into a championship-level course with an 18-hole layout, strategic hazards and expensive maintenance, Trump is inching the course away from being a public good and toward a private enclave for the elites.

Yes, I’m talking about golf here. I understand the irony of trying to separate this sport from elitism. This isn’t exactly soccer, which you could play in a backyard, the street or inside your parents’ house until you knock a ball through the flatscreen TV.

East Potomac is a popular course with the residents of DC. It has two nine-hole courses, an 18-hole course and a miniature golf area. The mini golf area has, as you’d hope, hazards shaped like national landmarks. Unfortunately, it doesn’t seem like there’s a way to putt a golf ball into Teddy Roosevelt’s mouth. At least not yet.

This is yet another instance of the priorities of one person taking precedent over the needs of literally anyone else. Trump clearly wants to play on a fancy, private golf course in DC. All three DC golf courses are publicly owned and operated by the National Park Service (though the park service has a partnership with the non-profit National Links Trust to renovate and operate the courses, which Trump tried to terminate in December of 2025). East Potomac, being the largest, has the most opportunity to be the shrine to our commander-in-chief’s favorite leisure obsession.

I can’t stop myself from picturing what the new East Potomac Golf Links would look like under Trump’s control. The first thing is, it would surely become Trump-East Potomac Golf Links, since a facility without his name on it is a facility wasted.

Would the mini golf course survive? Doubtful, as mini golf is strictly for poor people, and the PGA and the United States Golf Association would be too busy laughing at the windmill hazards to schedule the US Open there.

But if it stayed, I’d guess there’d be at least a few changes to the layout of the course. Perhaps you’d have to knock your ball past recreations of Trump Tower, a gold-plated toilet and the outstretched fist of the president himself.

As much as I care about the beautiful old trees being torn out for no reason, I’m equally flabbergasted by what’s at the core of this project – the lust to turn Washington DC into Graceland, or a worse, Donald Trump-themed version of that. Graceland is the final home of Elvis Presley, and has become a popular tourist attraction since his passing.

It’s a shrine to all things Elvis, full of merchandise and memorabilia. The area of Memphis around the home is designed to facilitate tourism and commerce.

I love commerce as much as the next red-blooded American, and DC has long been dependent on tourism to prop up its economy. But the lure of DC was American history, not one man’s vanity project.

Without oversight or lawful procedure, DC will become Graceland – a place for fans of a famous person to get their picture taken with his old shoes. As Trump’s tenure at the center of American life comes to an end in the next two years, he’s only going to accelerate his attempts to turn the nation’s capital into an extension of his own, very lucrative brand ventures.

There are already numerous golf courses with Trump’s name on them, so the novelty isn’t even that potent. It’s that this course is ours, and by that, I mean it belongs to the taxpayers of this country. Taking it and its history and molding it to his will is the fun of it for Donald Trump. That it isn’t his, but it can be, makes it a conquest worthy of his time. Like the Kennedy Center, he can put his name on it, he can try to change it, but it will never truly be his.

Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humorist

Ali G answers his critics: ‘Me ain’t the first intellectual to get haterz’

The Guardian Sun, 18 Oct 2026 09:00:55 GMT

Staines’s finest nailed the zeitgeist of the late 90s and early 00s, and now he’s back – but how does he fit into 2026? He discusses the backlash against his return, his worst ever interviewee and how he’s going to prevent world war two

“Can you tell people that you’re from Hustler?” Ali G asks me. “Or The Source. Or Guns & Ammo. Speaking to a Guardian journalist ain’t a good look for me in the hood.”

At Ali’s request, we are meeting in an independent chicken shop in Staines because – due to some sort of mix-up – he thought the one interview he had agreed to for his new film was Chicken Shop Date, which was “90% likely to lead to boning”. He follows this with an entirely unprintable reminiscence about the first time he and “me Julie” had sex in the disabled toilets of Egham KFC.

Now that we have established I am not in fact Amelia Dimoldenberg – and that any boning today will be strictly chicken-related – Ali changes tack. Whenever anyone comes near our table, he loudly explains, to my embarrassment, that we are actually conducting a major drug deal. Having seemingly worked his way through the entire menu, he starts asking what else he would need to buy to get the bill up to £500, after discovering that the Guardian is footing it.

It is, in other words, reassuringly easy to tell that not everything about Ali G has changed, even though a lot has happened in the “20 decades” (he means 24 years) since he was last on the big screen in Ali G Indahouse. In that time, the UK has had nine prime ministers, survived a global pandemic and seen the rise of #MeToo and Black Lives Matter. Or, as Ali puts it rather more succinctly in the trailer: “The world went to crap: there was Covid, wars and Ed Sheeran”.

Now he’s back in Ali G: Who Iz I? – and, inevitably, not everybody is delighted. The trailer alone has prompted accusations that the fake dreadlocks, Rastafarian imagery and faux-Jamaican persona now look less like satire and more like an outdated racial caricature. Which is how, 24 years after Ali G first took his home town of Staines global, I find myself sitting opposite him in his old manor, trying to work out whether the UK is ready to show him some respect again.

Parked outside is the same yellow Renault 5 I remember from Indahouse, now with a homemade Uber sign stuck in the windscreen. Around his neck hangs a diamond teddy bear clutching two sacks of money. It “used to be part of the crown jewels and was worn by the queen, RIP. A bloke who worked as a dog washer at Windsor palace nicked it and then came into the Crooked Billet pub in Iver Heath, where me bought it off him for 20K when me was rich,” he claims.

More bafflingly, he is wearing four watches. “Dem are for different time zones – dis one is Staines, dis one is Egham, dis one iz Langley Village and dis one iz Scrotland.” There is plenty more to take in, but I should probably attempt to conduct the interview I actually came here for.

So how should I address you – Ali, Ali G or Mr G? Me iz known by me mates as “De G”, “G-Dog” and “De Ali-torney G-eneral” … and by Staines Benefits Office as Richard Watkins, Kelvin Matthews and Priyanka Patel.

And what happened to the dreads? Me ain’t never had dreads. Me wears the Rasta bonnet because – and me iz trusting you to keep dis secret – dat’s where me keeps me stash, the ganja. Perfect place because the cops ain’t allowed to look under it for religious reasons, innit.

We find out in the trailer that you’re about to become a dad. How are you preparing? Are you and your Julie going to NCT classes? Me has actually already become a daddy, something dat for the last 40 years me has prepared for five times every day. Me usually just prepared with me Julie, although one time we also prepared with Cheryl from Abrakebabra in dis marble Jacuzzi me bought off eBay, which tragically didn’t end well. Me put it upstairs at Nan’s house, when me filled it with water and the three of us got in, it was too heavy and broke through the floor and landed on me Nan, who was sitting in the room downstairs. Luckily it killed her instantly, completely squashed her. She died happy because just one week before, me had bought her a new pair of double-F swingaz for her 88th birthday. The weight of the Jacuzzi caused them to literally explode; one of her nipples was found three streets away. Anyway, when one life ends, another one starts, and me iz loving being a dad.

What sort of dad are you? There have been some discipline issues. No matter how many times me tells the baby, “Hands off, dem iz mine!”, him keeps trying to grab me Julie’s swingaz. But there you go – like his dad, he iz a boobs man, innit. Me loves him and he iz well brainy, at six months old him can already read audiobooks.

Staines officially became Staines-upon-Thames in 2012, partly to improve the town’s image after years of association with you – but now there’s a petition calling for a statue of you in the town. Do you feel vindicated? And if they build it, would you pose for it – perhaps naked, like Michelangelo’s David? Firstly, it ain’t because of me they changed the name of Staines. It’s because in 2012 the River Thames started flowing through the town, so they added it to the name, innit. Thirdly, me iz well proud dat they want to put a statute of me in the middle of Staines. Me Julie says the only difference between dat and the real thing iz dat the statute won’t be selling ganja – they’ll both be hanging around the town centre doing nothing, ha ha ha! Unfortunately, as well as loads of people wanting the statute, there are also loads of people who don’t, because of racialism. Me ain’t gonna let them win and iz willing to pay out of me Julie’s pocket for an Ali G erection in the middle of Staines.
