When you watch the acclaimed TV drama Time, remember this: I’ve seen inside our prisons and they are just as bleak

The Guardian Sun, 18 Oct 2026 07:00:53 GMT

The show depicts prisons as places characterised by violence and isolation, with no focus on rehabilitation. It’s depressingly accurate

Alex South is a former prison officer and the author of the memoir Behind These Doors

The new series of Time is not an easy watch. The opening seconds of Jimmy McGovern’s prison drama show a normal woman on a normal bus, as it drives up a normal road. But to the right of that road is a huge concrete wall, topped with barbed wire and CCTV cameras.

The wall is only partly visible, just as prisons themselves tend to occupy a space towards the very edges of our thoughts. They exist, but not as part of normal life. But McGovern’s drama shows just how permeable that wall is.

The show’s fictional young offender institution, HMYOI Alderwick, is a place that boils with anger. As new arrivals enter the prison, an officer tells them: “Keep going, ignore the noise.” As if you ever could. The sound of prisoners shouting and kicking their cell doors is an assault on the ears. Those scenes are louder than any headline, of which there are plenty these days; overcrowding, escapes from custody, the latest early-release scheme. What McGovern does is crank the volume so loud it’s impossible to block out.

The reality is that prisons are closer to us than they might seem. The Sentencing Act 2026 allows prisoners serving standard determinate sentences to be released after serving only a third of their sentence in custody. The early-release scheme is intended to help relieve the prison capacity crisis, but as the recent recall rate demonstrates, this solution is temporary.

Many of the boys in Time would not be eligible for early release. Murder, manslaughter and rape are among the stated exemptions. But the value of time in prison is not only determined by its length, but by how it is spent. Just as David Tennant’s character bemoans the lack of training or education for young men in custody, so do prison staff across the country. They know what is blindingly obvious: angry people don’t come out of prison less angry if they’ve been banged up for 23 hours a day.

Life inside Alderwick demonstrates the futility of keeping people locked up for hours on end, isolated from one another and with nothing to do. The culture of “keep-aparts” is firmly entrenched in many English prisons, particularly those housing young adults. “Keep aparts” are as they sound; groups of prisoners who are quite literally kept apart, often due to gang issues or postcode wars. Prisoners known to have conflict with others end up with a long list of “keep-aparts” on their file. They must associate separately from their “keep aparts” – they cannot attend the gym, education or visits with anyone on that list. This results in staggered regimes that are increasingly complex to manage. Rather than everyone having three or four hours out a day, each group only has one hour.

Short-term, this works. But in the long-term, this stifling conflict-management tactic only exacerbates division and violence.

In Time, an officer suggests a solution to this issue – perhaps all new entrants could be told that, from now on, they would have to associate with everyone living in their unit. No more “keep aparts”. The governor’s response is: “We’ll park that one for now.” But that’s the problem. We are parking it and never coming back. We are releasing people from prison but not addressing the issues that put them there in the first place. Letting people out early was inevitable; prisons are full. But when 80% of all offending in England and Wales is reoffending, it suggests only a small minority come out changed for the better.

Most institutions are depressingly similar to Alderwick: no education, no libraries, with prisoners barely allowed any time out of their cells at all. A report this year on children in custody found that, at almost every establishment in the youth custody estate, prisoners were locked behind their doors for as long as 19 hours a day. The overstretched, understaffed system does not allow for integration, socialisation, healthy forms of argument and discussion, or opportunities for conflict resolution. If it did, perhaps early release might not feel like such a bad thing.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Being banished to a place characterised by violence and being locked up may seem an appropriate punishment for criminals. But on release day, the only ones being punished are us. Because those angry boys who fight and kick and slash, the ones with the baby faces and sprinkling of acne, are the same boys who grow into men behind that imposing wall. They are the same boys who board that normal bus on that normal road, right next to you and I.

This series of Time is beautiful and ugly and exact, all at once. The least realistic bit is the surplus of toilet roll in one boy’s cell. There’s never enough toilet roll inside. But the major flaw of the show is that it only lasts three episodes. Because the boys represented in those fictionalised prisons are still banged up in the real ones, while the rest of us ignore the noise.

Alex South is a former prison officer and the author of the memoir Behind These Doors

Blunder in, abandon allies and court a dictator: it’s the Trump doctrine, now playing out in Myanmar

The Guardian Sun, 18 Oct 2026 05:00:50 GMT

The US condemned the genocide and military rule there, but now that Trump craves its rare earths, that’s all changed. For democracy activists, that’s a disaster

Marco Rubio was once adamant that the US had to do everything in its power to end what he described as the “ethnic cleansing” of the Rohingya in Myanmar. In a 2017 letter he signed along with 20 other US senators, Rubio called for “strong multilateral sanctions against specific senior Burmese military officials associated with the gross human rights abuses”. Those responsible for the atrocities should be prosecuted, he argued.

In the years since, the Myanmar military’s crimes have only increased. What was then deemed ethnic cleansing of the Rohingya is now widely viewed, including by the US, as genocide. What little democracy existed in Myanmar was eradicated in 2021 when Aung San Suu Kyi was arrested and imprisoned and her party’s election victory overturned, and the military took full control.

This sparked a civil war that has now turned into a brutal series of overlapping conflicts between the military, resistance forces and a medley of ethnic militias. Around 100,000 people have been killed in the conflict, which has forced 5 million people to flee their homes. The UN estimates that 16 million are now in need of urgent assistance. It is one of the world’s biggest humanitarian disasters – and entirely human-made.

Earlier this year, Myanmar held sham elections, and Min Aung Hlaing – the general most responsible for Myanmar’s genocide and one of the targets of Rubio’s letter – became president.

But Rubio, now the US secretary of state, no longer believes that Min Aung Hlaing should be prosecuted. Instead he’d rather like him to become an ally. This month the Trump administration decided to upend nearly a decade of united western policy and open direct talks with the Myanmar regime. The possibility of lifting sanctions is now being discussed. The move has shocked other western nations – none of which, it appears, was warned.

Inevitably, a Maga figure lingers in the background. This time it’s Roger Stone, the Donald Trump ally who was found guilty in 2019 of lying to Congress, witness tampering and obstructing the investigation into whether the Trump campaign conspired with Russia in the 2016 presidential election.

Stone, who was spared jail after Trump commuted his sentence, recently started working as a lobbyist for the Myanmar regime, helping to “rebuild relations between the Republic of the Union of Myanmar and the United States”.

It seems to be working. Earlier this month Michael Vance, the assistant secretary of ​state for intelligence and research, travelled to Myanmar’s capital Naypyidaw. The trip was supposedly to secure the release of a US citizen, but Vance also held talks with the generals. The purpose of the talks was not to persuade the military regime to reintroduce democracy or stop its brutal war. Instead it appeared to be about securing American access to Myanmar’s rare earth minerals.

In recent years, the race to control a steady supply of rare-earth minerals – elements used in a host of military technology and hi-tech manufacturing applications – has become increasingly fraught. China controls most of the world’s rare-earth mines and almost all of the processing capacity. The Trump administration’s desire to turn the tables has led it to strike one-sided deals with Ukraine and the Democratic Republic of Congo that have placed US business interests over practically everything else.

There are more than 600 rare earth mines in Myanmar, most of which currently supply China. Since the 2021 coup, rare-earth shipments from Myanmar to China have totalled $3.6bn, making up the majority of China’s rare-earth imports. This is the prize the US appears to have its eyes on.

Vance’s trip has handed Myanmar’s generals a propaganda victory at a moment when they are doing everything they can to legitimise the regime. The US, unfortunately, is not the only country welcoming Myanmar’s generals back into the fold. Min Aung Hlaing this month flew to Malaysia, once a strong opponent of the junta, where the prime minister Anwar Imbrahim floated the idea of Myanmar being welcomed back into the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean). Trips to Indonesia and Brunei are also on the cards, while the Philippines has indicated that it too would like to see relations normalised.

The junta’s diplomatic victories follow growing military success. Over the last two and a half years, with the help of more sophisticated drones supplied by Russia and China, and the conscription of another 100,000 young men, the junta has regained control over several towns and pushed the resistance back into the countryside.

For Myanmar’s civilians, the long nightmare continues. Last month more than 50 people were killed when the military bombed a busy market in a rebel-held area. Every week brings fresh atrocities, while the hope of a peaceful, democratic Myanmar slips further into the distance.

The one silver lining that those fighting for Myanmar’s freedom can cling to is that the rest of the west hasn’t given up on it yet. British diplomats are adamant that there will be no change in the UK’s position, while Canada, Australia and the EU are all likely to hold the line too. But even here there are concerns.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Campaigners point to the UK’s recent reduction in aid to Myanmar from £66m a year to £55m. Just half of the $889.6m the UN has requested for Myanmar this year has been provided by international donors. They would also like to see Britain and others engage more directly with Myanmar’s pro-democracy camp, including the resistance.

Trump is not the first president to prioritise resources over democracy, as a cursory glance at US relations with Saudi Arabia since it discovered oil in 1938 shows. But Trump’s rapacious attitude to oil and minerals, his willingness to enrich his friends and family, and his brazen support for dictators makes this a very different America. Myanmar is simply another example of the corrosive nature that Trump’s foreign policy is having in every corner of the globe.

The question is whether Trump will get what he wants. US policy on Myanmar has been driven by Congress, and there remains bipartisan support for keeping it in place. The House of Representatives recently passed a bill that would extend the sanctions regime for another six years. Particularly at a time when his support is waning, Trump is unlikely to have much joy in persuading senators and members of Congress who have long supported Myanmar’s pro-democracy movement to turn a blind eye to genocide and war crimes.

Even if he did, the bigger question is whether Myanmar’s generals can give Trump what he wants. The vast majority of Myanmar’s rare earth mines are near the border with China and many are controlled by militia groups, not the junta. “There is no way China is going to let the US get anywhere near the rare earths,” Joshua Kurlantzick at the Council on Foreign Relations told me.

And yet even if none of this leads to any real change, the Trump administration’s decision to open talks with a genocidal regime responsible for one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises is a disaster for those in Myanmar fighting for their freedom. Many Myanmar resistance figures, including Aung San Suu Kyi, have placed their hope in US help. Like other democrats fighting demagogues, such as Volodymyr Zelenskyy, they have been deserted.

Here is yet another example of the Trump administration blundering into a part of the world where it knows little, offering a prize to an authoritarian and leaving with not much to show for it.

Steve Bloomfield is the former international editor of the Observer

‘4,000 people minding our own business’: four decades on, Falklands again face a hostile Argentina

The Guardian Sun, 18 Oct 2026 04:00:49 GMT

Facing a slump in the polls, Argentina’s president is making economic attacks on the islands’ oil industry, and suggesting its key fisheries industry could be next

A dozen local people and a uniformed military police officer (“Do you mind if I sit in?”) took their seats at the back of the handsome wood-panelled courtroom that doubles as the Falkland Islands’ legislative assembly. Outside, it was a typically blowy early evening. It may nominally be spring in the south Atlantic, but Stanley harbour, with its dark grey water speckled with historical shipwrecks, was a cauldron of swells and churn.

Six of the assembly’s eight members – five men, one woman – waited patiently at a row of desks and microphones. The heating had been turned up to just short of uncomfortable. Behind them, a portrait of King Charles. From the other walls, dusty photographs of governors peered down on the scene.

Proceedings started at the raised hand of a bored-looking young man wearing headphones in the corner. He was transmitting the question and answer session via radio across the dozen or so inhabited islands that make up the 778-strong archipelago.

It was not clear how many of the Falklands’ 3,600 residents were listening in from their farm houses out in the diddle-dee shrub that coats much of the islands, or in the front rooms of Port Stanley’s white clapboard cottages with the pretty coloured roofs; likely not on a par with the number who learned 44 years ago from the Falkland Islands broadcasting station that their lands had been invaded.

“There’s no turning back, we can expect them by dawn,” the governor, Rex Hunt, had said then.

But for those who did tune in on Monday evening, there was much to dwell on. Not so much the answers about the local internet contract or the consultation on the contentious plan for a salmon farm.

“I have another one for you,” piped up one enthusiastic quizzer with a heavy local accent, a West Country burr with a slight antipodean lift. That intervention prompted a little shuffling of tired bums. But a rather more significant announcement was to come.

Lewis Clifton, an assembly member who can date his family’s residence on the Falklands to the late 1870s, advised the islanders that an unprecedented economic war was being waged against them – a community no bigger than an English village – by a country of 46 million people.

“I am concerned that the level of Argentinian thrust this time has been at a different level,” Clifton said. “Perhaps a more vehement and belligerent tone than [seen since] 1982, because it has the potential to threaten our very economic development.”

Facing a downturn in his domestic polling and with an upcoming election, Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, has legislated to criminalise companies and individuals involved in the Falklands’ nascent oil industry, and suggested the fisheries industry on which it currently relies for its prosperity could be next.

The British forces capability at Mount Pleasant airbase – 1,800 personnel there and on Ascension island, four typhoon jets, a ground-based air defence system and with HMS Medway patrolling the waters – makes a military threat from Argentina largely hypothetical. But Buenos Aires has launched a full spectrum attack of another sort.

In response this week, Andy Burnham and his foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, restated the UK’s solidarity with the islanders’ desire to remain British, and promised legislation that might offer some protection against the financial damage imposed by Argentina’s economic sanctions. Interpol received Foreign Office representations suggesting they reject an Argentinian request for arrests relating to the dispute.

For the islanders, it was a welcome show of muscularity. They have never felt entirely confident in the spine of those in power back on the homeland. It was arguably the indifference of Westminster that led Argentina to launch its invasion in the first place back in 1982.

“I have never trusted the Foreign Office and I have been proven right,” said Norma Edwards, 84, whose husband, Roger, 80, a former Royal Marine, was attached to the SAS in the 1982 conflict. “Catching up time,” said Clifton, of what he saw as a belated toughness from London this week. But things remain precarious.

The Falkland Islands might be described as a British success story. Four decades ago, there were 1,800 inhabitants, and its tiny wool-centric economy, 300 miles (480km) east of mainland South America, was dependent on UK government handouts.

Today the population, growing at 3% year-on-year in recent times, includes about 70 different nationalities, attracted by the 26% top rate of tax, good pay and opportunities in a growing and entirely self-reliant economy.

There are Zimbabweans who came to de-mine after the war. Construction workers from South Africa who came to rebuild. Chileans who found something they liked after taking a Latam Airlines flight. The largest minority group is the Filipinos, who came to work in social care and the service industry in the late 1980s and 90s.

Working behind the bar at Groovy’s, a Nepalese waiter said he had come from Dubai. The money was better in the Falklands, he said, and “the people are nicer”. “The locals start at Deano’s bar, then it’s the Victory bar and here – then it is the Globe, for dancing,” he said with a smile. “After that they go to house parties.”

Such has been the Falklands’ success in attracting people that a permanent residency scheme, capped at 90 people a year, has been frozen for 12 months. The islands, for all their challenges, are somewhere people want to be.

All of this had been made possible because of squid, said John Barton, chair of the fishing companies association. “It has been transformational,” he said.

In 1986, the UK allowed the Falklands to establish a 200-nautical-mile exclusive fishing zone in which those wanting to operate had to be licensed by the islands’ government. Licences sold to fleets of Spanish, Korean and Taiwanese “jiggers” have delivered major revenues, but the locals are increasingly running the vessels too.

The islands’ gross domestic production per capita soared as a result, from about £2,000 in 1982 to £85,000 in 2025, putting the islands sixth in the world league table, just behind Norway. The tourism industry is also going strong, with 75,000 or more people spilling out of cruise ships every year at Stanley port, but that is at best a nice addition.

James Wallace, 41, is chief executive of Fortuna, the largest fishing company on the island. It is a growing operation, which last year acquired Cornwall’s oldest fishing business, the Ocean Fish Group. But he is diversifying his business for a reason.

The squid populations in the Falklands waters, on which his company and the islands rely, are hugely variable and it is clear that “catches are declining”, he said. “We have commissioned a bunch of inshore work to see what is happening but the answer is that we don’t yet know,” he said. But there is another natural resource on which the islanders’ hopes are pinned.

About 136 miles north of the Falkland Islands, work is continuing at pace on the Sea Lion oil project led by Israeli firm Navitas and its British partner, Rockhopper Exploration.

Independent estimates suggest the offshore oil field could triple the Falkland Islands’ GDP and deliver a Norway-style sovereign wealth fund. The companies involved remain confident that drilling will commence within months. A new jetty is busy with activity. But the impact of Argentinian pressure cannot be discounted. Two major contractors recently pulled out of the project.

Andrea Clausen, as chief executive of the Falklands government, its top civil servant, works from a building on Thatcher Drive. Her office is opposite the room where Brig Gen Mario Menéndez signed Argentina’s letter of surrender on 14 June 1982. The letter remains on the wall.

Clausen was 10 at the time of the invasion and remembers the Argentinian solders’ arrival. She also recalls cowering with her family in their home in Goose Green, 60 miles west of Stanley, as the British Harrier jets came in with their cluster bombs. “Even now I struggle to cope with the sound of fast jets,” she said.

Clausen sees trauma throughout the islands. “I guess, some extreme behaviour,” she said. “Anger, aggression on certain political subjects.” She is evidently frustrated by the recent Argentinian actions.

“The Falklands has since [19]82 ensured that we are financially independent – save for defence,” she said. “We had no money in 82 and we never want to be in that position again.”

The oil is their insurance, she suggested. “I like to think that better people will de-escalate this because, honestly, we are 4,000 people minding our own business, we have a history deeper and older than theirs.”

There are cycles to Argentinian bellicosity. The opportunistic but ill-fated invasion ordered by Argentina’s dictator general Leopoldo Galtieri, leading to the death of 649 Argentinians and 255 British military personnel, along with three islanders, has cast a pall over Argentinian-UK relations ever since.

But at times, notably in the 1990s, Buenos Aires adopted a hearts-and-minds approach to the islanders, sending videos of the animated series Pingu to their children. Such kindness has tended to evaporate away, though, when an Argentinian government is losing public support at home, as Milei is experiencing now.

But if any one attribute sums up the islanders, it is resilience, said Dot Gould, an assembly member who owns Pebble, a 20-mile long island north-west of the Falklands. She and her husband share the island with a couple who run a lodge, 5,000 sheep, 100 cattle, a load of spectacular wildlife, but not much else.

Rampaging around the undulating terrain in her 4x4 vehicle, avoiding colonies of Rockhopper and Gentoo penguins, Gould points out the scattered remains of an Argentinian fighter jet and the graves of two of the airmen killed during battle. As a child on Pebble, she used to play with the parachutes left by the Argentinians, using them as sails for a go-kart.

“I think, since 1982, this is probably the most serious it’s been for us,” she said. “How effective they will be, we don’t know yet … it’s almost two fingers up: we’ll get on with it, we have to.” But there is much that they want to do.

The islands are dependent on a narrow range of freight links from the UK and South America for much of their fresh produce. Any glitch, and peculiar shortages can emerge. There was a period without milk. A time without beer. During one cherry tomato shortage, which saw their price shoot up, the main supermarket opted to cut them in half and sell them like that to spread the joy.

A sorry-looking cabbage will set you back £8 at the West Store on the front. The local newspaper is the Penguin News (“This one’s not for Penguin News but …” is the traditional opening when disseminating islands gossip). But Facebook is the key means of communication. “Grown men and women use Snapchat like teenagers, often to arrange their extramarital affairs,” said one local.

Other peculiarities include the Falklands government paying for children from the age of 16 to complete their secondary and university education in the UK. The size of the islands’ population makes it impractical to offer such levels of education at home, said Sarah Stannard, the islands’ director of education.

But if the oil money comes online, she would rebuild the primary school. Children from the countryside – it is known locally as “camp” – are offered board in Stanley, although there are also peripatetic teachers and lessons done on the telephone.

The children grow up quickly here, and tend to be keen to broaden their horizons. Oliver Lee, 15, was keen to join the merchant navy. “I would like to see other places,” he said. “The Mediterranean, hotter places basically.” Layla-May Vatemanu, 14, said: “A lot of the boys especially in my class do a lot of sport. Our [friendship group] doesn’t have a lot to do.”

There are no bus services anywhere, and the more distant parts of the islands are only accessible via boat or the Falkland government’s twin-engine aircraft service. On a landmass half the size of Wales, there is only one cashpoint.

Touch rugby – rather than full-contact rugby – is played, in part because the islands’ hospital does not have the capability to deal with complex injuries. Much of the health budget goes on medi-evacs to South America. Yet, for all that, most of the children who leave at 16 do return.

All places are shaped by their history and geography, but some have more history and geography than others. “We are British with a twist,” said Stacy Bragger, a former journalist who represents the Stanley constituency in the assembly.

“We have our own identity. If you were to ask what are the traits of a Falkland islander – resourcefulness, resilience, making do. Because if something breaks you can’t just go down the road. You have to make do. That’s our version of Britishness.”

The islanders also have long memories. “I used to read the Guardian when I was a good deal younger,” said Mike Summers, 73, who sits on the board of the local chamber of commerce. “But I stopped reading it in 1982 when [the editor] Peter Preston just fucked me off so much. He was: ‘Oh well they are a long way away and there is only a few of them – so why don’t we just sell them?’”

On the Argentinian rhetoric, Summers added: “There are a lot of people who still suffer effects from the war – PTSD among the older people. I bumped into someone at the supermarket the other day who I have known for ever. She said: ‘Oh, I’m wondering if I should sell my house and move away. The Argies are going to invade again.’ It seriously affects some people and it is cruel actually.”

Roxy King-Clarke, 40, describes herself as the Falklands’ biggest influencer, with about 60,000 followers. She picked up a major following when posting in response to the Argentinian men’s football team brandishing a “Las Malvinas son Argentinas” [The Malvinas are Argentinian] banner at the World Cup.

She is regularly subjected to abuse for her posts. “The most common insults are to call us pirates, usurpers and colonisers,” she said. “It’s a bizarre thing to be on the receiving end of it all as they speak like we’ve just tipped up here. I can trace my family back to my earliest ancestor arriving here in 1842.”

Her generation too, she suggests, have taken lessons from what happened four decades ago. King-Clarke said she would take a “hard line” to avoid any misinterpretation. “We need to learn from history,” she said, “and not make the same mistakes.”

Jonathan Glazer was ‘shocked into silence’ by NAZA documentary

The Guardian Sat, 17 Oct 2026 22:30:50 GMT

Film’s executive producer talks about first time he watched film detailing Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza

The director Jonathan Glazer said he was “shocked into silence” the first time he watched NAZA, an award-winning documentary about Israel’s systems of mass killing in the war on Gaza.

Glazer appeared on a panel at NAZA’s UK premiere in London on Thursday night alongside key figures behind the documentary, including its Israeli co-directors, Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor.

Since the film’s release, the Israeli government has denounced it and pursued those involved, announcing plans aimed at stripping citizenship from Abraham and Szor, who government ministers have accused of treason.

Responding to questions from the Guardian’s editor-in-chief, Katharine Viner, who chaired the event, Glazer, who is an executive producer on the film, said he was “shocked into silence” the first time he watched NAZA, which is produced by the Guardian.

“It wasn’t really a question for me of getting involved once Yuval and Rachel had asked me to,” he said. “Partly because of the power of the testimonies. But also the filmmaking: the way they had presented those testimonies was cinematic and eloquent in terms of form.”

He noted that NAZA was “clearly in dialogue” with and “deals with very similar themes” to The Zone of Interest, the 2023 historical drama he directed and that depicted the mundane daily lives of Nazi officers overseeing the extermination of Jews at Auschwitz.

“Both films deal with dehumanisation,” Glazer said. “And how we get to where we do as a species by othering and dehumanising, and what that then leads to.”

Asked whether he was surprised by the intense reaction of the Israeli government to NAZA, Glazer replied: “We had conversations before the film about what Yuval and Rachel were anticipating. But certainly from my point of view [the reaction] was much more venal than I thought it was going to be.”

Glazer’s long-time collaborator, James Wilson, who was a producer on NAZA, made similar remarks at the BFI London Film Festival earlier this month. Wilson condemned the “hysterical, vituperative, aggressive backlash from members of the Israeli government and Israeli politicians.”

Expanding on those comments on Thursday, Wilson noted how the Israeli government reaction occurred before anyone in the country had even seen the film. He said while the response in Israel makes him “angry” he believes it reveals something about “perpetrator psyche”. “When confronted by reality, it’s the rage of cognitive dissonance.”

Abraham said the film allows viewers to look at the “mechanisms that allow human beings to do this to other human beings”, and Szor said the idea to shoot footage looking inside Tel Aviv citizens’ apartments was to focus on the “ritual” of people gathering around the TV to watch the “news and to see the absence or justification” of the devastation happening in Gaza.

She said she and Abraham began recording interviews before they had begun thinking about the form or visual language of the film. “We thought this is our responsibility as Israelis who have access to [soldiers and officers involved in the war in Gaza] to try to just record those interviews.”

Paul Lewis, the Guardian’s head of investigations, and an executive producer on NAZA, said many other Israeli journalists would not have done this work because of the risks. He said of Abraham and Szor: “They deserve a huge plaudit from everyone for their courage. There is a cost to them both. The response from the Israeli government is absolutely appalling. No-one who works as a filmmaker or a journalist should be punished for an exercise in telling the truth.”

NAZA is in UK cinemas and will be shown in more than 50 countries. As well as its global cinema releases, NAZA will be available free on the Guardian’s website from late November. When the film opened in Italy last month, it surpassed the Marvel movie Avengers Endgame: Encore to open at No 1.

The film contains 24 interviews with Israeli military insiders who detail how an AI-assisted apparatus of mass surveillance was activated during the Gaza war, revealing the systems that were used to target Hamas operatives in the knowledge that large numbers of Palestinian civilians would also die.

Various bodies, including the UN, Amnesty International, B’Tselem and Physicians for Human Rights, the latter two of which are Israeli-based, have said Israel is committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.

The film premiered at the Venice film festival, where it was met with a 25-minute standing ovation – a festival record. The documentary went on to win the special jury prize.

Israeli government officials have attempted to discredit NAZA’s content, while far-right activists have threatened to hunt down the directors.

The Israel Defense Forces’ chief of staff, Eyal Zamir, has said they will use “every tool at our disposal” against the film, while the military has issued a 10-page response to NAZA, which was based on interviews with more than 100 sources with knowledge of the military systems used in the war.

Demonstrators have gathered outside the home of Szor’s parents, demanding that she face the death penalty, and a mural depicting the film-makers through the sights of a gun appeared in the Israeli city of Ashdod.

Szor and Abraham addressed the backlash to their documentary at a Q&A after its New York premiere. “Our country is doing so much to hide these systems,” Szor told the audience. “It’s not a world that is open even to the Israeli public.”

The Zone of Interest won the Oscar for best international film in 2024.

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

A social media star comes a cropper in timely horror, and the Spice Girls ledge takes her disco- and indie-tinged bops out on a short tour

The Influencer Project Out now When your career involves constantly posting footage of everything you do to social media, it makes things a cakewalk for stalkers. And lo, the influencer-in-peril horror subgenre was born. British social media star Chiara King plays herself in this chilling iteration, set in Copenhagen.

Naza Out now The ongoing genocide in Gaza has proven an urgent subject for documentaries and drama alike. Here, directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor (two of the four film-makers behind the 2025 Oscar winner No Other Land) construct a doc made up of interviews with Israeli Intelligence Corps agents, who map out the details of targeted airstrikes in civilian areas.

Whalefall Out now What if you were swallowed by a whale but survived? That’s the vivid premise of this – what to call it? Eco horror? Monster movie? Survival thriller? Maybe all three? – in which scuba diver Jay (Austin Abrams) has one hour to find a way to escape before his oxygen runs out. Also starring Josh Brolin (sadly not as the whale).

Street Fighter Out now This reboot marks the third live-action movie based on the hit video game to make it to the big screen, and features Jason Momoa as Blanka, 50 Cent as Balrog, and Callina Liang as Chun-Li. Ready… set… fight! Catherine Bray

Melanie C 18 to 24 October; tour starts Dublin The seemingly indefatigable Melanie C, whose dancefloor-focused ninth solo album Sweat peaked at No 3 earlier in the year, takes her solo oeuvre for a spin around a collection of mid-sized venues. As well as the raft of recent bangers, there should be space for some Northern Star-era pop gems, too. Michael Cragg

A star-studded, 24-track behemoth, it’s quite the swansong, so chances are these arena shows will carry a similar sense of celebratory closure. MC

Mingus Big Band Ronnie Scott’s, London, 19 to 24 October Charles Mingus, one of the most soulfully creative jazz composers, died in 1979, but the powerful legacy band bearing his name has cherished his repertoire for three decades. The classy lineup includes saxists Wayne Escoffery and Craig Handy, trumpter Alex Sipiagin, and uncannily Mingus-echoing bassist Boris Kozlov. John Fordham

The programme culminates in Stravinsky’s Rite of Spring – still thrilling, more than a century after its own premiere provoked a riot. Flora Willson

Sturtevant Raven Row, London, to 20 December Sturtevant was the ultimate appropriator, a satirical copycat who had been mimicking the work of other artists since the 1960s. This first UK institutional show since her death in 2014 is a celebration of her radical take on conceptualism.

Hokusai: 36 Views of Mount Fuji Dulwich Picture Gallery, London, 13 October to 17 January Hokusai’s iconic depiction of Mount Fuji, one of the most famous images in the history of art, wasn’t a one-off. It was part of a series, and this exhibition brings the full set together.

Joy Gregory Arnolfini, Bristol, 17 October to 7 February A celebration of four decades of experimental photography by this leading voice in Black and feminist art, working across historic photographic processes and digital manipulation.

Larry Achiampong Karst, Plymouth, to 12 December Using the visual language of science fiction, this British Ghanaian artist tackles big ideas of colonialism, class, diaspora and displacement in this continuation of his ambitious film project. Eddy Frankel

Lyndsey Winship

It’s a blurred and beguiling tale about a young boy who goes missing: is it foul play, the work of an ancient shape-shifting figure or something else? MG

TED-Ed: Public Speaking 101 YouTube This ongoing and insightful series of lectures on public speaking is sure to give even the shyest person confidence to talk to a crowd. The most recent episode covers succinct ways to explain complex ideas.

Five Great Reads: cocaine nation, a 28-year walk home, and Americans give their verdict on Trump

The Guardian Fri, 16 Oct 2026 22:03:56 GMT

The Guardian’s weekend wrap of essential reads from the past seven days, selected by Miles Herbert

Get this in your inbox every weekend. Sign up for Five Great Reads here

Hello and happy weekend to you all.

We have reads for you today from all over the world. So sit back, ease into the weekend and be transported by mysteries in Cuba, mountains in Colombia and midterms in the US – just to name a few.

Enjoy.

Cocaine seizures in Europe have increased more than fivefold in the past 10 years. A host of drug cartels have taken root as the continent’s “insatiable appetite” for cocaine grows. One man, Jos Leijdekkers, has successfully turned Sierra Leone into the world’s first true narco state, according to intelligence sources. A Guardian investigation, which drew on dozens of interviews with intelligence and police officers across two continents, has revealed the murderous cost of the drug trade.

‘It is state capture by a criminal network on a scale never seen’: Leijdekkers is Europe’s pre-eminent cocaine baron. The Dutchman is credited with importing volumes “vast enough to repeatedly crash Europe’s cocaine market”. He is also comfortable with deadly violence. It is reported that high-ranking police officers are among at least 14 people killed in Sierra Leone on Leijdekkers’ orders. The cocaine kingpin is also the son-in-law of Julius Maada Bio – the president of Sierra Leone. Sources say Leijdekkers’ empire was at one time generating a $150m (£113m) monthly profit – greater than the cost of running the entire country. In 2025, the Netherlands sent a request to extradite Leijdekkers – one of Europe’s most wanted men. But Sierra Leone denied even knowing who he was.

Notable quote: “We’ve had cocaine disputes before, but nothing like this. We’ve entered a new era.” – European police source

How long will it take to read: just over nine minutes.

Further reading: As drug cartels take root in Europe, what is state capture and why does it matter?

Come 3 November, millions of Americans will head to the polls and cast their vote in the midterm elections. The stakes are high, with the results predicted to have a huge impact on Donald Trump’s last two years in office. Voters are set to decide whether they trust the president’s Maga allies to keep control of Congress, or return Democrats to the majority. With the cost-of-living continuing to hurt households, and the US-Israel war on Iran unpopular with many across the political spectrum, Democrats have a shot at taking back control of the House of Representatives and the Senate – potentially giving them the power to block Trump’s authoritarian agenda. What really matters to Americans? When the Guardian asked readers what issue mattered most to them and if they were optimistic about the future of America, common themes emerged. Most voters were concerned about the state of the economy. Justin Daniels from Michigan said: “I don’t understand why so many CEOs are saying companies are making record profits while people have to have two and three jobs.” Morgan from California saw a discrepancy between ordinary citizens and Donald Trump: “He is benefiting from his office, increasing his income [by] billions of dollars, while Americans are suffering with high gas prices and food prices and so forth.” Another theme was the Trump administration’s assault on migrants. Scott from Georgia told the Guardian: “I feel like [ICE] right now is having the largest, most powerful negative impact on people in this country. And it’s very blatant, and I feel like stopping that would be a good touchstone for how we all move forward.” How long will it take to read: less than six minutes. Giving US readers plenty of time to register to vote. Further reading: Everything you need to know about the US midterms in one place.

How far would you be willing to walk home? More than a kilometre and I am probably calling a cab. But Karl Bushby has walked more than 36,000 miles (58,000km) since he left his home in Hull back in 1998. After bush-bashing through deserts, surviving kidnappers and being held at gunpoint, Bushby says “some things are worth dying for”. But why walk? What is Bushby running from?

An overwhelming sense of his own mortality: A keen distance runner, Bushby would suffer from anxiety attacks if he went a day without running. Poor mental health pushed him to finally lace up his hiking boots and walk across the world. But his biggest driver was death. “I took death seriously. You’re dying, you’ve got one life, and what are you going to do with it? That really resonated with me,” Bushby said.

Notable quote: “I always say 99.999% of the people I met represented the very best of humanity. Every country has been the same.”

How long will it take to read: 11 minutes. But don’t worry, Bushby’s trek may be coming to a screen near you. German film-maker Werner Herzog is making a documentary about the journey.

Further reading: Are there places on Earth where humans haven’t been?

Sign up to Five Great Reads

Each week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morning

after newsletter promotion

It’s a mystery that has haunted American intelligence services for the last decade. Dozens of CIA officers have been afflicted by the strange and debilitating symptoms often referred to as Havana Syndrome (official documents refer to it as anomalous health incidents). This read asks: is it just hysteria, or is there something more nefarious behind the unexplained phenomenon?

Is Russia behind Havana Syndrome? A new book by two CBS journalists asserts that Russia was behind at least some of the documented episodes of the strange illness. The theory posits Russian intelligence found a way to wound or intimidate covert US operatives using a previously unknown weapon that delivers sonic or pulsed microwave energy. The book also suggests that parts of the US government and intelligence community covered up the evidence. But others, like Douglas Fields, a cellular neuroscientist and author of several books about the brain, claim that theories of an energy weapon should be taken no more seriously than sightings of the Loch Ness monster.

How long will it take to read: a bit under 10 minutes.

Further reading: What the experts say about Havana Syndrome.

Sarah Collard, Indigenous affairs correspondent for Guardian Australia, spoke to four young men who have lodged civil proceedings alleging historical sexual abuse by staff and fellow detainees at youth detention centres in Canberra. They give eerily similar accounts, despite their experiences being separated by years and occurring at different centres. They allege they were not believed, were dismissed or had no way of disclosing their abuse at the time.

Notable quote: “It seemed to be a bit of a protect-the-perpetrators club there … The few that did [speak up] were shunned out.” – Kirsten Nasser, from the legal firm Maliganis Edwards Johnson, a solicitor specialising in cases alleging institutional abuse.

How long will it take to read: just over five minutes.

Further reading: Sarah Collard talks to the First Nations children’s commissioner.

Another stellar cast assembles for British Champions Day, with Gstaad front and centre in the Queen Elizabeth II Stakes. Having been second best to Bow Echo for so long, Gstaad flourished at the Curragh in the Irish Guineas and can shine again at Ascot. In the Champion Stakes, Calandagan seeks to defend his crown. No horse has been able to better Kalpana in the last two running of the Fillies and Mares Stakes and it is hard to envisage anything stopping her hat-trick bid. Almeraq must surely be hard to beat in the British Champions Sprint, while in the Long Distance Cup, Caballo De Mar, will have plenty of backers against the St Leger winner Highwayman. Victory Gold has enough form in the book to give him claims in the opening British Champions Day Two-Year-Old Conditions Stakes, while Hickory is worth a dart in the lucky last, the Balmoral Handicap. Tony Paley giddy-ups the blog, with Greg Wood reporting from the Berkshire track.

Chelsea head to Hill Dickinson Stadium having responded to the 3-0 defeat at Brentford by bludgeoning Bournemouth 5-1. That marked the return of João Pedro, a key player for Xabi Alonso’s Blues, with five goals and three assists this season, though their poor defensive record is a worry. The hosts will be hoping Thierno Barry continues his hot streak after scoring in his past two games. David Moyes’s side are one of only three unbeaten teams, along with the leaders, Manchester City, and Brentford. Scott Murray helms the blog, with Andy Hunter reporting.

Simon Burnton ringmasters the mid-afternoon kick-offs, with two cracking matches to the fore. Liverpool touch down at Brentford with a different kind of momentum after a spectacular 6-3 Champions League victory at Lask in midweek. The night in Austria belonged to Bradley Barcola, whose hat-trick represented his first goals for Liverpool after going scoreless in his opening six appearances for the club. It was a badly needed breakthrough for the 24-year-old and a welcome response from Liverpool after their humbling home defeat by Manchester City three days earlier. Liverpool are ninth in the league on nine points and face a Brentford side sitting a point above them in fourth. Manchester City will ⁠attempt to keep their perfect start rolling at home to Ipswich, with uncertainty over their punishment for financial rule breaches continuing to cast a dark pall over the leaders. Enzo Maresca’s side have won their opening six league games and sit three points clear of Arsenal while their future remains unresolved. They did lose 4-2 at home to Paris Saint-Germain, the Champions League holders, on Wednesday but return to the Etihad Stadium to face an ⁠Ipswich side sitting 10th on nine points.

Newcastle rebounded from last month’s 4-1 hammering at Leeds by overcoming Hull and Matthias Jaissle, their head coach, will be hoping for a similar response against Villa after his side’s damaging setback at Coventry. But their defensive record is troubling and in 2026 only Tottenham (13) have lost more Premier League games than Newcastle’s 12. Villa are also leaking goals galore but Unai Emery’s side banged six past Fenerbahce without reply in midweek. Rob Smyth brings live coverage of the late game, with Louise Taylor reporting from St James’ Park.

Daniel Dubois was knocked down twice in the early rounds when the British heavyweight rivals clashed for the first time in May but recovered to seize control of the fight and force a brutal late stoppage against Fabio Wardley. They meet again at London’s O2 Arena for the WBO world title. If Dubois wins this, his 27th professional fight, he will set about unifying the heavyweight division by dethroning his rival champions: Agit Kabayel, Filip Hrgovic and Murat Gassiev. Alex Reid blogs the fight round by round, with Donald McRae reporting.

Rob Smyth hosts as we build towards Sunday’s big games. Manchester United’s problems are mounting as they make the short trip to Elland Road to face Leeds, desperate to breathe life into a troubled campaign. Arsenal will be determined to stay on Manchester City’s heels at the summit when they travel to the City Ground for a meeting with Nottingham Forest in the late game. Breaking news and vibes from around grounds, plus readers’ observations – Matchday live is the unbeatable gateway to the day’s big stories. Why not join the conversation by emailing your thoughts to matchday. live@theguardian. com?

Australia made good use of the reversing ball in the fourth innings in Durban, with a similar wicket expected at St George’s Park for the second Test. Reverse swing was, of course, a major talking point on Australia’s last tour of South Africa in 2018, headlined by the ball-tampering scandal in Cape Town. In Durban, it was a matter of conditions and Australia playing a rare five-day Test with a red ball on a more docile wicket. We will be picking the up action with over-by-over coverage of the first day’s play.

Spurs’ bright start to the campaign ended before the international break thanks to a 6-1 drubbing by London City Lionesses. By contrast, their London rivals are on a roll under Sonia Bompastor, unbeaten in 13 WSL games and with four wins on the spin. Six consecutive clean sheets in all competitions – their longest such run since December 2021 – underline the Blues’ glowing form. Taha Hashim is on the blog, with Suzanne Wrack reporting from Stamford Bridge.

Manchester United travel to old rivals Leeds with pressure mounting on Michael Carrick. United are off to their worst league start in 40 years and were plunged further into chaos by the defender Lisandro Martínez’s attack on the club’s hierarchy over a lack of investment in the squad after Tuesday’s 2-0 defeat by Atlético Madrid. The Argentinian pulled no punches despite being one of those most culpable for a miserable start to the campaign for his part in goals conceded to Fulham and Tottenham in recent weeks. United have won just one of their opening six league games and were also dumped out of the League Cup by Brighton. Leeds last beat the Red Devils at Elland Road back in 2002, but did inflict the only home defeat of Carrick’s interim spell in charge last season when the sides met in April. There is no love lost in this footballing War of the Roses and Michael Butler dons heavy armour at the helm of our live blog while Jamie Jackson and Barney Ronay will file reports and analysis.

Graham Searles kicks off his compelling live blog of Sunday’s key NFL action with the week six headliner in London. The Houston Texans fly in to face the Jacksonville ⁠Jaguars, but without two injured starters: the running back David Montgomery (groin) and ⁠safety Jalen Pitre (shoulder) ⁠have been ​ruled out. Still, Houston are seeking a fourth win over Jacksonville in their past five meetings and those seeking omens will note the Texans won the only previous match-up in London 26-3 in 2019.

Arsenal demolished Lille 3-0 in the Champions League on Tuesday, but Mikel Arteta’s side have little wriggle room to surrender points if they are to keep pace in the title race. The Gunners sit second on 15 points and visit Forest knowing any slip could allow Manchester City to open a significant early gap. Forest stand 15th with five points and have a frightful home record. Their last league win at the City Ground came in April, a 4-1 defeat of relegated Burnley. Daniel Harris helms the blog, while David Hytner and Jonathan Wilson watch on at the City Ground.

‘Tough to watch, impossible to ignore’: reviewers on NAZA documentary

The Guardian Fri, 16 Oct 2026 15:42:46 GMT

Film interviewing military insiders about mass killing of civilians in Gaza wins widespread praise around the world

Critics around the world have hailed the award-winning documentary NAZA as a “brilliant and harrowing” film that is “impossible to ignore”.

NAZA, which is produced by the Guardian and details Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza, was released in UK cinemas this week and will be shown in more than 50 countries. As well as its global cinema releases, NAZA will be available free on the Guardian’s website from late November.

The investigative documentary, which contains 24 interviews with Israeli military insiders speaking anonymously on the rooftops of Tel Aviv at night, has received widespread praise.

In a five-star review, the Financial Times’s Danny Leigh says that as a piece of cinema, “journalism and film-making brilliantly entwine”. The Times calls the film “hugely provocative and a disturbing account” of Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza, and the Irish Times brands NAZA an “essential record of engineered nightmare”. In a four-star review, the Guardian’s Peter Bradshaw says the “anguish of Gaza is brought into pin-sharp focus”.

British Vogue calls NAZA a “brilliant and harrowing film” that outlines the “restrained, meticulous, bone-chilling depiction of the progressive erasure of Gaza”. The magazine says the film “feels destined to become an enduring historical document, one which will and should be seen by generations to come”.

Time Out magazine says NAZA “puts together a restrained, intelligent, articulate, precise and utterly damning case against Israel’s actions in Gaza and their ongoing actions through the region. As a work of cinema, it is exemplary. As a work of journalism, it is inarguable. As a document, it is an indictment.”

The New York Times makes the film a “critic’s choice” and calls NAZA a “haunting” documentary that is “tough to watch, and impossible to ignore”. The Los Angeles Times says NAZA is a “stone-cold frightening” film that “burns the conscience”. And in New York magazine, it is described as “one of the most important films of our time”.

The Hollywood Reporter praises NAZA as a “sober and thoroughly documented bombshell of an exposé” that “leaves one with a deadening feeling, as if humanity may have lost all hope”. The Toronto Star says “NAZA is heartbreaking but essential viewing, questioning the systems that cause and quantify civilian death in modern warfare”.

The Spanish outlet El Mundo hailed NAZA as “the film of our time, a superb, electrifying, and devastating documentary about the systematic model of annihilation of the Palestinian people” that ultimately “points the finger at us. At night, in silence.”

The French newspaper Le Monde says the film “has the effect of an uppercut that leaves the viewer stunned”, while the Danish culture magazine Soundvenue calls NAZA a “soul-crushing testimony to the genocide in Gaza” that is an “example of how the world increasingly seems like a dystopia”.

The United Arab Emirates’ state-owned newspaper the National calls NAZA a “sickeningly tough film to watch”, and an editorial in the Israeli-outlet Haaretz says the film is “trying to force Israelis to confront what they already know: that Israel’s conduct of the war in Gaza has left a black stain”.

When the film opened in Italy last month, it topped the charts. The Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera says NAZA lasts “only 80 minutes, but no more is needed: the ‘scientific’ coldness with which the interviewees reconstruct how they are destroying Gaza is something unforgettable”.

The film contains 24 interviews with Israeli military insiders who detail how an AI-assisted apparatus of mass surveillance was activated during the Gaza war, revealing the systems that were used to target Hamas operatives in the knowledge that large numbers of Palestinian civilians would also die.

Various organisations, including the UN, Amnesty International, B’Tselem and Physicians for Human Rights, the latter two of which are Israeli-based, have said Israel is committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.

The film premiered at the Venice film festival, where it was received a 25-minute standing ovation – a festival record. The documentary went on to win the special jury prize.

A Day After Huge Riots in France, Shock and Recrimination

The New York Times October 18, 2026

Student Protests in France

Advertisement

Supported by

After anti-government protests devolved into chaos, leaders from across the political spectrum blamed one another for the unrest, even as it largely subsided on Sunday.

By Catherine Porter and Ségolène Le Stradic

Reporting from Paris

A day after some of the worst riots in decades in France, President Emmanuel Macron on Sunday vowed to address some of the protesters’ demands without offering many specifics as the waves of violence largely yielded to a furious political debate on who was to blame.

Mr. Macron said in an evening broadcast interview that he would seek to lower gas prices — a key complaint from some protesters — during a diplomatic trip to the Persian Gulf this week.

But he offered no concrete concessions, and appealed for “order, calm, not an escalation,” criticizing calls to “take to the streets, to protest, to create disorder.”

He also warned that “Those who looted will have to pay back, and those who sought to bring down the Republic will be held accountable.”

On Sunday, the violence and protests had largely subsided, apart from sporadic skirmishes and looting involving small numbers of rioters in Paris, as the unrest gave way to political finger pointing.

Politicians from the far left to the far right criticized the government for a police response deemed too weak or ill-prepared — with some calling for the interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, to resign.

Mr. Nuñez told journalists on Saturday that the police had not been understaffed, but that it was hard to contain rioters “when they’re scattered in small groups.”

Saturday’s unrest, which led to nearly 2,400 arrests, caused widespread damage to several symbols of the state. Among them was a 19th-century city hall largely destroyed by fire in Limoges, a town in central France renowned for its porcelain. Nearly 1,000 police officers were injured, France’s interior ministry said on Sunday, including seven suffering from serious injuries.

Rioters also attacked city halls from Lille in northern France to Marseille in the south, where they broke into the local government headquarters and tipped over a bust of Marianne, a symbol of the French Republic. A fire destroyed a tourist office in Lyon, and 1,500 shops were damaged or looted nationwide, according to Alexandre Bompard, head of the French federation of commerce and distribution, who estimated that the cost of repairs could run into hundreds of millions of dollars.

“I’ve never seen this before, I am disgusted,” said Sophie Vanpoperinghe, 47, as she gazed at ransacked shops on Boulevard Magenta, the road in Paris where she has lived for 22 years and which is frequently used for demonstrations.

More than half a million demonstrators marched on Saturday to protest the rising cost of living and poor conditions in schools, among other grievances. Many were stunned on Sunday at how rioters had used those demonstrations as a smoke screen for vandalism.

Estelle Grandidier, a nonprofit worker who had marched in Paris, said she was “shocked” to see scenes reminiscent of those she has observed in crisis zones overseas.

But Ms. Grandidier said that a clear distinction should be made between the rioters and the protesters, who came “onto the streets to present their demands in a completely peaceful manner.”

Government officials and far right leaders accused the far left of stirring up the unrest, and left-wing leaders blamed the government for budget decisions and heavy-handed policing that they said had spurred public anger.

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu placed the blame for the chaos squarely on a far-left party, France Unbowed. The leader of that party, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, stands a chance of beating centrists to the runoff in next year’s presidential election to succeed President Emmanuel Macron.

Mr. Lecornu accused France Unbowed of sowing distrust about the police among student protesters all week. He also said that the earliest rioters had started attacking riot police and government buildings before official protests were set to begin and were members of the “ultra-left.”

“Behind all this, there is obviously a political battle to wage,” Mr. Lecornu said, adding that the country was at “the point of no return.”

“It’s also time to choose sides,” he said. “Either you are in the camp of the Republic, and therefore of law enforcement — and of those who protect people and property and enforce the laws — or you are on the side of the rioters.”

In response, Mr. Mélenchon blamed the government. He said on social media that Mr. Lecornu was “responsible for the chaos” — due to “incompetence or a worst-case strategy to create a party of order that would make people forget his failure in public finances.”

Mr. Lecornu did not respond to that accusation, but had earlier urged Mr. Mélenchon to call out the perpetrators of looting and violence.

Mr. Mélenchon had offered a qualified condemnation of the violence, stating that “those who share our fight have no place in looting, in pillaging.”

Regardless of the “responsibilities of those in power,” he said on Saturday night, the left “must refuse to take part in actions without political meaning and contrary to our methods.”

Marine Le Pen, a far-right leader who leads the polls for next year’s presidential election, said that “legitimate social demands” had been “hijacked by the far left and the rhetoric of Jean-Luc Mélenchon” and his colleagues, whom she accused of fostering chaos by “legitimizing violence.”

Protest organizers had hoped that the demonstrations on Saturday would lead to a convergence between the student demonstrations demanding better school conditions that have roiled France since September, and a broader social movement addressing a wider array of concerns, including the rising cost of living.

What emerged on Saturday, as more than half a million people protested nationwide, seemed like a split-screen event. Students, farmers, teachers and trade unionists often marched peacefully through one part of a city, while groups of black-clad agitators sparred with police and caused damage in other areas.

Then, as things unraveled, opportunist rioters joined in, exploiting the chaos, government officials said.

“It’s sad, people got angry,” said Laure Monloubou, 50, as she gazed at the aftermath in Paris near Place de la République, where dozens of shops were looted and cars were burned on Saturday.

But she, too, emphasized that the anger of those who looted was “not to be mixed up” with that of people peacefully walking in the streets.

In Paris, the police said they were confronted first by “wildcat marches” and violent groups of 500 to 1,000 people. The situation changed in the late afternoon, the Paris police prefecture said in a statement on Sunday morning, with “the massive arrival of individuals whose sole objective was to commit theft and looting, taking advantage of the disorder to act.”

Sorin Moraru, 48, the owner of a cleaning company, was working on Sunday to restore a bank agency that had been attacked in Paris. He said the vandalism was “unacceptable.”

The damage, he estimated, would take days for his team of six to clean up. The looters “should be caught and punished, they should pay,” Mr. Moraru said.

“One can demonstrate, one can express oneself, but not destroy,” he added.

Though the scale of the protests on Saturday led some union leaders to consider it a success, the movement faced an uncertain future on Sunday as French society processed the violence and looting that accompanied the demonstrations.

With French schools starting a two-week half-term holiday, the high school movement is expected to lose steam — though some labor unions, including the C. G. T., one of France’s largest, have called for another day of mass demonstrations on Nov. 5.

“It feels like society is spinning out of control,” said Henri Parent, 56, a tourist from Belgium who was surveying broken storefronts in central Paris on Sunday morning.

Catherine Porter is an international reporter for The Times, covering France. She is based in Paris.

Ségolène Le Stradic a reporter and researcher for The Times, based in Paris.

Migrants From Ukraine and Sudan to Keep Deportation Protections for Now

The New York Times October 18, 2026

U. S. Immigration Crackdown

Advertisement

Supported by

Temporary Protected Status for the two countries was set to expire on Monday. The Trump administration said an announcement would be made “at the appropriate time.”

By Madeleine Ngo

Reporting from Washington

The Trump administration said on Sunday that people from Ukraine and Sudan would be able to keep their temporary humanitarian protections for now, allowing them to continue living in the United States.

Temporary Protected Status, a program meant to help foreign nationals who cannot safely return home because of armed conflict or natural disasters in their countries, was set to expire for about 100,000 Ukrainians and about 1,800 Sudanese on Monday.

The Homeland Security Department said that an announcement on the future of both programs would be “made at the appropriate time” and that people covered by them would be protected until then. But the department did not provide more information on the timing of the announcement.

Ukraine is nearly five years into a war that has battered the country, and civilian casualties have hit the highest levels since the beginning of the full-scale invasion by Russia. Sudan is in the middle of a devastating civil war that has engulfed the country for more than three years, leading to a severe food crisis.

The decision to hold off making an announcement mirrored a similar move by the Trump administration last month to allow people from El Salvador to keep their deportation protections for now. Since then, no announcement has been made and more than 170,000 Salvadorans have been left in limbo.

The moves notably diverge from the Trump administration’s previous attempts to swiftly dismantle T. P. S. programs as part of its broader campaign to restrict immigration, ending the protections for 13 of the 17 countries once covered. They also sharply differ from the administration’s treatment of about 350,000 Haitians who lost their temporary deportation protections this summer, despite ongoing unrest in their country. In a barrage of social media posts, homeland security officials cheered on deportation flights to Haiti.

But President Trump’s aggressive immigration crackdown has become a political problem for Republicans ahead of the midterm elections on Nov. 3, and his party is at risk of losing control of one or both chambers of Congress. The decision to keep the protections for Ukrainians also comes as tensions between Mr. Trump and President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine have erupted over Mr. Trump’s thawing relationship and deal-making with Moscow, raising questions about the future of U. S. support for Ukraine.

This month, the United States lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports that were first put in place to limit Moscow’s ability to finance the war. On Friday, Mr. Trump signed an order exempting Russia from new sanctions approved by Congress that were intended to target Russian officials, oligarchs and financial institutions.

Mr. Trump’s efforts stem from concerns that high fuel prices could hurt Republicans in the midterms. He has demanded that Ukraine stop striking Russian oil refineries so that Moscow can send more diesel to global markets. But Mr. Zelensky said last week that he would resume the strikes after Russia refused to halt its own attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, defying Mr. Trump.

The Trump administration’s decision to keep the deportation protections, at least for now, is a sign that the United States is still committed to providing some assistance for Ukrainians.

Kate, a recent high school graduate in Nebraska, said she was glad that T. P. S. would not immediately end for Ukrainians. She said that she fled the country with her mother and brother four years ago, and that the program had allowed them to live in the United States.

But Kate, who agreed to be interviewed on the condition that only her first name be used because she fears being targeted by immigration agents, said she worried that the United States could still terminate the protections before the war ended.

She recalled living in a bomb shelter shortly after the war broke out and frequently hearing rockets fly over her hometown. “I’m very scared to go back,” she said. “Nobody’s safe there.”

The administration’s decision to hold off making an announcement about the programs was also criticized by some former homeland security officials who said the moves created uncertainty for families and employers across the country.

“In light of the armed conflicts that continue in Ukraine and Sudan, extending T. P. S. is the right decision,” said Royce Murray, an assistant secretary at the Homeland Security Department during the Biden administration. “But the lack of clarity about the decision — including for how long T. P. S. will last — creates incredible instability for T. P. S. holders and the employers who rely on them.”

Hamed Aleaziz contributed reporting.

Madeleine Ngo covers immigration and economic policy for The Times.

On the Campaign Trail, Trump Tries to Outrun a Bad Week in Washington

The New York Times October 18, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

News Analysis

As Trump rallies around the nation, his White House was consumed by dramas that reinforce how his presidency has become a drag on his party’s prospects in the midterms.

By Tyler Pager

Tyler Pager is a White House correspondent. He reported Wasilla, Alaska; Kalispell, Montana; Dalton, Georgia; and Highland Heights, Kentucky.

President Trump continued to sell himself as the Republican Party’s savior as he crisscrossed the country in recent days, making it clear in words and sheer presence that this midterm election is about him.

But back in the nation’s capital, Mr. Trump’s White House was consumed by dramas that reinforced why polls show that his presidency itself has become a drag on Republican tickets.

On Monday, Mr. Trump asked for the resignation of Kimberly Guilfoyle, his ambassador to Greece, after a string of embarrassing reports, including that she urged a donor to pay for her $100,000 credit card debt. The president on Thursday canceled the Pentagon’s planned livestream of an execution of the Army officer convicted in the 2009 Fort Hood mass shooting after bipartisan outrage. And on Friday, he ousted his press secretary of five days after her bumpy debut.

Meantime, the White House Counsel’s Office was investigating a dispute between two prominent Trump allies and former administration officials over claims one of them misallocated funds for the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, a heated conflict stemming from a transaction from the Democratic Republic of Congo to a Texas defense company. And the administration deepened its standoff with the federal judge presiding over a lawsuit challenging the president’s plan for a golf course, pushing to disqualify her after she excoriated federal officials for ripping up hundreds of mature trees with little notice.

Together, the string of controversies invoked the chaos of Mr. Trump’s first term, when infighting among his aides regularly burst into public view. The week also encapsulated how Mr. Trump’s approval ratings have been dragged down by his administration’s policies and allegations of self-dealing that have shadowed much of his inner circle.

“It feels like late 2020,” said Alyssa Farah Griffin, who served in Mr. Trump’s White House during his first term. “There’s almost too much chaos. It's drinking from the fire hose, and you can’t anticipate the next plot twist from this administration.”

She added: “You couldn’t dream up a worse week for the White House heading into the midterms.”

Mr. Trump's approval rating sits around 37 percent, the lowest of his presidency, according to The New York Times average of polls. A Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll conducted Oct. 9-13 and released on Sunday shows his approval among Republicans dropped from 88 percent near the start of his term to 79 percent. The survey also found, for the first time in a decade, that voters trust Democrats more on the economy, and 66 percent of voters said Mr. Trump is using the presidency to enrich himself.

A Fox News poll from this month found that government corruption ranked first among voters’s concerns, followed by inflation, gas prices, government leadership and health care. Democrats are making the case that corruption is in fact a cause of higher prices.

“To the extent that Republicans are successful in keeping the Senate, it will be because of their success in distancing themselves from some of the president’s policies,” former Senator Jeff Flake, Republican of Arizona and longtime Trump critic who served as ambassador to Turkey in the Biden administration, said in an interview. “And that’s not a position you want to be in. And it’s not just the policies. It’s the weirdness of it. The crass and crude and vulgar language. It’s awful. It doesn’t help Republicans.”

On the road, Mr. Trump made no mention of the latest controversies. He held rallies in six different states, stretching from Alaska to Georgia, serving up a familiar message: His presidency has been an unbridled success, and Democratic victories next month threaten America’s future.

Inside the cosseted bubble of a Trump rally, composed largely of MAGA superfans, that message was met with hearty concurrence from the president’s adoring fans.

Tara Green, a front desk office administrator who attended the rally in Wasilla, Alaska, said seeing Mr. Trump was “an opportunity of a lifetime.”

“Trump has a vision, and it might take time, but it is fixing things,” she said. “I have every belief and trust in him.”

Still, there were signs of Mr. Trump’s eroding support, even inside his bubble. The president was interrupted by protesters at each of his rallies, once a rare occurrence. And swaths of the arenas, which Mr. Trump used to pack with ease, remained empty.

At a check-in desk for special guests on Saturday outside Truist Arena in Highland Heights, Ky., one volunteer asked a staffer for Mr. Trump how many people they were expecting at the rally. The staffer, outfitted in a “Team Trump” jacket, said they had expected a larger audience than was on hand. (The entire upper level of the arena remained empty during the rally.) The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

Mr. Trump’s closing message also was notably meandering, even for a man who boasts about “the weave,” his description of how he bounces from one topic to another without any discernible connection.

The president kicked off most rallies this week by praising the appearance of Republican male candidates. (He seemed particularly enthralled by the backside of Senator Jon Husted, Republican of Ohio, bringing it up at two different rallies this week.)

He recounted his own political successes and margins of victory in the states he was visiting, most of which are historically Republican strongholds and a sign of how much ground his party is defending this year.

And he reminded voters of the basket of incentives he’s offering if they elect Republicans, expanding it from cash bonuses to pardons and investments from the Pentagon.

But even the president downplayed the impact of his signature midterm giveaway: a controversial promise to give $5,000 for every American adult — which he calls the “Trump dividend” — if Republicans retain control of Congress.

Describing a hypothetical conversation about a couple looking to spend the money, “Let’s go to Palm Beach and join the president for lunch. Let’s have lunch at Mar-a-Lago, where for $5,000, you’ll get one hamburger and a small dessert,” he said, with a laugh. “I shouldn’t say that.”

That line in particular underscored how Mr. Trump has repeatedly seemed to minimize voter anxieties about rising costs, one reason Republicans have tried distancing themselves from the president.

Even among rally-goers, there seemed more wariness than in earlier elections, and loyalty to Mr. Trump seemed more important than concerns about policy or the turbulence in his administration.

Ustun Yuksel, a Trump supporter who has a Ph. D in political science and lives in Dawsonville, Ga., acknowledged that he needs to work on addressing cost of living issues.

“They can definitely do better,” he said, while waiting for Mr. Trump in Dalton, Ga.

But he said he likes Mr. Trump’s foreign policy. And he had no interest in discussing the latest headlines out of the White House.

“I don’t want to talk about it,” Mr. Yuksel said just after the news broke that Katie Zacharia, the White House press secretary, was ousted. “I don’t want to say anything.”

A few hours later, as Amy Thomas, a bail bonds agent from Cleveland, Tennessee, waited in traffic to exit the rally, she jumped out of her car to capture Mr. Trump depart on Marine One. She said Mr. Trump was “getting the job done” and demurred when asked about the turmoil in the administration.

“My friend follows it more than I do,” she said of the firings and latest drama.

Tyler Pager is a White House correspondent for The Times, covering President Trump and his administration.
