The 2028 Presidential ‘Shadow Primary’ Descends on the Midterms

The New York Times October 18, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The schedule is especially packed in New Hampshire, an early presidential nominating state where there is a competitive Senate race Democrats are flocking to this month.

By Evan Gorelick

Gov. Gavin Newsom of California spent his Saturday weaving through New Hampshire, campaigning with midterm candidates as he faced questions about his presidential ambitions. Next weekend, former Vice President Kamala Harris, who is weighing another White House bid, plans to be in the state with the Democratic Senate nominee. And days after that, Senator Mark Kelly of Arizona, who is also considering a run, will appear there, too.

In the final stage of this year’s midterms, prospective presidential candidates are parachuting into battleground states to rally support for candidates on the ballot this fall, road-test their stump speeches, and introduce themselves to voters and activists. The Democratic schedule is especially packed in New Hampshire, an early presidential nominating state where there is a competitive Senate race. While New Hampshire has lost its long vaunted first-in-the-nation Democratic primary status to South Carolina, it will go third in 2028.

“Got here last night from the most un-Trump state in the United States of America, California,” Mr. Newsom told the crowd in Exeter, N. H., at a rally on Saturday with Representative Chris Pappas, the Democratic Senate nominee, as well as other Democratic candidates. His 10-minute speech focused primarily on Mr. Trump.

Ambitious Republicans, too, are trying to leave lasting marks across the country in this year’s high-stakes elections. Vice President JD Vance and Senator Ted Cruz of Texas are hitting the road for midterm candidates, including in states expected to figure prominently in the next G. O. P. presidential race.

In both parties, the possible presidential candidates’ itineraries reflect their standings, showing where they are in demand and where they are not. At times, midterm candidates have subtly or loudly distanced themselves from some of them.

In other cases, midterm contenders have welcomed the extra attention and support. Mr. Newsom’s trip to New Hampshire follows recent visits by Senator Raphael Warnock, Democrat of Georgia, and Pete Buttigieg, the former transportation secretary, among others. Mr. Pappas, whose roster of surrogates from outside New Hampshire has grown, is facing former Senator John E. Sununu, a Republican.

“I think of political campaigns like building a house. You have to build the foundation first before building the walls. That’s what these visits are,” said Jim Demers, a veteran New Hampshire Democratic strategist, who like other operatives refers to the current phase as the “shadow primary.”

At the town hall event in Exeter, Mr. Newsom popped out from behind a curtain, beaming as Macklemore and Ryan Lewis’s “Can’t Hold Us” played in the background. Asked about his political future, he waved his hand and said, “It’s all about 2026.”

While others similarly say they are solely focused on this year’s elections, Democratic and Republican strategists see multiple purposes in these visits.

“A campaign for president is like having an endoscopy and a colonoscopy at the same time,” said Jesse Ferguson, a Democratic strategist. “A lot of candidates are truly deciding whether they want to do this.”

Midterm travel may be especially attractive to lesser-known politicians looking to raise their national profiles, and to those who don’t hold public office.

Mr. Buttigieg, who left his post in the Biden administration in early 2025, has endorsed more than 100 candidates this cycle and campaigned for them in more than 30 states. Gov. Andy Beshear of Kentucky has headlined Democratic Party dinners or conventions in nine states, including several that will hold early presidential primaries. Representative Ro Khanna of California has campaigned for more than 70 candidates.

Others have been more selective with their travels. Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Democrat of New York, recently campaigned in Michigan, another early-nominating state, with Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for Senate. She plans to appear in Maine this week with Troy Jackson, the Democratic Senate nominee there.

The country faces a “pivotal and consequential moment,” Ms. Ocasio-Cortez said in Michigan on Friday. She brushed aside speculation about her 2028 plans, saying, “What matters right now is the next 19 days.”

Ms. Harris also recently appeared with Dr. El-Sayed. She plans to visit Nevada, an early-nominating state, as well as Mississippi, Georgia and Wisconsin.

But Senate candidates in Alaska, Iowa and Kansas have publicly and pre-emptively uninvited Ms. Harris, whose ties to the Biden administration have made her unwelcome in some conservative-leaning states.

Tensions have flared in other ways. In recent weeks, Latino leaders became angry that the Democratic Governors Association, chaired by Mr. Beshear, was not investing more money into Gina Hinojosa’s race for Texas governor against Greg Abbott, the Republican incumbent. They made veiled threats to withhold their support from Mr. Beshear should he run for president in 2028.

Within a week, the D. G. A. made a seven-figure donation to help elect Ms. Hinojosa.

Some potential presidential candidates have sought to balance their own re-elections: Govs. JB Pritzker of Illinois and Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania are on the ballot in November. Mr. Shapiro recently started a federal political-action committee that enables him to give money to congressional candidates.

On the Republican side, Mr. Vance has campaigned in Kansas, Michigan and other battlegrounds. In Michigan on Thursday, he called the Senate contest “the most important race in the United States of America,” as he stumped for Mike Rogers, the Republican nominee.

Mr. Trump’s sinking approval ratings have made the president and, by extension, Mr. Vance a liability for some battleground candidates, as they seek to energize the party’s base voters. When Mr. Vance held a rally in Iowa last month, Ashley Hinson, the Republican nominee for Senate, didn’t attend, citing scheduling conflicts.

Republican “candidates in swing seats want his voters, not necessarily his baggage,” said Matt Klink, a Republican strategist in California, speaking of Mr. Trump.

Mr. Cruz, who has clashed publicly with Mr. Vance, has raised money and campaigned in his home state of Texas for Ken Paxton, the Republican Senate nominee in a tight contest, and visited Iowa, which has been an early Republican nominating state, among other places.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, a frequent target in Democrats’ campaign attacks, has also campaigned for Republicans this cycle in Iowa and Kentucky, a departure from past Pentagon officials who have stayed out of politics.

In New Hampshire, Derek Thibeault, 55, the chair of the Nashua Democratic City Committee, said he approached Mr. Newsom at an event on Saturday and asked the governor to let him know when he’d be back to campaign for the White House.

“He gave me a big laugh, but he didn’t say no,” Mr. Thibeault said.

Andrew Sylvia contributed reporting from New Hampshire.

Evan Gorelick is a New York-based writer for The Morning, the flagship daily newsletter of The Times.

Trump Outlines Rapid Plan to Close and Overhaul D. C. Golf Course

The New York Times October 18, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

The plan to begin work transforming the course in four weeks injected fresh urgency into a federal lawsuit opposing changes to East Potomac Golf Links.

By Zach Montague

Reporting from Washington

President Trump said on Sunday that his administration had finalized plans to transform East Potomac Golf Links in Washington into a “World Class Championship Golf Course,” saying the municipal course would close within four weeks and that its replacement would be playable in about 15 months.

The announcement set up another frantic legal clash over the site. A federal judge ordered the administration in July to present her with any long-term plans for the course and not to carry out a surprise overhaul as the president had with the East Wing of the White House and the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

The Interior Department appeared to have done just that earlier this month, taking down hundreds of trees over a holiday weekend and giving the court and a group suing to stop any changes to the course less than a day to react.

In a post on social media on Sunday morning, Mr. Trump appeared to affirm what a historical-preservation group and two Washington residents had warned of in a federal lawsuit: that the administration might move to seize the existing course before they had a real chance to oppose the plan.

Mr. Trump wrote that he had already notified professional golf organizations that “they will soon have one of the Best and Most Spectacular Golf Courses anywhere in the World to put on their list of great places to play, and hold Major Events.” He added that he had secured a design by Tom Fazio, a well-known designer who has planned other courses owned by the Trump Organization.

The president shared a rendering of the planned course that resembled a blurred-out image sitting on his desk in a photo shared on Friday by Katie Zacharia, his press secretary who was ousted from the role after less than a week.

In response to the post, Judge Ana C. Reyes, who has presided over the case, ordered the Justice Department to reconcile the announcement with what had been said in court by Sunday at 8 p. m.

She noted that the government had consistently denied that any decisions on the future of the course had been made along the lines of the vision Mr. Trump has shared publicly. She quoted a Justice Department lawyer who, as recently as Friday, said that Mr. Trump “at most” had given only “preliminary thought to” the future of the course.

The group opposing the plan has argued that the existing course provided an affordable and accessible option to players in the Washington area who would be harmed by its conversion into a more exclusive, professional-level destination. Critics and local golfers have also expressed doubt that the isolated Hains Point peninsula, where the course is situated, could handle the traffic that professional tournaments would demand.

The map Mr. Trump shared on Sunday showed the new course covering the bulk of East Potomac Park, with the proposed 12th hole situated over what is now a public picnic area and playground at Hains Point. In addition to the current municipal course, the perimeter of the island is also a popular cycling circuit.

“East Potomac Park is a national park, golf course and recreational facility that is meant for everyone to enjoy,” said Skye Perryman, the president of Democracy Forward, which is representing the group challenging the plan. “Our litigation is intended to protect this community jewel for the people and communities it serves.”

Mr. Trump has signaled for months that he intended to realize the plan, and he was photographed touring the site and studying blueprints with Doug Burgum, the interior secretary, and Mr. Fazio in June.

But because there had not previously been imminent plans to move forward with the redevelopment, Judge Reyes was hesitant for months to preemptively block the Trump administration from making any changes to the existing course. Instead, she had prevailed upon the Justice Department to notify her before making any major changes.

During a hearing in July, a Justice Department lawyer said that no decision had been reached on the fate of the course.

After it was revealed that the Interior Department cleared hundreds of trees last weekend, Judge Reyes excoriated the Justice Department for failing to keep her apprised during a fiery hearing on Monday. She accused the government of “double speak” for representing in court that the work was planned maintenance, despite Mr. Trump’s public vision to transform the course.

Seething at a government lawyer, Judge Reyes turned an extended portion of the four-hour hearing into an effort to identify who had given the go-ahead to begin the work. She ordered the government to track down several senior officials in the Interior Department to testify on the spot but was able to reach only one.

Judge Reyes lamented that she had tried to avoid “playing parks and rec” or policing landscaping decisions at the course. But confronted with signs that the administration was rushing forward, she ordered the government not to remove any more trees until Oct. 26 to give the group opposing the plan time to respond.

The question of who authorized the work is expected to be the focus of a hearing on Monday, at which Judge Reyes had ordered Gregory Wischer, a Trump appointee at the Interior Department, and Jessica Bowron, the acting director of the National Park Service, to testify.

But the Justice Department escalated the standoff on Friday and filed a motion to disqualify Judge Reyes, citing her frustration at the hearing in order to question her impartiality and ask that she recuse herself from the case. She ordered both sides to file a response to the request by Sunday afternoon.

On Sunday, Judge Reyes also ordered Stanley Woodward Jr., the associate attorney general who filed the motion to disqualify her, to attend the hearing on Monday in which more senior Interior Department officials are scheduled to testify.

In the post on Sunday, Mr. Trump repeated an argument the government had made in court that clearing trees from the course was meant to return it to its original 1920s design, which featured open sight lines. But while the government indicated last week that the tree removal was proposed in a seven-year-old historic-restoration concept, Mr. Trump appeared to suggest that it was linked to the “Fazio Design” that he said would be built starting on Nov. 15.

Zach Montague is a Times reporter covering the federal courts, including the legal disputes over the Trump administration’s agenda.

Three Scenarios for a Leaderless World

The New York Times October 18, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Serge Schmemann

By Serge Schmemann

Mr. Schmemann, an Opinion writer, is a former Moscow, Bonn and Jerusalem bureau chief of The Times.

This essay concludes The New World Disorder, a series exploring the disintegration of the postwar international system and how countries are adjusting as America steps aside. Read more in the series below.

By now it is clear to most of America and much of the world that America and what it stands for have changed. The dominant face of that change is President Trump and his determined and deliberate efforts to accumulate greater powers than the Constitution apportioned to the president, to create a cult of personality based on grievance and vengeance and to challenge every aspect of the postwar global order, demeaning allies and courting autocrats.

Is that the future of America in the world? An increasingly autocratic, rude and unpredictable superpower guided by populism, rancor and whim? Or will Americans, once Mr. Trump is gone, try to restore the United States as the world’s repository of democratic values and human rights?

It is hard to imagine that even a MAGA-minded successor to Mr. Trump (say, Marco Rubio or JD Vance) would be as petulant, inconsistent and vindictive as this president has been. Yet too much has already shifted in the world — beyond anything Mr. Trump has done — to believe that the liberal, rules-based and values-driven order shaped by America and its allies after World War II can ever fully return to what it was.

New realities have come to the fore since the Berlin Wall came down almost four decades ago: the emergence of China as a greater economic and military rival to the United States than the Soviet Union ever was; the re-emergence of Russia as a menacing police state and its starting of a European war; the global retreat of liberal democracy, led by the premier democracy, the United States; fast-evolving technology undertaking tasks once reserved for the human brain. Globalization, once promising a borderless world and worldwide prosperity, has revealed its dark side: mass migration, inequality, cybercrime, polarization.

There is no reboot mechanism in history; there is no way back to the conveniently binary world of the last century any more than Mr. Trump can realize the illusions of Make America Great Again. The world is moving on.

What lies ahead? There is no way to know. But we must consider possible scenarios, if only to prepare as best we can. The exercise is especially critical for Americans, because any coherent action against global disarray will have to begin with the return of American democracy, as Charles A. Kupchan argues in his book “Bringing Order to Anarchy: Governing the World to Come.” Though Mark Carney, Canada’s prime minister, might have articulated a widespread longing at Davos in January when he urged middle powers to join forces and “create a third path,” the power, wealth and traditions of a renewed United States would be critical for any meaningful reversal of illiberal and autocratic trends.

The scenarios below, looking a dozen years or so into the future, are drawn from conversations with and the writings of people who professionally gaze into the crystal balls of politics and world affairs, as well as with people who are concerned with what we leave behind. They are meant not to be scientific or comprehensive but to reflect on this critical moment, because, as the great American sage Yogi Berra once said, “If you don’t know where you are going, you might wind up someplace else.”

This is our most hopeful scenario. A leader committed to the primacy of law, honest governance and liberal democracy across the globe is back in the White House, and the United States has begun to clamber back to its place as the “shining city on a hill.”

Europeans have taken on greater responsibility for their defense and are warily coming to accept the United States as a friend and ally again. Vladimir Putin has been ousted and the conflict with Ukraine frozen, allowing Ukraine to make a rapid economic recovery and eventually have its territory returned. China has surpassed the United States economically but not militarily, and the two superpowers work to avoid conflict and find a modus vivendi.

A reinvigorated and re-empowered United Nations, no longer undermined by Washington, is mobilizing once again to combat climate change and public health challenges and find ways to regulate artificial intelligence. The consensus formed among rich nations after World War II — that aid to poor countries builds stability, fosters growth and reduces suffering — is restored as America retreats from Mr. Trump’s “America first” use of foreign aid purely as a transactional lever.

Before exiting, Mr. Trump called off the war in Iran, declaring victory even though Tehran retains its mullahs and its nuclear fuel. But at least the Middle East is calm, and with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel voted out of power, the new administration in Washington gets to work on beginning another peace process between Israelis and Palestinians.

Its own house in order and its democratic allies behind it, the United States is able to begin guiding the world to a new order. The verities long taken for granted about the benefits of globalization, free trade, automation, digital technology and liberal democracy have given way to a far more fragmented world, with multiple centers of power competing over influence and status, but at the same time, as Mr. Kupchan writes, “more tethered together and interdependent than it was during the 20th century.” A new system of global governance begins to take shape, perhaps along the lines of what Mr. Kupchan envisions: a global concert of major nations to preserve peace and cooperation while acknowledging the ideological and cultural diversity of a complex world.

The recovery of America is central to this future. However great the degradation of American ideals in the MAGA era, the United States remains unique in its power, resources and embedded values and in its ability to overcome serious failings. It took fourscore and seven years and a cruel civil war before the proposition that all men are created equal was expanded to include Black people and an additional century to translate that into law. Women have had the vote for only a bit more than 100 years, and the struggle for equality is far from finished. Yet to borrow further from Abraham Lincoln, America has succeeded in “a new birth of freedom” again and again, and it can do it once more.

In this version of our collective future, the world carries on much as it is. A new U. S. administration ends Mr. Trump’s tariffs and tries to restore relations with allies and avoid conflicts, but a deep polarization continues to grip American politics, feeding constant tensions among the branches of government and destabilizing the executive.

America’s wealth and military power command fear and respect, but after all the back and forth of the Trump and Biden administrations, most of the world — including Europe and Canada — can no longer view the United States as either the democratic standard or a moral leader. American-led alliances and economic institutions weaken. Governments around the globe form shifting economic groupings and increasingly turn to China for trade and security.

As China surpasses the United States economically and draws closer militarily, Beijing forges ever closer economic ties to Europe and emerging economies and escalates pressure on Taiwan, though it avoids confrontations that could provoke American action. Several of the countries once relegated to the developing world — like India, Mexico, Brazil and Indonesia — approach first rank but without a shared vision for how the world should work together.

In the Middle East, Mr. Trump finally found an exit ramp in Iran before leaving office, restoring passage through the Strait of Hormuz, but the mullahs, with much of their enriched uranium, remain in power in Iran. Mr. Netanyahu is gone, but Gaza remains devastated, and new Israeli settlements in the West Bank continue to fan Palestinian resentment. Mr. Putin has been overthrown by a junta of siloviki — the military and security barons through whom he ruled — but the war with Ukraine remains a smoldering stalemate. Europe accepts greater responsibility for its own defense but struggles to find a unified approach to China, Russia or the problems of the world.

Global tasks like battling climate change continue in fits and starts, without major commitments or progress. The United Nations and its major agencies, like the World Health Organization and UNICEF, remain suspect to much of America and thereby limited in reach and financing. The world is largely at peace, but this can change at any moment as China rapidly gathers force.

Here, polarization and recriminations paralyze the United States. NATO and other American-led alliances lose meaning in a maelstrom of tariff wars and mutual rancor. Major international organizations — the United Nations, the World Trade Organization, the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund — founder as countries north and south seek security and trade in shifting alliances and trading blocs. Beijing succeeds in annexing Taiwan without international military resistance, but China’s growth stalls, leaving the world without a dominant center. Unregulated A. I. leads to a host of new crises — rogue incursions and raids, proliferation of misinformation, loss of countless jobs, dangerous advances in cyberwarfare.

An America distrusted by other nations and trapped in debilitating internal struggles leads to a deeply fragmented and unstable world, increasingly vulnerable to Chinese demands. Xenophobia and ancient grievances become the stuff of local politics and international relations, leading to flare-ups in the Caucasus, the Balkans, the Horn of Africa and other places where demagogues fan animosities.

Unchecked global warming creates chaos the world over, from seawater sloshing through the Bowery to flooding and drought in Africa and Asia, setting off vast new migrations and conflicts. A total breakdown of alliances and international organizations leaves the world vulnerable to the full range of historical scourges, from famine to war.

Russia, its oil and gas fields battered by Ukrainian drones, threatens a tactical nuclear strike against Ukraine. The United States and Iran remain at a yearslong stalemate, rendering passage through the Strait of Hormuz sporadic and dangerous, pushing the price of oil ever higher and adding, most grievously, to the woes of developing countries and the poor with rising energy, transportation and food costs. Saudi Arabia and other Middle Eastern powers lose faith in America. Terrorist attacks multiply in Israel and the occupied territories, the threat of war hanging over the region.

Even in this scenario, a major clash of great powers — the United States, China, Russia or even Europe — remains unlikely, given that such conflicts tend to be over historical wrongs, artificial crises or regional borders, but the threat of regional conflicts going out of control is ever present. The strongmen in power are not above using conflict to extend control over their subjects.

The world is a dark place, and America is no longer there to offer light.

There are, of course, innumerable other ways things could play out in coming years and decades. As our great American sage, again, reputedly said, “It’s tough to make predictions, especially about the future.”

The dangers are huge, but the future need not be dystopian. However the old liberal order is viewed, its achievements cannot be denied — or quickly undone. Even as autocracies spread, the yearning for freedom remains strong. Ukrainians have demonstrated an extraordinary determination to stay free; American judges still often stand up to Mr. Trump’s efforts to subvert the law; journalists the world over risk freedom and even death to report the truth; countries still rush to help others when catastrophe strikes, as they did when floods ravaged Nepal and Tibet in August.

Elections can reverse an extremist drift, as they did in Poland and Hungary, but they can also raise warning signals, as with the gains of the Alternative for Germany in Germany’s recent regional elections. The midterm contests in the United States next month will be scrutinized the world over, the presidential race in 2028 even more.

In the words of the hymn, the fate of humanity still turns on the decisions that people and nations take “in the strife of truth with falsehood.” They do not always make the wrong choice. The key is not to wait too long.

Serge Schmemann joined The Times in 1980 and worked as the bureau chief in Moscow, Bonn and Jerusalem and at the United Nations. He was editorial page editor of The International Herald Tribune in Paris from 2003 to 2013.

Connections: Sports Edition

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

Books

The works of the British art critic John Berger offer the antidote to our age of infinite scrolling.

Credit... Photo illustration by Mike McQuade

Supported by

By A. O. Scott

As a critic, which is to say someone whose job is to pay attention to things, and as a reader of criticism, which means someone who pays attention to the ways attention is paid, I’ve been fixated recently on the works of John Berger.

Berger, a British art critic, novelist and political polemicist who died in 2017, devoted much of his writing life to the theory and practice of looking — at paintings, at animals, at the natural world. This wasn’t merely an aesthetic preoccupation. “You can’t talk about aesthetics,” he wrote, “without talking about the principle of hope and the existence of evil.” Attention, for him, was a matter of life and death, or at least of their cultural equivalents, remembering and forgetting.

One of my favorite Berger essays, first published in 1973, is called “Between Two Colmars.” It recounts his experience of going to see a renaissance altarpiece near that Alsatian cathedral town in 1963, and again 10 years later.

I’ve never been to Colmar, and there’s no picture of the altarpiece, which was painted by the German master Matthias Grunewald, in the edition of “About Looking” that I’m consulting. I could search online, of course (something I couldn’t have done when the piece first appeared or when I first read it a decade or so later), to see what Berger was talking about. But I don’t think I’ve ever done that, because even though he describes the altarpiece in careful detail — “It was painted on hinged panels of wood. When these were shut, those before the altar saw the Crucifixion, flanked by St. Anthony and St. Sebastian. When the panels were opened, they saw a Concert of Angels and a Madonna and Child, flanked by an Annunciation and Resurrection” — what matters to me more is his experiences of looking at it.

An artifact of early-16th-century Europe — an era experienced by many, according to Berger, as “a time of damnation” — that depicts scenes of biblical history strikes Berger as brutal and despairing when he sees it first in 1963, and as hopeful and compassionate when he revisits it. Those impressions are the mirror images of his own state of mind at the beginning and end of a period that started in personal and political optimism and ended in disorientation and defeat. The hope of the early ’60s gave him the security to embrace gloom, while the desolation of the ’70s left him in need of solace. A single work of art answered to both needs. “In a period of revolutionary expectation,” Berger concludes, “I saw a work of art which had survived as evidence of the past’s despair; in a period which has to be endured, I see the same work miraculously offering a narrow pass across despair.”

I find that sentence moving enough that I may never need to see the altarpiece for myself. The idea that art can offer a measure of hope in bad times is a commonplace these days and can easily slide toward sentimentality and escapism. But for Berger art offers not a refuge so much as a way of living in history, of grasping the complexity of the past and the individual’s changing relationship to it. The altarpiece, anchored in the facts of its own epoch — wars of religion; rapid technological change; plague and paranoia — reaches across the centuries as a reminder of the kind of meaning only art can provide.

Similarly, “Between Two Colmars” can remind a 21st-century reader of the urgency and complexity of looking at art. Right now, we’re in the midst of an attention crisis, individually and collectively snared in an infinite scroll of disruption and distraction. Berger saw this crisis coming and foresaw its consequences. In 1978, writing about photography and its impact on the modern world, he argued that the dominance of images “creates an eternal present of immediate expectation: Memory ceases to be necessary or desirable. With the loss of memory, the continuities of meaning and judgment are also lost to us.” That diagnosis seems even truer today, as the functions of remembering, judging and interpreting are increasingly offloaded from human minds and communities into the ether of social media feeds and artificial intelligence. We’re in danger of forgetting how to look.

Berger’s centennial will arrive on Nov. 5. Almost 10 years after his death, his presence is still felt in pockets of the culture. His best-known book, “Ways of Seeing,” has been a staple of art-history classes and a fixture on the bookshelves of critically minded young people for more than half a century. New York Review Books has been steadily reissuing his fiction and criticism, including, earlier this fall, the 1980 collection “About Looking,” which includes the essay I just quoted. A new biography, by Tom Overton, has just been published, the second in a decade.

On the internet, in addition to finding his four-part BBC series “Ways of Seeing,” you can stream “The Seasons in Quincy,” a meditative documentary from 2015 in which Berger participates in a public conversation with Ben Lerner, peels apples with Tilda Swinton and offers motorcycle lessons to her daughter, Honor Swinton Byrne. Berger appears in the film as an elfin, grandfatherly figure with a mop of silver curls and piercing blue eyes — charismatic in a way that feels a little old-fashioned.

His persona on the page is not quite as playful but just as magnetic. Berger liked to think of himself as a storyteller. His fourth novel, “G.” — an earthy, experimental picaresque that often reads like “Tristram Shandy” by way of Thomas Pynchon — won the Booker Prize in 1972. He spent much of the 1970s and ’80s toiling on “Into Their Labors,” a sweeping trilogy of novels about the history and fate of European peasantry. Other books of his are hybrids — documentary, polemical, lyrical, personal — exploring history, ecology and political and economic injustice.

But it’s his essays about art and artists that matter most to me now. Reading them, you often feel you’re standing next to him in the museum or even looking through his eyes at a painting or a sculpture. You pay attention to his attention.

Berger trained as a painter before shifting to criticism. For him, attention was not a passive, individual state but rather an action. We don’t just see what’s in front of our eyes. We interpret it, looking for patterns and meanings and associations. How we do this depends on where we are, who we’re with and how we see ourselves.

This, in the abstract, was the argument of “Ways of Seeing,” both the book and the broadcast.

Berger’s mop of curls was brown in those days, his eyes no less alive. Speaking in an accent that is educated but not posh, with a tendency to melt his R’s into W’s, he zigzags through the history of art, focusing not on masterpieces and movements but on — the title sums it up.

In the excitable, democratic manner of a hip young professor (Berger never held a full-time academic post), he begins by pointing out how works of art change when they’re reproduced on postcards, merchandise and television screens. This wasn’t an entirely original observation. Berger acknowledged the influence of the essay “The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction,” by the prewar German-Jewish critic Walter Benjamin, which would become a staple of the cultural studies syllabus in subsequent decades, partly thanks to the influence of “Ways of Seeing.”

The second episode, which featured a panel of feminist critics and writers, did the same for the idea of the “male gaze.” (In Berger’s summary: “Men look at women. Women watch themselves being looked at.”) A later installment proposed a link between the popularity of oil painting in early modern Europe and the rise of capitalism. (“Oil paintings often depict things,” he says. “Things which in reality are buyable. To have a thing painted and put on a canvas is not unlike buying it and putting it in your house. If you buy a painting, you buy also the look of the thing it represents.”)

“Ways of Seeing” popularized an approach to art — and to culture more generally — that has since become ubiquitous. Rather than focusing on the achievement of individual artists or on the traditions that connect them, this approach insists on context: the social forces that shape artists and schools; the relationships among art, money and power; the ways that making and appreciating are mediated by history, ideology and institutions.

By now the frisson of new awareness that greeted the first viewers of “Ways of Seeing” has been experienced by several generations of readers. The notion that art is socially embedded is such a piece of conventional wisdom that it can be hard to imagine what the alternative view might have been. And there is a facile, debunking version of the argument, one that promises an easy kind of mastery, an ability to see through art instead of seeing it, a substitution of knowingness for aesthetic experience. Reams of criticism have been written exposing the complicity of countless artists and artworks with colonialism, capitalism, patriarchy and every other system of domination. Berger is never not aware of those connections — and does not hesitate to judge the political and moral failings of artists — but he always puts the experience of making and viewing the art first.

For him, the act of looking — the artist’s and the spectator’s — carries primal human impulses of curiosity, pleasure and awe. While art doesn’t exist in a vacuum, neither is it reducible to politics or commerce or anything else. An oil painting may be an object, a commodity in the marketplace, but it’s never only that. It is also the expression of the painter’s subjectivity, the work of hands that reach across time and geography to find receptive eyes. And to communicate a utopian possibility: “Art,” he wrote, “supposes that beauty is not an exception — is not in despite of — but is the basis for an order.”

Even as the world of commodities is ruled by equivalence, part of the allure of a painting lies in its uniqueness. A Caravaggio is not the same as a Courbet. You can’t swap Picasso for Francis Bacon. What that means is that art — even art that is anonymously made or consumed en masse — is personal. Somebody made it. Somebody sees it.

This idealism — often described, by him and others, as humanism — is what separates Berger from the postmodernist strain of critical thought that “Ways of Seeing” in other ways anticipates. It’s also what gives his art criticism moral force and political relevance.

Like many other British intellectuals of his background and generation, Berger, a child of the London middle class with some Jewish ancestry, gravitated leftward during and after World War II. He never joined the British Communist Party; his Marxism provided less a body of doctrine than a set of prompts and hunches. He was biased in favor of realism and suspicious of abstraction; he found traces of class struggle in every corner of the history of art; he mined the lives of painters for clues about the social implications of their work. When he won the Booker Prize in 1972, he made headlines (and enemies) by donating half the prize money to the British Black Panthers — to draw attention to the prize funders’ role in colonialism and the slave trade.

But in the second half of his career, Berger’s leftist principles — his hatred of inequality, his reverence for labor, his conviction that a more human alternative to capitalism was possible — were increasingly filtered through a sensibility tinted with conservatism. He grew skeptical of modernity and acutely aware of the costs of technological progress, which brings in its wake dispossession, alienation and amnesia along with efficiency, speed and convenience. While he would remain engaged in a familiar array of leftist causes until the end of his life, his center of gravity shifted radically in the ’70s and ’80s because of his intensifying connection to rural life.

While working on a documentary project about migrant laborers with the Swiss photographer Jean Mohr, Berger discovered that most of the people he interviewed had been small farmers or agricultural workers uprooted from land where their families lived for generations. He realized that he had no way to understand that background, even though it was shared by (in his estimate) hundreds of millions of people around the world.

He had spent time in the French countryside before, but in the mid-’70s, he relocated permanently to Haute-Savoie in the French Alps, settling in Quincy, a remote hamlet, and making his life among the peasants there.

Plenty of writers move to the country, seeking refuge or respite from the swirl of metropolitan literary life. Berger’s rustication was a more serious and sustained project. After moving to Quincy, he would devote much of his creative and critical energy to witnessing and trying to explain to himself and his readers the contours of a mode of existence in the process of vanishing, and to understanding why that vanishing mattered. He came to believe that an essential piece of human experience was disappearing from memory.

Go back far enough in your family tree, and you are likely to find people who can be classified as peasants. Small-scale farming, supplemented by cottage industry, handicraft, hunting and foraging, has organized much of human life for most of our history as a species. From his neighbors in Quincy, Berger extrapolated the intellectual, aesthetic and spiritual dimensions of the peasant world — its distinctive understanding of a person’s relationships with animals, family, nature and the dead.

To the extent that Berger’s point of view is contradictory, a perspective that ties the desire for a better future with a stubborn attachment to the past, it’s summed up in the figure of the peasant, a human type that is both ubiquitous and nearly invisible for much of human recorded history. “Very few peasants become artists,” he noted. “This is not a question of talent, but of opportunity and free time.” As a result, “the peasant’s soul is as unfamiliar or unknown to most urban people as is his physical endurance and the material conditions of his labor.”

In the European literature and art Berger knew best, people who work the land, if they are present at all, tend to be subjected to mockery, pity or sentimental idealization, all of which are forms of condescension. This isn’t just a matter of metropolitan prejudice or bourgeois elitism. The 19th-century French realist Jean-François Millet was for Berger a “unique” artist: “No other European painter had treated rural labor as the central theme of his art.” But he was nonetheless a failure “because the language of traditional oil painting could not accommodate the subject he brought with him.” That is because landscape painting and rural portraiture are based on observational detachment. In this tradition, Millet found “no formula for representing the close, harsh, patient physicality of a peasant’s labor on, instead of in front of, the land.”

Berger’s own essays, which approach the question of peasant experience more abstractly and obliquely, may come closer to capturing its importance. Exploring the question “Why look at animals?” (in an essay of the same title collected in “About Looking”), Berger zeros in on an essential aspect of the human connection to other species by observing that “a peasant becomes fond of his pig and is glad to salt away its pork. What is significant, and is so difficult for the urban stranger to understand, is that the two statements in that sentence are connected by an and and not by a but.”

Berger had a romantic streak, but he didn’t sentimentalize life on the land or paint a nostalgic picture of an existence defined by grueling labor, frequent hardship and particular vulnerability to natural and economic disaster. The question he asked — of the migrants and displaced rural people he encountered in Europe, Africa and the Middle East and of modern civilization as a whole — was: What happens when that continuity is disrupted, when that sense of place, of home, of animals as a source of companionship and labor and food, is lost?

The answer goes back to his criticism. The peasant’s survival depends on attention: to the weather; to customs and traditions; to a host of practical considerations that are also aesthetic and ethical choices. How do you plant a field? Build a chair? Raise a child? Mourn the dead?

The knowledge that provides answers to those questions is acquired by paying attention, in a way that is not qualitatively different from what a painter brings to a landscape or a critic to a painting.

That is what we are at risk of losing. Or what, Berger might say, is being stolen from us, not least by the technologies that offer us endless novelty and seem to fulfill desires we never even knew we had. The loss is a foreclosure of memory, of the knowledge that we exist in history. It’s not abstract: The rage that defines so much modern politics, in the developed world and the global South, on the right as well as the left, can be understood as a reaction to the feeling that something we once had is gone. Grief manifests itself as grievance.

Art — and art criticism, for that matter — suggest a fragile, conditional alternative. As Berger put it: “We live in a world of suffering in which evil is rampant, a world whose events do not confirm our Being, a world that has to be resisted. It is in this situation that the aesthetic moment offers hope.”

A. O. Scott is a critic at large for The New York Times Book Review, writing about literature and ideas.

Source photographs for illustration: Leonardo Cendamo/Getty Images

This French City Was Rarely Linked With Unrest. Then Arsonists Attacked.

The New York Times October 18, 2026

Student Protests in France

Advertisement

Supported by

As unrest surged across France this weekend, the most surprising attack came in the quiet city of Limoges, where rioters set fire to the city hall.

By Giulia Imbert

Reporting from Limoges, France

Gathered in the heart of Limoges, a small city in central France, more than a hundred people gazed in shock on Sunday afternoon at what remained of their city hall.

Some stood in silence. Others took pictures of the building’s skeletal frame, still smoking from a fire that had largely destroyed it the night before.

Apart from the building’s gray stone walls, erected in the late 19th century, and a few broken windows, not much remained. Not the roof, not the clock on the facade, not even the metal bell tower that once loomed over the building.

“All we have left are pictures,” said Gilles Peignelin, 64, who was staring at the ruin alongside his wife, Sylvie, 61. They married in the building 35 years ago, they said, recalling its grand staircase and painting collection. Now, that staircase seemed to have collapsed, Mr. Peignelin noted, pointing through a shattered window.

“I’m outraged — it’s shameful, deplorable,” Ms. Peignelin added.

The damage at Limoges was among the most serious and surprising stemming from the nationwide unrest that swept across France yesterday, as huge anti-government marches gave way to rioting.

Some 2,000 people were arrested nationwide as rioters attacked government buildings and roughly 1,500 shops.

Limoges, a quiet city renowned for its porcelain and far from the unrest of Paris, is the only place that saw its city hall burn down, though a tourist office was also set on fire in Lyon.

The rallies in the city, which has roughly 130,000 residents, began relatively calmly, the authorities said. Several thousands demonstrators marched through the streets in the late morning to protest rising living costs and express solidarity with high school students calling for better school conditions.

The authorities said that rioters headed toward the city center at 5 p. m. with the “sole objective to burn, break and loot.” By 6 p. m., rioters forced their way into the city hall and set it on fire while staff and visitors were still inside, the authorities said. Despite firefighters’ swift response, the building was largely destroyed — with its burning bell tower toppling over several hours later.

“Today, the entire facade and the historic front section have been almost 100 percent destroyed,” Maurice Barate, the top official for the region, announced on national television. Mr. Barate said that firefighters had been disadvantaged by the wind, and that the city hall’s wooden roof had “collapsed onto the rest of the building.”

Listed as a historical monument, Limoges’s city hall was built by a Parisian architect, Charles-Alfred Leclerc, in the 1880s. A jewel of late-19th-century French architecture, the building featured a metal bell tower, ornate details on its facade and mosaic portraits of local figures. At the start of World War II, the monument hosted exiled Belgian lawmakers after Belgium surrendered to Nazi Germany.

Many saw the burning of the hall as a direct assault on the French state.

To attack the city hall is “to attack the Republic,” said Guillaume Guérin, the Limoges mayor, on social media on Sunday morning. Mr. Guérin, of the main conservative party, the Republicans, also accused the perpetrators of being affiliated with or manipulated by the far left and promised to hold them accountable.

The local prosecutor’s office has announced that 17 people were arrested in the city this weekend, including seven minors, though it did not clarify if they were accused of involvement in the arson.

Lino Cardona, an art student who joined the peaceful protests earlier in the day, said the atmosphere at the demonstrations turned sour as soon as the city hall attack began.

“That’s when the joyful, inclusive atmosphere disappeared,” said Ms. Cardona, 26, who lamented how the violence would now overshadow the goals of the peaceful protesters.

The attack was a powerful symbol of “the fragility of our institutions,” she added. “We now need to ask ourselves: How do we move forward?”

The Peignelins said they were shocked at how such violence could reach a city usually untouched by unrest — and they were angry at the government’s failure to prevent it.

“We didn’t expect this in Limoges, but today we realize that even a small town in France can be a hotbed of chaos,” Mr. Peignelin said.

Ms. Peignelin added: “I’m sickened by a government that does nothing. We know full well that the people who did this won’t be brought to justice.”

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu and other government leaders have pledged consequences for perpetrators across France, including by making them pay for the damage. In a message to Mr. Guérin, the mayor, that was reviewed by The New York Times, Mr. Lecornu said the state would help cover costs from the blaze and pledged to visit the city this week.

Mr. Guérin complained that the national government had done too little to prevent the fire, saying that local law enforcement “had simply run out of ammunition” by 3:30 p. m. on Saturday.

“This country is in bad shape,” Mr. Guérin said, adding, “If there isn’t a change in policy, if there isn’t a shift in direction, things are going to end very, very badly.”

How a Dominican Migrant in New York Became an ICE Target

The New York Times October 18, 2026

ICE Shooting in New York

Oscar Belgal arrived in the city from the Dominican Republic in 2022. Chaos appeared to follow, ending in a fateful encounter with immigration agents.

Oscar Belgal arrived in the city from the Dominican Republic in 2022. Chaos appeared to follow, ending in a fateful encounter with immigration agents.

Immigration agents descended upon Oscar Belgal, a Dominican immigrant, along a strip of small stores in New York as people made their way home from work or accompanied their children after school. Credit... Karsten Moran for The New York Times

Supported by

By Luis Ferré-SadurníAna LeyMaria Cramer and Hamed Aleaziz

The reporters interviewed more than a dozen people, in New York and the Dominican Republic, and reviewed internal federal records and hundreds of pages of court documents.

The young man from the Dominican Republic slipped into the United States through the southern border about four years ago, acquaintances said, evading U. S. immigration authorities.

He was in his mid-20s and headed to New York, but his attempts to fly under the radar — and to find his footing in a new country — quickly spiraled.

He got a job at a carwash, and then selling carpets, but couldn’t hold down either job. He rented a bedroom in Upper Manhattan, but was taken to court after failing to pay thousands of dollars in rent.

About a year after arriving, the man, Oscar Belgal, was arrested after being accused of stealing cash and jewelry from two acquaintances, with help from an associate who had a gun. Two years later, he was arrested again, this time charged with drug dealing, after he sold bags of cocaine to an undercover police officer outside his apartment building, according to prosecutors.

By 2026, his past had caught up to him: The Trump administration was going after undocumented immigrants, and he was on its radar.

Mr. Belgal’s collision course with Immigration and Customs Enforcement came to a violent climax on Oct. 8, bringing a sudden hail of gunfire to a residential pocket of the city that straddles Manhattan and the Bronx.

It was a sunny autumn afternoon, and Mr. Belgal had just picked up his 5-year-old son from school and taken him to McDonald’s. While they were parked, with the boy in the back seat, a team of ICE officers in plain clothes surprised them.

Two officers in hats and sweatshirts, one with his gun drawn, rushed at the car and Mr. Belgal accelerated his vehicle. At least one officer fired multiple rounds, striking Mr. Belgal on the left side of the neck as he crashed into a concrete traffic barrier. His son was not injured.

Mr. Belgal, 28, was taken to a hospital and later transported to a federal prison in Brooklyn, where he was being held in solitary confinement, a bullet still lodged in his neck, his lawyers say.

Key elements of the encounter — most critically, whether the officer’s use of deadly force was legally justified — remain fiercely contested. In court filings, Mr. Belgal’s lawyers said that the officers never identified themselves — which ICE denied — and said that “Oscar was terrified for his and his son’s lives.”

While the New York Police Department released footage that shows the lead up to and aftermath of the shooting, ICE has not released body camera footage from its officers that could show the shooting itself. Local and federal officials said they are investigating the incident.

Since the start of President Trump’s immigration crackdown, shootings by ICE officers — of immigrants and of demonstrators — in Minneapolis and Maine, Chicago and Los Angeles have ignited furious protests.

Now, that tumult has arrived in New York.

For ICE, the encounter cast a spotlight anew on its tactics and provoked criticism from city and state leaders, including Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who renewed calls to abolish the agency.

For Mr. Belgal, a father of two whom ICE said had entered the country illegally, the shooting marked the culmination of a brief but turbulent time in New York. Some who knew him — particularly those who felt harmed by his actions — were outraged by the shooting but said that a string of bad decisions had paved a direct path to his arrest and potential deportation.

The New York Times interviewed more than a dozen people who knew Mr. Belgal, obtained internal federal records of his apprehension by ICE and reviewed hundreds of pages of court records.

From the moment Mr. Belgal arrived in New York, his life was fraught with turmoil.

Mr. Belgal hailed from a poor urban neighborhood in Santo Domingo, the capital of the Dominican Republic.

In an interview there last week, his grandmother, Juana de León, said she had raised Mr. Belgal, as well as other grandchildren, because his mother was absent.

Mr. Belgal, a slim man with long dark hair he often braided, bounced between low-wage day jobs in construction and moved out of the house after meeting a woman and having a son with her, Ms. de León said.

“He got by through odd jobs,” Ms. de León said outside her home on Thursday, as she sold shoes and clothes that had been shipped from the United States. “One day he would go work with one bricklayer, the next with another.”

Like other migrants, Mr. Belgal left the Dominican Republic alone in search of better economic prospects and made it to Colombia by October 2022, according to Carlos Martínez, a Dominican man he befriended there.

Together, they made the same journey that thousands of migrants undertook on foot during the Biden administration, cutting through the treacherous Darién Gap in Panama until reaching Mexico.

“We slept together, we ate together, we did everything together,” Mr. Martínez, 25, said in an interview.

They split up before crossing the border, though they would reunite in New York.

Mr. Belgal told acquaintances that he crossed the U. S.-Mexico border in late 2022 without being apprehended. He soon found refuge in Washington Heights, the Upper Manhattan neighborhood bustling with immigrants from the Dominican Republic.

A pair of Dominican sisters whose relatives knew Mr. Belgal said they extended him a hand when he arrived in November 2022, apparently penniless.

Cruz María Reyes, 49, one of the sisters, said that they let him stay in a spare bedroom for free over nine months. They helped him find a gig washing cars, which he abandoned once it got colder, she said, and later selling carpets at a store in downtown Manhattan.

By late 2023, Ms. Reyes, who lived in the three-bedroom apartment with Mr. Belgal, said she began charging him $250 a week for the room.

A few months later, in December 2023, Ms. Reyes heard loud knocks at the door.

It was two police officers looking for Mr. Belgal. They handcuffed him and took him away.

Police officers arrested him because two months before, according to prosecutors, Mr. Belgal and another man had robbed two people Mr. Belgal knew: Mr. Martínez and his wife, Yesica Torres.

The couple told the officers that they had gone clubbing in the Bronx on Oct. 2, 2023, with Mr. Belgal and the other man, whom they did not know, according to court filings.

While they were all sitting inside a car, Mr. Belgal’s accomplice pointed a gun from the driver’s seat at the couple, who were seated in the back, and demanded they hand over their jewelry, prosecutors said. Mr. Belgal, seated in the passenger’s seat, took their chains and rings, and about $1,100 in cash, before kicking them out of the car, according to prosecutors.

Mr. Belgal faced 18 criminal charges, but his lawyer, who argued at the time that Mr. Belgal was in the car but not involved in the robbery, negotiated a deal with prosecutors. Mr. Belgal pleaded guilty to just one charge: grand larceny in the fourth degree, a nonviolent felony.

He received five years of probation.

Mr. Martínez and Ms. Torres, who said they were scarred by Mr. Belgal’s betrayal, said they fled to the Dominican Republic after his arrest because they felt intimidated by him.

“We put him in jail, and he stayed in touch with us,” Ms. Torres, 35, said in a phone interview last week from the Dominican Republic, describing how Mr. Belgal had accused them of “snitching” on him. “He threatened us.”

The Times was unable to interview Mr. Belgal.

In a statement, the Legal Aid Society, which is representing Mr. Belgal, denied that he had “threatened or intimidated witnesses.”

Mr. Belgal continued to share the apartment with Ms. Reyes after his first arrest.

Soon, his partner and their son, a toddler at the time, arrived from the Dominican Republic and moved in, Ms. Reyes said.

Mr. Belgal later left his job selling carpets and the couple stopped paying rent at the end of 2024, said Ms. Reyes, who took them to housing court.

Around that time, Mr. Belgal also appeared to have turned to drug dealing, according to Manhattan prosecutors.

From January to June 2025, Mr. Belgal sold plastic bags of cocaine to an undercover officer during multiple exchanges near his building on Wadsworth Avenue, and on at least one occasion, a bag that also had fentanyl and heroin, prosecutors said in a criminal complaint.

Mr. Belgal was arrested in August 2025 and charged with 10 counts of criminal sale of a controlled substance. He pleaded not guilty to all counts; the case has not been resolved.

Some of Mr. Belgal’s neighbors said the arrests didn’t define him, adding that he was generally a kind person who helped older residents with their groceries and even took them to their doctor’s appointments.

“You knew he was often out of a job,” said Aldenia Casanova, 53, who said that Mr. Belgal replaced the locks on her door in his free time. “But he was very well-behaved and mild-mannered.”

When Mr. Belgal was released from custody after his second arrest, he never returned to the apartment. His partner and their son also moved out after a judge ordered them to vacate the premises because of the lapsed rent payments, records show.

Ms. Reyes said that she is owed seven months of rent, or about $7,000.

She criticized ICE’s conduct in the shooting, but said that Mr. Belgal’s run-ins with the law had ultimately exposed him.

“I’m not out for revenge,” Ms. Reyes said. “But he’s paying for the consequences of his actions.”

In a statement, the Legal Aid Society said that Mr. Belgal’s “past does not diminish his humanity, lessen the gravity of what happened to him or erase the profound trauma his child has experienced.”

ICE first tried to arrest Mr. Belgal last month.

When officers found him in the Bronx on Sept. 18, he ran into a nearby building and got away before he could be arrested, according to internal federal records.

Federal agents tried again 20 days later.

They fanned out in plain clothes and unmarked vehicles on Oct. 8 in the Marble Hill neighborhood, where Mr. Belgal had moved.

They spotted him at about 4 p. m. inside a gray Honda, parked in front of a fire hydrant on West 225th Street, his blinkers still on.

Moments later, surveillance footage shows, two officers run up to the driver’s side of his car, one with his gun pointed at Mr. Belgal, who puts his car in reverse and backs up a few feet.

Then, he accelerates, steering away from the officers, as one smashes the side window of the car and the other points his gun at the windshield, the video shows.

At least one officer fired multiple shots at Mr. Belgal’s vehicle, according to local and federal officials.

After the crash, Mr. Belgal emerged from his car, its back window shattered and its windshield pierced. His son, unharmed in the back seat, was crying. Mr. Belgal held his neck, and shouted in Spanish.

“He yelled, ‘Help me!’” Viely Herrera, 21, a bystander, said. “‘Help me! I’m dying!’”

ICE officers forced Mr. Belgal onto the pavement and handcuffed him, according to witnesses.

Minutes later, New York police officers carried Mr. Belgal into an S. U. V., and drove him to a hospital.

ICE officials argued that Mr. Belgal had refused orders to exit his vehicle and accused him of “weaponizing” his car.

The agency said that Mr. Belgal smashed his car into two ICE vehicles and tried to run over an officer, an account that has not been corroborated by the publicly available footage.

Federal officials said that they would release ICE body camera footage upon concluding their investigation. The Bronx district attorney, Darcel Clark, said her office was investigating the shooting, which she described as “a matter of grave concern.”

Arianna Montero, the mother of Mr. Belgal’s son, said in a brief interview that her son had been “traumatized,” speaking little and having nightmares.

“Why fire so much at a single person, and a child?” she said.

Federal officials said that the officers did not know the boy was in the car.

Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, said that officials believed Mr. Belgal had “indirect or direct knowledge” about a shooting that injured an off-duty customs officer in Manhattan in July 2025, but Mr. Mullin did not elaborate.

ICE officials said that Mr. Belgal had ties to a gang known as the Trinitarios, but offered no evidence. His lawyers said in filings that Mr. Belgal — whom they said most recently worked in construction — “vehemently” denied any gang affiliations.

In a statement, the Department of Homeland Security blamed New York’s so-called sanctuary laws, which they said prevented the city from transferring Mr. Belgal to ICE when he had been previously arrested.

“Make no mistake: ICE is not going anywhere, and we will continue to target the worst of the worst in sanctuary cities who refuse to jail criminal illegal aliens,” the agency said.

Mr. Belgal’s lawyers argued that his arrest was illegal because the officers arrested him without a valid warrant and without having started deportation proceedings against him.

His lawyers said he was semiconscious when he arrived at NewYork-Presbyterian Allen Hospital the night of the shooting. Inside, doctors stopped his bleeding and, when he awoke, ICE officers handcuffed him to his bed, his lawyers said.

Mr. Belgal spent about five hours in the hospital and was discharged after doctors found that he was medically stable, the federal records say.

ICE officers moved him the next day to the Metropolitan Detention Center, a federal prison in Brooklyn.

His lawyers, who are suing for his release, said that he was being held without proper medical care while awaiting surgery that doctors had told him he needed to remove the bullet, adding that “the left side of his face is numb, and he can barely hear out of his left ear.”

Anusha Bayya, Hurubie Meko, Oishika Neogi, Wesley Parnell, Nate Schweber and Ed Shanahan contributed reporting from New York. Hogla Enecia Pérez contributed reporting from the Dominican Republic. Susan C. Beachy contributed research.

Luis Ferré-Sadurní is an immigration reporter for The New York Times.

Ana Ley is a Times reporter covering immigration in New York City.

Maria Cramer is a Times reporter covering the New York Police Department and crime in the city and surrounding areas.

Hamed Aleaziz covers the Department of Homeland Security and immigration policy for The Times.

Huge Riots and Anti-Government Protests in France: What to Know

The New York Times October 18, 2026

Student Protests in France

Advertisement

Supported by

Rioters attacked city halls and shops over the weekend amid protests over living costs and poor school conditions.

By Amelia NierenbergLynsey Chutel and Catherine Porter

Catherine Porter, who reported from Paris, has covered the protests for weeks.

France is reeling from its largest unrest in years, after anti-government demonstrations devolved into riots and looting that caused nationwide damage and deepened a sense of national reckoning.

As the chaos subsided on Sunday, political leaders blamed each other for the unrest and citizens looked on with shock at their cities, littered with broken glass and the charred skeletons of burned cars.

The violence marked a convergence between a weeks-old student movement for better school conditions, an emerging national movement to protest high living costs, and opportunistic rioters who used the demonstrations as a cover for looting.

The protests have heightened a sense of fiscal and social crisis in France, the European Union’s second-largest economy. The government is trying to pass an unpopular belt-tightening budget while facing public anger that has helped position Marine Le Pen, a far-right leader, as the favorite to win the presidency in an election next spring.

More than half a million people joined some 110 marches throughout France on Saturday, the interior ministry said, in the biggest day of protest since the demonstrations began about a month ago. A major union, the C. G. T., gave a higher estimate, saying 800,000 protesters had turned out.

Amid many peaceful demonstrations, rioters vandalized roughly 1,500 shops and many symbols of the French state, leading to roughly 2,000 arrests. An arson attack largely destroyed the town hall in Limoges, in central France. In Marseille, the second-largest city, masked people broke into a government building and tipped over a bust of Marianne, a symbol of the Republic.

High school students started protesting last month to express frustration with the condition of their schools.

They have pointed to crumbling infrastructure, overcrowded classrooms, overloaded schedules, a shortage of teachers and staff, and underfunding in schools. Many are also calling for an overhaul of state-run admissions platforms for higher education and universities that they call unfairly selective.

Students have blockaded hundreds of schools. They have set fire to, or damaged, at least 24 of them, according to the government. Thousands have been arrested since September and over 1,000 police officers, students and school staff have been hurt.

The students’ anger has been exacerbated by the police’s forceful response. Prosecutors and a police watchdog are investigating at least 34 cases involving accusations of police misconduct during the protests.

The cases include a 15-year-old boy whose left hand was ripped off, officials said, likely by the explosion of a police stun grenade; and a 14-year-old boy maimed by a tear-gas grenade that an officer had fired at close range.

Throughout October, labor unions and other campaign groups have increasingly joined the students’ demonstrations. They have held bigger rallies to express solidarity with the students as well as to protest a broader range of issues.

Some are angry over the cost of living and rising fuel prices that have surged, in part, because of the Iran war. Farmers have joined in, angry at agricultural costs.

Social media accounts associated with the “yellow vest” protest movement, which beset France nearly a decade ago with roadside demonstrations against high gas prices and other issues, have joined calls for demonstrations.

And left-wing parties have also seized on the protests as part of a wider expression of discontent at President Emmanuel Macron, who is limited to two terms and is nearing the end of his time in office.

Such discontent has a long history in France, where student-led protests in 1968 nearly toppled the government and helped transform French society.

On Sunday, far-right leaders and the centrist government blamed the far left for the chaos. They pointed in particular to a major far-left party, France Unbowed, that they said provoked the unrest.

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has accused party leaders of sowing distrust about the police among student protesters, and said some rioters were members of the “ultra-left.”

France Unbowed has rejected that accusation and its leader, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, has instead blamed the government for actions that he said made the unrest more likely.

Mr. Mélenchon said on social media that Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu was “responsible for the chaos, because of “incompetence or a worst-case strategy to create a party of order that would make people forget his failure in public finances.” Mr. Lecornu did not respond to that accusation.

Giulia Imbert, Ségolène Le Stradic and Zane Irwin contributed reporting.

Amelia Nierenberg is a Times reporter covering international news from London.

Lynsey Chutel is a Times reporter based in London who covers breaking news in Africa, the Middle East and Europe.

Catherine Porter is an international reporter for The Times, covering France. She is based in Paris.
