O. J. Simpson, a Secret Informant and a Decades-Old Mystery

The New York Times October 18, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Times Exclusive

An “extremely reliable” informant told authorities about the missing murder weapon, according to newly unsealed records. The informant’s brother told The Times his sibling was at the crime scene.

By Mike Baker and Tim Arango

The reporters knocked on the doors of former mobsters in California, combed through a dusty storage unit in Florida and persuaded a federal judge to unseal 30-year-old records in New York.

O. J. Simpson entered a Miami hotel suite in June 2006 and sank into a chair. His eyes scanned the room, as if looking for a way out. His fingers rapped on the armrest.

The former N. F. L. superstar, television pitchman, movie star and onetime murder suspect had agreed to this meeting with his ghostwriter. Mr. Simpson planned to publish a confession — or at least a “hypothetical” confession — to the murder of his ex-wife and her friend. But he seemed to be having second thoughts.

He leaned in and scooped up a handful of nuts. He reached for a water bottle. The ghostwriter turned on his audio recorder, signaling the start of a conversation.

Mr. Simpson paused for a moment, the room draped in silence.

“You know I couldn’t have done this alone,” he began.

In the story Mr. Simpson told that day, later published in the book “If I Did It,” he described a version of the 1994 murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman in which Mr. Simpson had help from a friend who got rid of the murder weapon and Mr. Simpson’s bloody clothes.

Prosecutors who had failed to convict Mr. Simpson of murder have given little credence to the notion of an accomplice. The police, too. Many people considered the details of Mr. Simpson’s hypothetical confession a fantasy, part of a desperate effort to cash in on his waning fame and notoriety amid growing money struggles and scrapes with the law.

But today, more than 30 years after the “trial of the century,” newly uncovered evidence suggests that Mr. Simpson’s account should not have been so readily dismissed.

A New York Times examination, based on recently unsealed court files, interviews and other evidence, details long-hidden information about the missing murder weapon, Mr. Simpson’s supposed efforts to cover up the crime, as well as the possibility of an accomplice. Together, the findings challenge the popular narrative around a case that has been dissected in countless books, podcasts and documentaries, and they stir doubts about law enforcement’s decision not to do more to pursue a promising lead.

A decades-old document filed in an unrelated, obscure criminal case in New York — recently unsealed at the request of The Times — outlines the account of a prized informant who came forward with tantalizing information while Mr. Simpson’s 1995 murder trial was proceeding.

The informant — a man considered “extremely reliable” by a veteran federal prosecutor and praised heartily by a longtime federal judge — was an associate of Mr. Simpson and a close friend of Mr. Simpson’s confidant, Al Cowlings. As part of his sweeping cooperation deal with law enforcement, the informant shared information about the supposed location of the murder weapon and the efforts to dispose of it. The document outlines the broad nature of what the informant offered prosecutors, but does not specify what he said, or to what degree he implicated himself or others.

His account was forwarded to Los Angeles prosecutors late in Mr. Simpson’s murder trial — so late that prosecutors had already presented their version of events to the jury and rested their case, but had yet to offer closing arguments. The documents in the New York case were ordered 30 years ago to be kept secret. They have remained so, until now.

The informant’s role in the case may go even deeper. Earlier this year, the informant’s brother told The Times that the siblings were in Los Angeles on the night of the murders. And he saw the informant with his hands apparently covered in blood after going out to help Mr. Simpson.

None of the new evidence uncovered by The Times definitively untangles the mystery. No one has come forward with new forensic evidence. Even the informant’s brother has since sought to disavow the explosive statements he made to The Times. Taken together, the material points in different directions but veers significantly from the official account that has been proffered by the police and prosecutors.

The double murder prosecution of Mr. Simpson, who was acquitted by a jury, remains one of the most scrutinized cases in popular culture, spawning endless theories. With many of the key players now dead, it’s possible the full truth will never be known.

Still, the notion that an accomplice participated in the murders has drawn the notice of Los Angeles Police cold case investigators, who as recently as last winter were quietly making calls about potential leads.

“The O. J. Simpson case remains an open and ongoing investigation,” a spokesman for the L. A. P. D. said. Because there was no conviction in the murders, “the department has an obligation to continue to pursue justice in this matter.” The spokesman added, “at a point that new evidence is found, detectives will follow those investigatory leads.”

As part of a re-examination of the Simpson case, The Times has unearthed tales of secret audiotapes, mafia links, a prison escape, and backchannel communications between state and federal prosecutors. The reporting also came across a dramatic account from the rapper Fat Joe that bolsters the informant’s supposed role in the case.

Much of the new information centers on the informant, a dead drug runner named Joseph Ippolito, known as Joey. He was a mafia associate, a serial felon, a prison escapee — and a friend of Mr. Simpson. The story of the New Jersey native’s high-flying life and his link to the Simpson case, were they not buttressed by police reports, court files and interviews, might seem too fantastical to be true.

Mr. Ippolito was raised in the mob underworld of New Jersey, where his father was part of the DeCavalcante crime family. As a young man, he went on to receive acclaim in Florida as a professional cigarette boat racer. He built a network of high-profile and well-heeled friends, such as the actor James Caan, and he built a reputation as a guy who embraced danger and took risks. Those risks included running drugs up the East Coast.

He was eventually caught in 1981, in a drug bust so large that it appeared on the front page of The Times. He served three years in prison for helping traffic 20 tons of marijuana from Colombia to Long Island.

In the late 1980s, fresh from prison, Mr. Ippolito moved to Los Angeles to start a new life.

He began managing an Italian restaurant, PCH Bar & Grill, which occupied a prime location near the Santa Monica beachfront. It offered sunset views across the Pacific Coast Highway, luring some of the city’s rich and famous. Among the people he hung out with: Al Cowlings, a former football star turned fledgling Hollywood actor.

Mr. Cowlings was also best friends with Mr. Simpson — they had been teammates in high school, college and the N. F. L.

Mr. Cowlings and Mr. Ippolito became fast friends. They went on hikes and took walks along the beach. They were so close, Mr. Cowlings later credited Mr. Ippolito for helping him kick his cocaine habit.

“My situation was getting so dismal that I know that if it were not for Joe, I probably would have died,” Mr. Cowlings wrote in a letter to a judge, while requesting leniency for Mr. Ippolito.

But while he helped Mr. Cowlings avoid cocaine, Mr. Ippolito was funneling it to others. Authorities found that Mr. Ippolito was trading on his proximity to Hollywood’s power brokers to move drugs. A major federal sting, involving secret recordings and an undercover mob informant, led to his arrest in Los Angeles in 1992. A jury found him guilty the following year.

Family and friends rushed to support Mr. Ippolito, lobbying the judge and attesting to his character. One friend, Julie Mijares, offered to house Mr. Ippolito in Los Angeles if he were released on bail. “I love Joe like a brother,” wrote Ms. Mijares, who met him more than a decade earlier in Florida.

A stylist to stars such as the pop group TLC, Ms. Mijares managed two retail shops of the Hollywood boutique Fred Segal in the 1990s. She was a regular at Mr. Ippolito’s restaurant.

Mr. Ippolito’s brother Sam, one of nine siblings in the Ippolito family, told the court that his brother had kept the family together after their father died, and served as the family’s figurehead.

“Joseph has worked hard his whole life, not for himself but for his family, and would not do anything to hurt them,” Sam wrote.

Mr. Ippolito was sentenced to 10 years in prison and sent to a minimum-security facility in Florida.

But prison couldn’t slow him.

In May 1994, eight months after his sentencing, he escaped by leaving a work duty before the 4 p. m. count. He stepped into a car he had called and got a ride to Panama City, Fla. His lawyer would later say in court it was the only known prison escape by way of private limousine.

His brother Sam said in an interview this year that he picked up Mr. Ippolito in Florida, began driving westward and eventually reached Los Angeles. He said they stayed at an apartment that belonged to Ms. Mijares, the stylist friend who had previously offered Joey refuge amid his legal troubles.

Records show that she once had an address in West Hollywood, in a four-story complex on Doheny Drive just off Sunset Boulevard.

Then one night — June 12, 1994 — Sam Ippolito recalled that his brother left the apartment. He said he needed to help a friend.

The authorities contended that, on that night, Mr. Simpson drove to his ex-wife’s condo. The former couple, who shared two children, had a volatile relationship, and he had a history of domestic violence.

Prosecutors said he stabbed her to death outside the home, and fatally slashed Mr. Goldman nearby.

At the crime scene, investigators found Mr. Simpson’s blood, along with footprints that matched both the style and size of his rare Bruno Magli shoes. They also found a single leather glove that matched the type Ms. Brown Simpson had once purchased for Mr. Simpson. Investigators also recovered a cap that contained hair consistent with Mr. Simpson’s hairs, and another hair on Mr. Goldman’s shirt, also consistent with Mr. Simpson. Another glove was found at Mr. Simpson’s home, with blood from both victims. Mr. Simpson had a cut on his hand.

The mountain of evidence against Mr. Simpson appeared clear-cut. The trial would be anything but.

When the authorities issued an arrest warrant for him five days after the killings, Mr. Simpson fled. The nation was transfixed as a white Ford Bronco, driven by Mr. Cowlings, with Mr. Simpson in the back seat, led the police on a slow-speed chase through the Los Angeles metro area.

Mr. Simpson eventually surrendered after returning to his home.

The chase not only captivated the country, it also drew the attention of authorities who were trying to track down Mr. Ippolito.

U. S. marshals knew Mr. Ippolito and Mr. Cowlings were friends. And the authorities knew the men were in close contact.

When Mr. Cowlings was briefly detained after the Bronco chase, the police found in his wallet the phone number to a mess hall where Mr. Ippolito worked while he was incarcerated, said John Cuff, one of the marshals tasked with finding Mr. Ippolito. In the Bronco, detectives also found photos of one of Mr. Ippolito’s girlfriends, along with her phone number.

The hunt for Mr. Ippolito grew more urgent, and the authorities began looking coast to coast. Their pursuit persisted for months. They conducted stakeouts and developed sources, at times believing they were on his tracks, only for Mr. Ippolito to slip through their fingers.

Then, as Mr. Cuff assessed a network of pager activity, he identified one likely belonging to Mr. Ippolito. Marshals made plans to apprehend him when he went to get the pager serviced at a store in New York’s Little Italy. They staked out the store for days until they saw a man who looked like Joey. Instead of a balding head, however, the man had flowing hair.

Still, they closed in.

“Joe,” Mr. Cuff said to the man.

“What do you mean? Who?” the man replied.

“What’s with this?” Mr. Cuff said, snatching at the man’s hair and pulling off Mr. Ippolito’s toupee. The escapee simply smiled, Mr. Cuff recalled, as he was brought back into custody.

Mr. Ippolito knew trouble and how to get out of it.

But options were limited for the repeat felon and recent prison escapee.

While Mr. Ippolito settled back behind bars in custody in New York, Mr. Simpson was on trial for murder, the proceedings playing out on television before a global audience.

Each man was fighting for his freedom. But Mr. Ippolito didn’t want to go to trial, or back to prison. So he turned snitch.

Drawing on his connections as a coast-to-coast drug trafficker, he quickly worked from behind bars to help undercover agents buy narcotics from high-priority targets. Records show he began to provide key information that helped federal agents piece together the racketeering activities of major mafia figures. Law enforcement officials said that Mr. Ippolito put himself “at great risk” to help them.

Through his close personal relationships with Al Cowlings, Simpson’s confidant, and others involved in the cases, including O. J. and Nicole Simpson, Ippolito had become privy to many facts relevant to the case, including Simpson’s alleged domestic violence, the Simpsons’ narcotics usage, Simpson’s attempted flight from justice, and his disposal of the murder weapon.

Full document: 1996 memo details Joey Ippolito’s tips about mafia, O. J. Simpson

His extraordinary assistance was later outlined in a sealed 5K letter, a legal document filed by federal prosecutors to reward a defendant’s service. The letter, filed in court in December 1996, detailed Mr. Ippolito’s cooperation “almost immediately” after his arrest in August 1995.

“From the outset, Ippolito was completely forthright in our debriefings, during which we found Ippolito to be a remarkable source of information,” the letter reads. “This information has proven valuable as both investigative leads and to buttress several cases under indictment, and is likely to result in significant prosecutions at which Ippolito, if called, should prove to be a valuable witness.”

The first example cited? The O. J. Simpson case.

While trafficking drugs in California, the letter stated, “Ippolito became close to several individuals at the center of the Simpson/Goldman murder case. Through his close personal relationships with Al Cowlings, Simpson’s confidant, and others involved in the cases, including O. J. and Nicole Simpson, Ippolito had become privy to many facts relevant to the case, including Simpson’s alleged domestic violence, the Simpsons’ narcotics usage, Simpson’s attempted flight from justice, and his disposal of the murder weapon.”

Mr. Ippolito’s claims may have seemed outlandish, the type of storytelling that spouts from inmates desperate for leniency. Except Mr. Ippolito had been a “tremendous resource” to authorities while the Simpson case was playing out in California.

Federal prosecutors in New York began quietly sharing information to local prosecutors in Los Angeles. Mr. Ippolito made himself available to the authorities, and his information was provided to prosecutors “during the murder trial,” which was “at that time important to their case, particularly Simpson’s flight and his remarks to Cowlings concerning a murder weapon,” the cooperation letter stated.

“While Ippolito ultimately was not called as a witness — he was arrested and began to cooperate as that trial drew to a close — my conversations with the Los Angeles authorities indicate that Ippolito’s information was, at the very least, very helpful to their case,” the letter, written by then-federal prosecutor David Kelley, said.

Reached recently, Mr. Kelley said that he remembered Mr. Ippolito speaking about a knife concealed around Mr. Simpson’s property and that Mr. Ippolito had learned of the information from a close associate of Mr. Simpson. He declined to name the person, though the cooperation letter he wrote years earlier suggested Mr. Cowlings was the conduit. Mr. Kelley added that he did not believe Mr. Ippolito was involved in the killings.

Mr. Cowlings did not respond to text messages, phone calls or a letter sent to his home.

Mr. Kelley said in an interview that he recalled having a series of conversations with the prosecution team in Los Angeles, including the lead prosecutors Marcia Clark and Christopher Darden.

Mr. Darden declined to comment.

Ms. Clark, in a recent message, said she had no knowledge of Mr. Ippolito. “If anyone had spoken to him and found him to have relevant and credible information, I surely would have been informed,” she said. “The fact that I was never so informed establishes he had no credible or relevant evidence to provide.”

But others said there was significant back-and-forth between the agencies. One Los Angeles law enforcement official who was involved in the prosecution recalled receiving a call in the summer of 1995 — in the middle of the murder trial — from a federal official in New York who said that Mr. Ippolito had information about the case and was willing to talk. The official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity around the case, recalled that Mr. Ippolito was later reluctant about “being the snitch of the century in the trial of the century.” With the prosecution of Mr. Simpson underway, and the L. A. P. D. and the district attorney’s office being inundated with tips, the official in Los Angeles said they didn’t press the matter.

Mr. Kelley, the former federal prosecutor, said he did not recall Mr. Ippolito being unwilling to help local authorities and that any such reluctance would have violated his cooperation agreement.

Mr. Ippolito was on the radar of L. A. P. D. investigators and prosecutors well before the murder trial, according to the case files reviewed by The Times.

Police detectives — with Mr. Darden, the prosecutor, present — interviewed Marcus Allen, an N. F. L. star and friend of Mr. Simpson, on Sept. 22, 1994, in Kansas City, according to investigative files. The interview took place months after the killings and while Mr. Ippolito was on the lam.

In the interview, investigators asked Mr. Allen whether he knew about Mr. Simpson’s friends and associates, including Joey. The report noted that Mr. Allen said he “did not know a Mr. Joey Ebalito” — an apparent misspelling of Mr. Ippolito’s name.

Around this time, Mr. Simpson’s defense lawyers also took interest in the drug runner with mafia ties. The group investigated whether Mr. Ippolito was linked to the murders, and at one point mulled whether he could be considered a suspect, according to Patrick J. McKenna, a private investigator from Florida who worked for the defense team.

Mr. McKenna said the team had another investigator, Jack McNally, a former New York Police Department detective with contacts in the city’s underworld, pursue this angle. Mr. McKenna recalled that Mr. McNally spoke to contacts in “the highest of the five families” in New York and reported back to the defense team, saying, “I don’t think he’s got any involvement.” (Mr. McNally died in 2023.)

Mr. Ippolito was never called — by the defense or the prosecution — to testify as a witness in the murder case. One of the complicating factors, as suggested in his cooperation letter, centered on timing.

At the time of Mr. Ippolito’s arrest in August 1995, the trial against Mr. Simpson had been underway for eight months. The prosecution had already rested its case. Closing arguments were approaching.

A jury acquitted Mr. Simpson in October 1995. The prosecution was marred by the police department’s history of racism and questions about the handling of key evidence. (A jury in a civil case later held Mr. Simpson liable for the deaths.)

At the time of Mr. Ippolito’s own sentencing in late 1996, federal prosecutors and a district judge heaped praise on him for his cooperation.

In addition to having him inform on mob associates, federal law enforcement placed him in a federal detention center in Brooklyn to spy on high-profile inmates, most notably suspects detained for their alleged roles in the 1993 World Trade Center bombing, according to two people who were close to Mr. Ippolito.

In a 1996 hearing closed to the public, Judge Kimba M. Wood said the government wrote on Mr. Ippolito’s behalf “one of the strongest letters I have ever received, possibly the strongest.”

Judge Wood said she was “inclined” to do whatever she could to “make sure” he received “the credit he deserves for this cooperation,” according to a transcript of the hearing.

She issued the most lenient sentence she could, under law.

For his prison escape, Mr. Ippolito was sentenced to time served. The government also agreed not to prosecute him for distributing drugs in California for the five years up until his arrest.

Records indicate that Mr. Ippolito was released from custody in 1998. He died in 2006. His obituary vastly understated his colorful life, describing him as “a self-employed restaurateur in the Florida area.”

The new information collected by The Times suggests that Mr. Ippolito’s role may have extended beyond what he told authorities.

Mr. Ippolito’s brother Sam said Joey was at the scene of the killings.

Sam Ippolito said that on the evening of the murders, Joey left the apartment around 6 p. m. Hours later, around midnight, his brother returned to their apartment carrying a bag with a heavy object inside and he appeared to have blood on his hands, Sam Ippolito said. Next, Joey undressed and stuffed his own clothes in the bag. He then asked Sam to get rid of it while he showered.

Sam also said he saw Joey call Mr. Cowlings from the apartment, and heard his brother say that he had just been “helping” Mr. Simpson.

Sam Ippolito told The Times he didn’t ask questions. He went outside and found a dumpster along Doheny Drive, near a construction site. He tossed the bag in.

Soon after, Sam said, he and his brother left Los Angeles and headed back to the East Coast. Sam brought up Mr. Simpson during the brothers’ trip. Sam said Joey refused to answer specific questions about what had transpired except to say that he “went to go help O. J.” that night.

An attorney for Ms. Mijares released a statement denying Sam Ippolito’s claim about Joey’s bloody appearance at her apartment, calling it absurd. “She has known Joey since she was a teenager,” the statement read. “She cannot be expected to remember every time they were together, especially events from 30 years ago.”

Ms. Mijares did not address questions about whether the Ippolitos stayed at her home in June 1994.

Sam Ippolito said in an interview that he was “100 percent” sure that Joey was with Mr. Simpson at the scene of the murders. He said he should have disclosed this information long ago.

But revealing secrets can have consequences. In 1997, two years after Joey became a federal informant, a mafia gunman shot Sam repeatedly and ran him over with a vehicle — authorities called it retaliation for Joey’s cooperation with the government. The gunman was later convicted of attempted murder and witness tampering.

In his conversations with a reporter earlier this year, Sam Ippolito maintained for months the story about his brother’s involvement.

Then, in a follow-up exchange this past summer, Sam Ippolito asked for compensation. He said he had been “offered a ton of money” and was under contract to tell his story elsewhere. And now, he wanted to recant what he previously told The Times, saying he previously could not differentiate what was real and what was not.

Peacock has announced that it is airing a documentary, “OJ’s Accomplice,” later this year about theories in the Simpson case.

Friends and some family members of Joey Ippolito have rejected any suggestion that he was involved on the night of the murders. They said that Sam Ippolito could not be trusted and might be trying to win attention and compensation.

Over the years, many have wondered about the case’s unexplained mysteries, such as where the murder weapon might have gone. Some have posited the brutal, efficient nature of the killings meant it likely that more than one person was involved.

Under the timeline presented by prosecutors, Mr. Simpson was in a hurry on the night of the murders, rushing home to catch a limousine that would take him to a previously scheduled flight.

Detectives hunted the route for the knife — in the woods, dumpsters and even the bowels of an airport waste tank that could have held the discharge from the airplane. None was ever found.

Tom Lange, who was the lead detective in the Simpson case and is now retired from the L. A. P. D., said he has never believed Mr. Simpson had help, and said if there was any evidence to support that theory it would have been disclosed by now.

Mr. Lange recalled Mr. Ippolito’s name coming up during the investigation of the murders, but that he “never really became an issue” for investigators. He said they received hundreds of tips during his time on the case and that only a handful were related to Mr. Ippolito.

During the criminal trial, Mr. Simpson’s defense team suggested there was evidence two people had been at the crime scene — an idea that prosecutors rejected. Robert Blasier, a lawyer who was part of Mr. Simpson’s defense team for both the criminal and civil trials and lived with him at his Brentwood home during the civil case, said Mr. Simpson had also maintained his innocence in private conversations. Still, Mr. Blasier believes the theories about having an accomplice could be true.

“My take is that these other theories are certainly possible,” he said. “But none of them amount to proof beyond a reasonable doubt.”

Got a confidential news tip? The New York Times would like to hear from readers who want to share messages and materials with our journalists.

Over the years, Mr. Ippolito told people varying stories about his role in the case.

Eddie Trotta, a longtime friend of Joey, said Mr. Ippolito phoned him, talking about how he was telling law enforcement that Mr. Cowlings was the one who hid the knife, and that Mr. Cowlings ultimately discarded the weapon. Mr. Trotta said it seemed to him Mr. Ippolito was inventing tales.

Rob Brisolari, a former Drug Enforcement Administration agent who regularly spoke with Joey Ippolito, was skeptical that Mr. Ippolito was involved in the murders. He believed Mr. Ippolito had no motive to do so. Still, Mr. Brisolari did not rule out the possibility.

“It seems a little far-fetched to me, but that doesn’t mean it didn’t happen,” he said in an interview.

Mr. Brisolari remembered that Mr. Ippolito did disclose to him that he had received a call from Mr. Cowlings after the murders, seeking help to get Mr. Simpson out of the area. Mr. Ippolito reported to Mr. Brisolari that he told Mr. Cowlings that it would be difficult to do so — Mr. Ippolito himself was on the run from the authorities.

That request for assistance was in line with yet another tale that has emerged about Mr. Ippolito. The rapper Fat Joe, the man behind the hit song “What’s Luv?”, told a seemingly random story on his podcast about a friend named “Joe” and O. J. Simpson.

He said this deceased friend in Miami went by the name Joe Bentley, a name used by Mr. Ippolito because of the many Bentleys he owned.

On the podcast, Fat Joe said that Joey, who was released from federal custody in 1998, confided to him that when Mr. Cowlings and Mr. Simpson were in the Bronco chase, Joey had been at an airport, waiting with a private jet to help them escape. (Investigators did find in the infamous white Bronco a travel bag with a passport and a disguise kit.)

Fat Joe said he once went to Joey’s home for the birthday of Joey’s wife. Mr. Simpson was there. When it came time to cut the cake, Joey handed a “machete” to Mr. Simpson and declared: “You did it!” Mr. Simpson then chased Joey around with the weapon, apparently all in jest.

Reached recently, a spokesperson for Fat Joe said the rapper declined to comment. Mr. Ippolito’s widow declined to comment.

The tale meant that there were at least three versions of Mr. Ippolito’s link to the murders. In one told to federal prosecutors, he shared information from Mr. Cowlings, including about the supposed location of the murder weapon. In another version, as told by his brother, Mr. Ippolito was at the scene of the killings and had apparent blood on his hands. In another version, as told to Fat Joe, Mr. Ippolito was ready to help Mr. Simpson escape.

He looked up and met my eyes, but for several moments it was as if he didn’t really see me. “Are you listening to me?” I said. “I asked you what happened here.”Charlie shook his head from side to side, his mouth still hanging open, his breathing still short, ragged, and in a voice that was no more than a frightened whisper, said, “Jesus Christ, O. J.—what have you done?”

Mr. Simpson, who died in 2024, was coy about the truth through the years. He vacillated between professing innocence and admitting guilt in a “hypothetical” confession.

In his hypothetical account of the night of June 12, 1994, Mr. Simpson told a ghostwriter that a friend of his, identified by the name “Charlie,” had come to his home that night, and their conversation triggered Mr. Simpson’s anger. The two hopped into Mr. Simpson’s white Ford Bronco and drove to Ms. Brown Simpson’s home to “scare” her. He described Charlie as a horrified observer to the bloodshed that ensued.

“Jesus Christ, O. J. — what have you done?” he quoted Charlie as saying as they looked over the scene of the two bodies crumpled on the ground. But after they arrived back in Mr. Simpson’s neighborhood, Mr. Simpson said he had handed Charlie a bundle of bloody clothes and the murder weapon. Charlie warily agreed to get rid of it.

But there’s yet another wrinkle to the “Charlie” story. A man whose real name is Charlie once suggested that he was the hypothetical accomplice.

Charlie Ehrlich was charged alongside Mr. Simpson during a robbery case in Las Vegas in 2007.

Mr. Ehrlich said in an interview that before the “If I Did It” book was published, Mr. Simpson told him over dinner that he had used his name as part of his hypothetical account.

Several years ago, Mr. Ehrlich went on to work with a producer, Erik Laibe, to tell his life story. The pair envisioned a film.

In hours of audiotapes never made public but reviewed by The Times, Mr. Laibe and Mr. Ehrlich do not directly confront the question of whether the “Charlie” in Mr. Simpson’s book was a reflection of Mr. Ehrlich. Mr. Ehrlich said on the tapes that he had met Mr. Simpson before the murders. Mr. Laibe at one point brings up that Mr. Simpson’s hypothetical account had used the name. “Regarding that: Use your imagination,” Mr. Ehrlich said. “I’ll leave it at that.”

Mr. Ehrlich suggested at another point that he had insights into Mr. Simpson’s mind-set on the night of the murders.

Those tapes fueled the theory that Mr. Ehrlich was the accomplice.

In a recent interview, Mr. Ehrlich said it was all a lie. He said he had played along with the idea that he was the hypothetical accomplice as part of an effort to cash in on the infamy.

Mr. Simpson’s ghostwriter, Pablo Fenjves, said he recalled being the one to propose Charlie as the pseudonym of Mr. Simpson’s supposed accomplice.

Mr. Ehrlich said he didn’t meet Mr. Simpson until Mr. Simpson moved to Florida in the years after his trial — well after the killings.

Mr. Ehrlich recalled that Mr. Simpson was impressed he had done seven years in prison, “kept his mouth shut” and “never ratted nobody out.”

“O. J. loved that about me,” Mr. Ehrlich said.

Unspoken was that the man who introduced them was himself a superstar snitch. His name? Joey Ippolito.

Kirsten Noyes, Alain Delaquérière, Kitty Bennett, Sheelagh McNeill and Susan C. Beachycontributed research.

I vividly remember when the O. J. Simpson verdict was announced in 1995. I was a senior in college, and my journalism professor canceled class so we could all gather at the student center to watch. I maintained an interest in the case over the years, but it wasn’t until I moved to L. A. that I came to fully understand how central it was to the city’s modern history — and to the fraught relationship between the L. A. P. D. and the Black community.

I was only in elementary school during the “trial of the century,” but in recent years, I was drawn back to whether there was an additional person at the murder scene that night. So we started digging. It is one of the most scrutinized criminal cases in American history — could there be anything left to learn?After knocking on mobsters' doors and unsealing missing court records, we discovered that reputed Mafia associate Joey Ippolito became a trusted government informant near the end of the trial. With the case still officially open, I have to wonder if these new revelations will lead detectives to take another look.

Mike Baker is a national investigative reporter for The Times, based in Seattle.

Tim Arango is a correspondent covering national news. He is based in Los Angeles.

This Is What America’s Utility Bill Crisis Looks Like

The New York Times October 18, 2026

Record heat and a rising demand for electricity are closing in on Oklahoma families trying to keep the lights on and the AC running.

Record heat and a rising demand for electricity are closing in on Oklahoma families trying to keep the lights on and the AC running.

Genia Weitz and her husband, Daryl Mason, confined themselves to their living room to try to keep their electricity bill down. Credit...

Supported by

By Eli Saslow

Photographs by Erin Schaff

The worst of the heat was just beginning to lift when Genia Weitz, 58, walked into the stubborn Oklahoma sun last month and found the next emergency waiting in her mailbox. “Disconnection notice,” the letter began. She scanned her electric bill and saw a total balance of $1,340.96, far more than her monthly income. State rules prevented the power company from shutting off someone’s electricity when the heat index was above 101 degrees, but now it had dropped to 99 in September, and Weitz had nine days to pay.

She went back inside, where the window shades were drawn and heavy blankets hung across the halls and doorways to trap cool air. The house had three bedrooms and two bathrooms, but for the past several months Weitz and her husband, Daryl Mason, had mostly confined themselves to their 300-square-foot living room, letting the rest of the house bake to save money on electricity. They had an air-conditioner mounted to the window that rattled all day. They had her oxygen machine plugged into the wall and his CPAP machine for sleep apnea hooked up in the corner.

Weitz had been sleeping on the couch while Mason slept in the recliner. Sometimes, their grandchildren would pile onto mattresses in the living room. On the most humid nights, the heat index outside barely dropped below 85, and their machines ran until morning.

“I can’t breathe if I don’t have my oxygen,” Weitz said, as she handed the bill to Mason. “I don’t think I’d last a single night.”

“We’d probably stroke out anyway in all this heat,” Mason said. “If we lose this room, we’re not going to make it.”

As fall sets in across the country, the bill is coming due for the hottest summer on record in the United States. The last three months were about three degrees above average, hotter than the Dust Bowl summer of 1936 and the heat dome of 2021, and tens of millions of people can’t afford to pay for the air-conditioning that helped keep them safe in the deadly heat. About one in six U. S. households is already behind on its utility bills, according to federal data. More than a dozen hot-weather states like Arizona, Georgia, Virginia and Oklahoma restrict shut-offs during the most dangerous heat, so disconnections tend to peak in October, when a climate crisis turns into a collection notice.

The Public Service Company of Oklahoma (PSO) had disconnected Weitz’s power before, so she knew the shut-off notice wasn’t an idle warning. PSO had told customers it was also facing rising costs: for fuel and equipment, for investments to update an aging power grid, for the rising demands of extreme weather and new large-load customers, including data centers being built for artificial intelligence. The company’s rates were still below the national average, and it attributed much of the summer’s higher bills to temperatures that kept air-conditioners running around the clock.

Weitz studied her bill and saw she was paying nearly $500 each month to live in a single room. “Turn the lamp off, Daryl,” she said. “Stop running the ceiling fan.”

She’d read on Facebook that power companies sometimes offered 30 days of relief to people with serious medical conditions, so she printed a form to bring to her doctor. “Please be advised that a life-threatening situation does not cause the debt to be forgiven, but merely postponed to a later date,” it read.

Their car was broken down in the driveway, so she boarded a shuttle bus and looked out the window at the faded brick buildings of McAlester. It was a town of 18,000 people built on a coal rush and sustained by an ammunition plant and the state penitentiary. Weitz had always known it as a hard place to live, but after five decades she also knew almost everyone, including the shuttle driver, Sondra Beck.

“Never thought I’d need to see the doctor just to keep my lights on,” Weitz said.

“I owe $700 by Friday,” Beck said. “Everybody’s getting shut off lately.”

They had worked together for several years at a nearby chicken plant, where Beck was a supervisor and Weitz worked on the deboning line. Weitz had stood in the refrigerated plant and deboned as many as a dozen birds a minute, hundreds an hour, thousands in an average 12-hour shift. She dug her fingers under the meat, peeling each fillet off the rib cage until her wrists went numb and her fingers swelled inside her gloves. Now she had arthritis in both hands, two artificial knees, a damaged back and $860 a month in government disability payments. She missed her job. She missed the chill of the factory floor.

The shuttle stopped at the clinic. Weitz tried the front door, but it was locked. A sign on the window said the office was closed for lunch. She went back to the shuttle, took out her phone and eventually texted her eldest daughter.

“You know I hate to ask,” she wrote.

Weitz’s daughter Shenia Mick put on a business suit and a necklace and left home in the dark to drive to her office in Tulsa. Mick, 36, had always believed in showing up early for her job at GasTech Engineering, but lately she was stretching her hours from 6 a. m. until early evening. What her bosses attributed to ambition and work ethic was also basic math. Her office was air-conditioned, and somebody else paid the bill.

Her house had been dangerously hot for much of the summer, as her two aging wall units failed to keep up with 17 consecutive days of 100-degree heat and high humidity. She pushed the AC to its limit around the clock and ran up electric bills of more than $500 each month, but her indoor thermometer rarely dipped below 80 degrees. She set up fans in her bedroom and still awoke sweating in the night. Once, she tried to cook dinner on the stove and became dizzy and then nauseated, suffering from what she believed to be heat stroke. Her boyfriend got her into the shower, and the ice-cold water felt hot against her skin.

She worked in her office until lunch, when she saw a text message from her mother in McAlester. Mick was already helping to pay for her mother’s water bill and car insurance, and here was a photograph of her mother’s electric bill.

“These numbers are getting crazy,” Weitz wrote.

“It’s bad here, too,” Mick wrote. “I’m constantly paying for something. I’m at work right now.”

“You’re doing so good. I’m proud of you.”

Her mother said it often and to everyone: Her eldest daughter had escaped McAlester and become the town’s most unlikely success story. Mick had dropped out of high school, run away from home several times, and returned with two children and a DUI before she turned 18. She lost years to alcohol and heroin before going into liver failure, and then she’d walked out of a Tulsa hospital in her mid-20s and somehow started clawing her way back: to a methadone clinic every day, to a G. E. D., to a manager’s job at IHOP. She signed up for college classes and went to night school for seven years, earning three associate degrees and eventually a job at GasTech.

She started in the shop, wearing T-shirts and jeans as she helped build equipment for natural gas plants, until a manager noticed Mick was organizing and running a team like a seasoned boss. The manager offered Mick a job on the business side, lent her a wardrobe of professional clothes and helped her pay back years’ worth of court fines. Now she was a senior buyer in the purchasing department, earning more than $80,000 a year to negotiate deals with suppliers around the world, with a LinkedIn profile her mother showed off around McAlester. She had her hair highlighted, her facial piercings removed, her suit jacket tailored. “A results-driven professional,” the profile read.

But lately it seemed to Mick as if the reward for so much transformation was more of the same bills, the same stress, the same debts that kept accumulating as she paid almost $1,500 for her own rent and just as much each month to help support her family in McAlester.

In August, she made three separate payments to PSO for her own electric bill, sending $150, $194 and then $101.42. After she became dizzy from heat in the kitchen, she borrowed money from an online lender to buy an extra portable AC unit for $379. The unit cooled parts of the house but drove up her electricity costs. Now she had another bill from PSO, and she would have to borrow to pay that balance, too.

Mick texted her mother with a photo of her own bill: $589.51. “Avoid disconnection,” the bill read. “Pay at least $169.59 to keep your power on.”

“I’m paying this every month, and it’s still so hot in our house,” Mick wrote.

“That’s way too much,” Weitz wrote.

“Is there anyone else who can help?” Mick asked her.

The heat held in the 90s. The window unit kept rattling in the living room. Weitz went back to the clinic and had her doctor sign and mail the medical form, certifying that losing power would be life-threatening. That bought her another 30 days, but her oxygen machine kept running and her debt continued to grow. One afternoon, she showed her electric bill to her daughter-in-law, Autumn Cooper, 24.

“I still don’t know what I’m going to do,” Weitz said.

“Even looking at that number gives me a heart attack,” Cooper said. “I’d panic if I was dealing with those big amounts.”

Instead of being billed hundreds of dollars each month, Cooper had switched to a prepaid plan with PSO so she could make small payments to her account every few days. As long as her account had a positive balance, she had power to cool her house, wash laundry and cook for her five children.

For the last month, she had been washing dishes by hand in the dark and still burning through an average of $12.29 in electricity each day as she monitored her balance constantly. Whenever it dipped below zero, PSO cut her off within a few days. She had received more than a dozen low-balance warnings over the course of the summer. Now she checked the latest balance on her phone and showed it to Weitz: $2.46, enough for a few more hours of power.

“See, that would stress me out even more,” Weitz said. “It’s hanging over your head every minute.”

“I can always come up with a few bucks,” Cooper said. “But every day is a hustle.”

Cooper was going to school to pursue a nursing certification during the week while her husband stayed home to care for their children — a 6-year-old, a 4-year-old, 2-year-old twins and an infant. On weekends, she worked back-to-back double shifts at the New Hope Retirement and Care Center, where she earned $16 an hour to bathe, feed and change residents in the memory care wing. She scraped together a little extra money by selling used baby gear online, borrowing from friends and doing odd jobs for a construction company. If everything went exactly right, she made just enough to keep her power on. One day in July, she sent PSO three separate payments: $7.15 in the morning, $3.65 a few hours later and another $3.14 before she went to bed.

She had come to believe that any real solution would take more than a few dollars at a time, so she went online to start researching electricity charges. Oklahoma was emerging as a major hub for data centers, luring companies like Google and Meta with the promise of tax breaks and cheap land in an effort to become “the high-tech data center capital of the world,” Gov. Kevin Stitt had said in 2025. One proposed data center outside McAlester would use more electricity each week at full capacity than all the homes in McAlester used in an entire year.

PSO was planning to invest $1.2 billion in new power generation and storage to keep up with the rising demands of a growing population, new homes and new businesses. A new state law aimed to make the largest new consumers pay their share, but some of the costs of adding more power had already fallen on ordinary customers.

PSO had cut off power 58 times for every 100 residential customers in 2024, the most recent year with federal data. It was the highest rate of any investor-owned utility in the country, and the company said most of those disconnections were on a small number of prepaid accounts like Cooper’s that shut off when they dipped below zero and then came back on within minutes of payment. On and then off again. On and then off.

PSO had promised to waive some late fees on high summer bills and offer extensions and payment plans. The company had written a public letter to customers saying “affordability is important” and “we do not take any change to customer bills lightly,” but Cooper went on social media and found hundreds of Oklahomans complaining about a similar crisis.

“My bill is unreal. I guess I’ll just burn up.”

“I use a flashlight on my phone before I turn a light on, and I pay $100 a week.”

“Single mom here. Cried on the phone with them last week because mine is so high.”

“My monthly bill is almost 900. I know it’s hot, but this is like an AC bill on Venus.”

Cooper read through the complaints in mid-September and started a petition online to demand more affordable and transparent electric bills. “We, the customers of PSO, are speaking up,” she wrote. “We want our voices heard and our concerns addressed.”

Now she sat in Weitz’s living room and checked the petition on her phone. It had 24 signatures.

She switched to her PSO account. “Urgent: low balance warning,” the app read.

“Here we go again,” Cooper said. “I could be waking up in the dark tomorrow.”

“They might cut you off before me,” Weitz said.

“Guess I have to figure this out,” Cooper said.

They got into Cooper’s car and drove into downtown, passing the cluster of churches that were losing members even as more people came to their doors for help. Cooper watched her gas gauge dip below the empty line as she pulled up to the post office. She had cut a deal online to sell 30 baby outfits to a buyer in Texas for a total of $10, but she wouldn’t get paid until the clothes arrived.

“How long until it gets there?” she asked the clerk.

“Two days, maybe three.”

“Nothing faster?”

“You could overnight it, but that’s not going to be cheap.”

Cooper shook her head and went outside. “It’s time to get creative,” Weitz said. She knew people in town who hired drivers for odd jobs and businesses that bought scrap metal or paid cash for gift cards. She knew all of the aid organizations in town and how much they gave to whom. Just a few weeks earlier, she had gotten almost $500 in energy assistance from a federal program for low-income families.

“Let’s try the churches,” Weitz said.

“I already feel guilty about not going to church,” Cooper said. “I don’t want to ask for help.”

“You have a better plan?”

Cooper stood in the parking lot for a moment and then got back into the car. They drove to the charity Shared Blessings, where the administrator said it had resources to help 10 people with electric bills each month, and Cooper’s request was the 43rd. They continued to All Saints Episcopal Church, where a woman came outside with her cellphone pressed to one ear and waved them away. “Sorry, all out,” she said. They walked a few blocks to Mike’s Club, a thrift store where the owner, Mike Brown, sometimes took money out of his register for families in need.

“I’ve got employees who’ve had their power cut,” Brown said. “The whole town’s going dark. I’m sorry, but I just can’t.”

Cooper thanked him and went back to her car. She started to drive home, but Weitz pointed to a building up the street. “Last stop,” she said.

Cooper groaned but then turned into the parking lot for First Baptist Church. A woman at the front desk greeted them with two bottles of water and a package of snack foods. “Let me guess — electric bill?” she said.

“I really just need maybe $10, $20 to keep my lights on,” Cooper said.

“I get it,” the woman said. “Let me talk to the pastor.”

Cooper and Weitz waited as she disappeared into the back of the church. A few minutes later, the pastor came out to the lobby, shaking his head. “My bill last month was $1,800, and I live in a double-wide,” he said. “We’re all out for the day. Will you try us again?”

“Sure,” Cooper said. “I’ll be in the same situation tomorrow.”

She drove back to Weitz’s house, parked out front and checked her account. “To prevent disconnection, please make a payment immediately,” the app read.

“The kids might stay over here with you for a few nights,” Cooper said.

“Of course,” Weitz said, and they walked through the dark house, past the hanging blankets and back into the living room.

I spent several days in Oklahoma with Genia Weitz, her daughter and her daughter-in-law as they scrambled to keep their power on. They leaned on one another constantly, texting photos of their bills back and forth and trading ideas, each trying to help the others while facing the same impossible equation.

Eli Saslow writes in-depth stories about the impact of major national issues on people’s lives.

Erin Schaff is a photojournalist for The Times, covering stories across the country.

5 Takeaways From The Times’s Re-Examination of the O. J. Simpson Case

The New York Times October 18, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Newly unsealed court files and interviews challenge the popular narrative around the murders and the “trial of the century.”

By Mike Baker and Tim Arango

In the failed murder prosecution of O. J. Simpson in 1995, the government professed that he alone had killed his ex-wife, Nicole Brown Simpson, and her friend Ronald Goldman.

Among the issues that hampered the case: the lack of a murder weapon, which has never been found. Its absence has long stoked speculation about whether the killer had assistance.

Now, records unsealed after 30 years at the request of The New York Times show that a prized government informant had told law enforcement key information about the killings, including the supposed location of the murder weapon and details about Mr. Simpson’s efforts to evade prosecution. Together, the findings challenge the popular narrative around the case.

This year, the informant’s brother told The Times that his sibling’s role in the case went much deeper. And the brother said he actually helped discard a bag, containing a heavy object, in the hours after the murders.

Joseph Ippolito, known as Joey, a convicted drug trafficker and mafia associate, escaped from a Florida prison a month before the 1994 murders.

Mr. Ippolito’s brother said the siblings went west after the escape to Los Angeles. Before his incarceration, Mr. Ippolito had operated a popular restaurant there and was a close friend of Al Cowlings, the longtime confidant of Mr. Simpson.

In the wake of the infamous Bronco chase with Mr. Simpson and Mr. Cowlings, investigators found photos in the vehicle of one of Mr. Ippolito’s girlfriends, along with her phone number.

Mr. Ippolito was eventually brought back into custody a year later. Right away, records show, he fed federal investigators in New York information about the mafia and set up meetings with undercover drug agents, with prosecutors saying that they “found Ippolito to be a remarkable source of information.” Mr. Ippolito risked his own safety to help them, prosecutors wrote in a memo lobbying a federal judge for leniency in his sentence.

He also divulged information about Mr. Simpson and the killings.

Prosecutors said that Mr. Ippolito’s close relationship with Mr. Cowlings and Mr. Simpson made him “privy to many facts relevant to the case, including Mr. Simpson’s alleged domestic violence, the Simpsons’ narcotics usage, Mr. Simpson’s attempted flight from justice, and his disposal of the murder weapon.”

Details of Mr. Ippolito’s cooperation were outlined in a federal court memo, as well as a sentencing hearing transcript, obtained by The Times. A federal prosecutor, a former U. S. marshal, a former agent for the Drug Enforcement Administration and an official involved in prosecuting the murder case also independently confirmed Mr. Ippolito’s cooperation.

Federal officials said they shared the information with prosecutors in Los Angeles. But the information arrived near the end of the murder trial, which was attracting global attention. Mr. Ippolito was never called as a witness. He died in 2006.

Earlier this year, one of Mr. Ippolito’s brothers, Sam, told The Times that they were staying at a West Hollywood apartment on the night of the murders in 1994. Joey told Sam he was going out for the night to help a friend. Sam said his brother came back hours later with what appeared to be blood on his hands and a bag that contained a heavy object. Joey asked his brother to get rid of the bag, Sam Ippolito recalled. Sam Ippolito said he tossed it into a construction site dumpster nearby.

Sam Ippolito said he was confident his brother had been at the scene of the murders. Months after the Times interview, Sam Ippolito asked for compensation. When a reporter declined, he recanted his story and said he “was offered a ton of money” to tell his story elsewhere, apparently for an upcoming documentary.

In 2007, Mr. Simpson went public with a “hypothetical” confession to the murders, published in the book “If I Did It.” In that account, he described a friend who was with him on the night of the murders, who first was a horrified bystander but then agreed to take the murder weapon and Mr. Simpson’s bloody clothes.

Prosecutors and investigators gave little credence to the details of Mr. Simpson’s tale, and they did little to follow up on the idea that someone may have aided in helping Mr. Simpson get rid of the murder weapon.

The Times found that Mr. Ippolito’s name had surfaced early — and repeatedly — in the murder investigation. Police investigators asked about him. The defense team examined him, checking into his mafia ties and exploring whether he could be considered a suspect.

Tom Lange, who was the lead detective in the Simpson case, said he recalled Mr. Ippolito’s name coming up but didn’t consider him a serious suspect. He still does not believe Mr. Simpson had help.

Mr. Simpson was eventually held civilly liable for the deaths. He died in 2024.

The Times learned that last year, investigators with the Los Angeles Police Department’s cold case unit were making calls to collect information about accomplice theories.

A police department spokesman said last week that the “O. J. Simpson case remains an open and ongoing investigation.” Because there was no conviction in the murders, “the department has an obligation to continue to pursue justice in this matter.” The spokesman added, “at a point that new evidence is found, detectives will follow those investigatory leads.”

Mike Baker is a national investigative reporter for The Times, based in Seattle.

Tim Arango is a correspondent covering national news. He is based in Los Angeles.

Connections: Sports Edition

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

OpinionGuest Essay

Credit... Ed Steed

Supported by

By Chris Marquis

Mr. Marquis is a professor at the University of Cambridge Judge Business School and the author of “The Profiteers: How Business Privatizes Profit and Socializes Cost.”

This fall, another cohort of ambitious young professionals has arrived at business schools around the world for two-year programs with price tags in the six figures. Their presence at some of the nicest and shiniest buildings on campus renews a familiar question: What exactly is an M. B. A. for?

This question has become more urgent as business education has expanded dramatically in the past decades. Today, nearly one in five American undergraduates majors in business, and the M. B. A. is the most popular graduate degree in the United States.

I have taught in business schools for over 20 years, at Harvard, Cornell and Cambridge. While some students appear to care only about their future compensation, I have met many with nobler goals: engineers who want to commercialize clean energy, physicians determined to fix the health care system, nonprofit leaders who have watched good missions fail for want of good management.

These students enroll hoping to learn what business schools say they teach: how to manage people, how to allocate capital and resources and how to make the world a better place through leadership. But I’ve come to see how the institution can reshape the worldviews of those who enter it, often undermining the very ambitions that brought them there.

This change can take place in a single semester. Again and again, I have watched students abandon their altruistic intentions, instead becoming consumed by whether to choose careers in consulting or finance and who will land a summer internship at McKinsey or Goldman Sachs.

The modern business school is designed to promote dealmaking, simplification and optimization. This mind-set has escaped containment and has spread to the wider world. Business-educated elites increasingly populate political leadership, bringing with them a transactional view of public life. One investigation found that out of 45 current heads of state who had studied in the United States, 10 were business majors, and six of those also earned M. B. A. s. President Trump, a Wharton graduate, has treated foreign policy and government itself as extensions of dealmaking and personal gain.

Surely, not every business graduate governs this way. But recent research by the Nobel laureate economist Daron Acemoglu and colleagues shows what tends to happen when you put an M. B. A. in charge. In both the United States and Denmark, firms that appointed managers with business degrees cut wages and reduced labor’s share of income. Yet these companies didn’t become more productive, nor did they grow sales, investment or employment any faster. What registers as managerial acumen turns out to be wealth transfer — value moved away from workers and toward profits, shareholders and executives.

I’ve come to realize that business schools don’t just reflect our economic system — they actively manufacture its priorities and normalize its harms, training the future leaders who will design and defend the structures driving our overlapping global crises. Tinkering at the margins with a class on corporate responsibility or ethics is not going to help. We don’t need to “fix” business schools. We need to abolish them.

Business schools have always struggled to justify their place in the university. A medical school’s core justification is health, and a law school’s is justice — undisputed public goods. Business schools are organized explicitly around a private good: the pursuit of profit. The American sociologist Thorstein Veblen identified this tension a century ago, criticizing university schools focused on commerce because they “need imply nothing in the way of serviceability to the common good.”

When schools like Wharton and Harvard Business School were established, they were seen as overly vocational, and to build legitimacy their founders framed management as a profession, on par with law and medicine. But education in those fields rested on established bodies of knowledge — centuries of case law, natural sciences like biology — that management lacked.

The solution, devised in the 1920s by the Harvard dean Wallace Donham, was to borrow the teaching style used in law and medicine: the case study. It became the signature method of business education. To this day, professors assign 10- to 20-page descriptions of business challenges culminating in a decision point that students then debate in class. The method is pervasive: In 2024, Harvard Business School sold nearly 17 million case studies to various business programs around the world.

One well-known case study that I have taught many times is “Rob Parson at Morgan Stanley.” The facts are simple enough to produce a lively classroom debate. Mr. Parson has delivered impressive results and is viewed as a star performer, but his abrasive and go-it-alone style has alienated people across the firm. In the classroom, students take the position of his manager, Paul Nasr, and decide whether to promote him, delay the promotion or push him out.

Nearly three decades after publication, it remains among H. B. S.’s most widely used cases, and the dilemma is enduring: Should results be rewarded even when the person producing them damages the culture around him? In class, students vote on Mr. Nasr’s options and often role-play the difficult conversation between him and Mr. Parson. The discussion can be dramatic, engaging and effective.

But my experience has shown that by asking students to inhabit Mr. Nasr’s role, the case study narrows their imaginations to the decision facing one senior manager. Deeper questions — like whether Mr. Parson is himself a product of investment-banking culture — are rarely raised. Mr. Parson becomes an individual problem, when the larger issue may be an industry that rewards rainmaking, hierarchy and masculine performance norms, then acts surprised when they cause conflict.

When the case method is used in medicine and law, it serves a different set of goals. Medical students work through detailed patient scenarios — symptoms, test results, histories and social and economic context. Law students read real court opinions, dissecting facts, arguments and judgments. In both fields, students are confronted by the messiness of reality, and the goal is to foster disciplined skepticism: ask what’s missing, challenge assumptions and test how an analysis could be wrong.

Business school cases operate on another logic, focused not on inquiry but on decision making. H. B. S.’s own overview of the method describes students imagining “themselves in the decision-maker’s role” and “taking decisive action.” The point is to practice acting like the person in charge — or, as George W. Bush, a graduate of Harvard Business School, put it, “the decider.”

By overestimating the importance of individual decision makers, the business school classroom avoids harder questions: Who made this person the legitimate protagonist? Whose knowledge is absent? Why are workers, regulators, communities, ecosystems or citizens rarely given equal standing?

I wrote dozens of case studies during my decade at H. B. S., some of which are described as classics and best sellers. These are not products of independent research, but carefully packaged corporate narratives. The disclaimer printed in tiny type on every H. B. S. case concedes this point: Cases “are not intended to serve … as sources of primary data.” The data they include can be selective, biased or even fabricated.

For the many cases I wrote under the guidance of senior faculty members, events that reflected poorly on the company were softened or omitted and the roles of certain executives were burnished. The companies held final approval, with drafts reviewed by their lawyers and P. R. staff. Rather than being vehicles for disinterested learning, as one might expect at a university, the case studies end up as instruments of reputation management.

Corporate influence feeds a larger problem: The cases almost always feature winners, making it easy to mistake luck or timing for a proven strategy. Failures, dead ends and nonmarket solutions are rarely considered. Before Enron’s fraud was exposed, its business model was presented in admiring terms by at least five H. B. S. case studies. More damning still, the strategies that later led to its collapse — its asset-light model, its trading platform — were portrayed as innovations. Questions about deregulated energy markets, revolving-door oversight and opaque accounting went unasked.

Furthermore, edits that push the case narratives away from reality are often meant to make it “work” in a classroom. Complexity is systematically shaved away, and dissenting voices often go unheard. Real organizations don’t move in clearly delineated phases toward a decision point, but business school teaching materials often do — compressing timelines, dropping messy subplots and smoothing over contradictions to produce clean narrative arcs and satisfying problems to debate.

The result is a curriculum built around false narratives. Some of the most celebrated ideas in management have not been the ones that survived peer review or replication, but the ones that could be turned into TED Talks, consulting frameworks or airport best sellers. Faculty members are rewarded not for knowledge but for performance — selling a big idea with a memorable label that promises “success” or “disruption.”

Business schools have a divided mission: They seek to legitimize an economic system focused on private gain while also developing guardrails to tame it. They found a remarkable way to manage this tension: the “win-win” story in which the conflict between private gain and public good simply evaporates.

A classic win-win is the contention that environmental programs like reducing waste or using LED lights can save money or that decent pay and benefits lower costs by reducing employee turnover. Business schools now claim to educate “leaders who make a difference in the world,” as H. B. S. proclaims in its mission, while Wharton pursues a “quest for positive global impact.”

These aspirations are built on the delusional but widely accepted idea of “stakeholder capitalism”: that companies can produce climate stability, fair wages, healthy communities and functioning democracies while also delivering profits. Executives promise that technology will solve our environmental problems; voluntary measurement systems are offered as appropriate alternatives to public accountability; ethics is rebranded as competitive advantage rather than moral obligation.

During the 2010s, stakeholder capitalism was quickly woven into M. B. A. syllabuses. But when researchers examined whether the corporations that signed on to a statement pledging commitment to this ethos actually changed their behavior on wages, investment, governance or climate, they found little evidence of a shift. The statement was less a new doctrine than an effort at reputation management — and a ploy to avoid oversight.

Recent evidence shows that many foundational studies supporting the win-win idea were based on flawed data or couldn’t be replicated. Yet faculty members keep researching, writing about and teaching the topic — suggesting an ideological project more than an academic exercise.

Much of what has happened in business schools turned out to be the leading edge of a broader transformation: the corporatization of the university itself. Institutions now chase rankings, donors and corporate partnerships, tout their contributions to innovation and growth and treat everything else as overhead. Students are “customers,” and the degrees are “products” with greater and lesser “market shares.” University strategic documents talk about “brand positioning” for departments and “R. O. I. s” on tenure lines.

Once you accept this frame, it becomes hard to defend the existence of a philosophy seminar or a history department for any reason other than the revenue it generates. The hiring of non-tenure-track adjunct professors follows: If education is “content” delivered to fee-paying “customers,” why keep full-time scholars on the payroll when you can hire contingent, low-wage instructors?

Business schools’ success in placing their graduates in high-paying jobs boosts their rankings; high rankings attract more applicants and allow higher tuitions; and wealthy alumni fund new programs and buildings that elevate the school’s status. It is a self-reinforcing cycle — a flywheel, in M. B. A. parlance — that pulls money, attention and legitimacy away from the disciplines best equipped to question this logic: history, philosophy, sociology, political theory.

The university’s capacity to cultivate historical memory, moral judgment and democratic imagination is weakened, even as its capacity to churn out data analysts, financial engineers and “innovation” managers grows. The irony — and danger — is that in the age of A. I., the thinking fostered in the arts and humanities is increasingly urgent. The domination of business schools is not only physical and financial; it is intellectual, and it is crowding out liberal education.

I’ve come to a grim conclusion: The problem with business schools is not repairable misalignment but the design itself. Business schools are not malfunctioning institutions; they are highly efficient machines doing exactly what they were designed to do. An ethics elective here, a sustainability center there, a “responsible leadership” badge — they all serve to legitimize the machine, not change its output.

The most honest solution I’ve come across is to replace the category entirely. Stuart Hart, an emeritus professor at Cornell and an early sustainability champion, told me he reached that conclusion after trying every internal route to make M. B. A. curriculums more responsible. The institution itself was the problem. At the University of Vermont, Dr. Hart has since developed a new form of business degree focused on societal impact — a small but concrete test of the case for starting over. In this program, sustainability is not a lone elective but run through the whole curriculum, and students spend the summer embedded in a mission-driven company.

What would that clean-sheet logic mean across an entire university? One starting point is the organization theorist Martin Parker’s call to create “schools for organizing” rather than schools for business, centered on how humans coordinate for shared ends. Students would study co-ops, unions and social movements alongside the shareholder corporation. The central question would shift from “How do we maximize shareholder value?” to “How do different forms of organization distribute power, risk and reward — and which should we strengthen?”

Dismantling the business school as a single high-status silo that professionalizes private gain may seem a heavy lift. But universities can create cross-disciplinary pathways for students who want to work in business without submitting them to the business school worldview. Some already offer “business and society” majors or master’s programs in organizations and public purpose, drawing on sociology, law and public policy. The point would not be to abolish the study of markets, but to return it to settings where questions of power, history, democracy and ecological limits cannot be so easily avoided.

For most of my career, I’ve taught electives focused on responsible business and sustainability — gratifying work, but largely preaching to the converted. Recently, at Cambridge, I introduced a required sustainability course filled with future bankers, consultants and tech executives who once would have steered clear.

Many arrive deeply skeptical, convinced that any time a corporation acts in a responsible way it must be a marketing ploy; some push back hard on ideas they see as threats to growth. But forcing them out of their bubbles into a shared conversation about the natural environment, inequality and discrimination has produced the kind of debate that is so often missing in education today.

This is not enough. One required course cannot redeem the business school model. If anything, teaching it has intensified my disappointment. The course is relegated to the very end of the program — a telling signal of its importance — and amid a growing backlash against sustainability, there is some pressure to reduce or eliminate the class, to appease the customers who now drive decisions in higher education.

Still, the experience has reminded me why abolishing business schools cannot mean abandoning the people in them. The goal is not to write off the students as aspiring selfish capitalists; it is to stop funneling them through a machine that narrows their sense of possibility. Many of my students arrive on campus wanting to work on the crises that our economic system has created. What they lack is an institution that is worthy of their better impulses.

Christopher Marquis is a professor at the University of Cambridge Judge Business School and the author of “The Profiteers.”
